In September, Markéta Čermáková will lecture on anarcho-capitalism; he will talk about the fact that the state guarantees children the right to education by imposing it on them as an obligation. The state promises to take into account the educational needs of the individual, mutual respect and tolerance, tolerance of opinions, solidarity and dignity of all participants in education. Among other things, it imposes on educators the obligation to create a positive and safe climate in the school environment and to support its development through their approach to education and training. Does that sound good to you? To Marquette (apart from that duty) yes. Does this sound like a description of most mainstream schools? Unfortunately not. We will look at the ways in which legislation and school practice most often differ. Four reasons why the state should not restrict freedom of speech!
All communication platform rules should be determined by their owners; including any restrictions. State intervention in any direction contradicts property rights.
If we ban the public presentation of some opinions, they will not disappear from society anyway; on the contrary, it will be much more difficult to oppose them than if we let them be heard.
I believe in finding the truth through dialogue. If we suppress criticism of a position, we limit the possibility of its constant review and possible reevaluation.
Words have great power to do much harm; however, they have exactly the same power in defense against such damage. Let us fight against word with word, against sword with sword.

Four reasons why the state does not need to build roads!
People want to be transported; and where there is demand, there is also supply in the free market.
The state has no additional resources available to it beyond those it collects from taxpayers. To give an idea: No company in the Czech Republic has such profits as the state earns from motorists after accounting for all costs. 
Notoriously known corruption - connected precisely with the construction of the road network - is, in principle, only possible where someone makes decisions about other people's finances - just like the state about taxpayers' money.
The private investor is motivated to manage and operate roads to the satisfaction of their users; not according to current – often ideological – political demand.

The third speaker of the "2023 Freeport Conference: Drugs and Guns Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his talk "Time of Prohibitions".

What happens when we ban something? Regardless of the reasons or the meaningfulness of such a ban, most people have a need to believe that the ban in question is meaningful; without knowing anything about the given issue, they can retroactively "invent" why this or that was forbidden and what would "certainly happen" if it was not forbidden. There's just one catch - very often it's simply not true; however, this does not prevent states from exploiting this ignorance (and fear) in enforcing bans. Drugs and guns used to be common "everyday" items a hundred years ago; until quite recently they were stigmatized and banned - yet it seems that only without them can our civilization function. It's interesting that a lot of people who have learned the futility of drug or gun bans are vehemently pushing for the regulation of the other... Why?

Urza is an anarcho-capitalist author; wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism. Space for corruption arises wherever someone makes decisions about other people's money. And deciding on foreign money is the very essence of the state.
Unfortunately, every control authority that should fight and combat corruption is also corruptible in principle. There is no reason why he shouldn't be; nor a way to ensure it.
In principle, incorruptible are those who manage their own – not other people's – money and property; bribing them then means nothing more than making a deal with them.
The only truly effective way to fight corruption is to eliminate public budgets and leave the money in the hands of those who earned it.

Four reasons why housing is so expensive!
Construction is such an extremely over-regulated industry that only entities large enough to dedicate enough people to just deal with the red tape can operate in it. This limits competition and raises prices.
Due to state regulations, construction procedures are extremely long, which increases costs. It is not built when the owner needs it, but when officials and politicians allow it. The offer then hardly responds to the demand.
The state's monetary policy consists in the permanent devaluation of the currency. Because of the state, money thus lost the ability to store value in the long term; people then store this in real estate, among other things, which increases their prices.
In addition to Czech regulations, European ones also affect us; of these, especially green policy requirements (for example, energy labels and the like) increase the price of housing.

Four reasons for the separation of healthcare from the state!
State socialist health care is killing people as a result of misallocation of resources; overworked, tired medical professionals or long waiting times for CT, MRI and other examinations can mean the difference between life and death.

The fifth speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2022: Money yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Mojmír Hampl with his lecture "Elastic money - the essence of the current monetary system".

It is surprising that we all use the monetary system on a daily basis, but often even the most educated people have only a vague or even zero idea of its nature and functioning. In the lecture, we will focus on how the current elastic money system is different from fixed money systems and explain how and where money is created and destroyed.

Mojmír Hampl is a Czech economist, banker and columnist with degrees from the University of Economics in Prague and the University of Surrey in Great Britain. He devoted most of his professional life to date to the Czech National Bank (ČNB), where he joined as an analyst after defending his diploma thesis with the then Vice-Governor of the CNB, Pavel Kysilka.
After a four-year break, when he worked as an economist at Česká spořitelna and later as a member of the management of the Czech Consolidation Agency, he returned to the CNB in 2006 when he was appointed to its banking board. Between 2008 and 2018, he held the position of Deputy Governor of the CNB. Throughout his life, he repeatedly returns to the topic of money, currencies and central banks in his works. This is also why he is known for his very sharp views on the subject of the euro and also European integration. He has published more than three hundred popular and professional articles in various areas of his broad interest - from macroeconomics, through economic history to contributions on the topic of cryptocurrencies. He lectured in many places around the world, especially on monetary policy and central banking.

The third speaker of the "2022 Freeport Conference: Money Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "The Internet of Ancient Times".

I sometimes refer to money in my lectures as the "Ancient Internet"; it is a wonderful means of communication between people, which in addition to information also conveys motivation. In my opinion, this is one of the most important inventions of mankind; it allows us to efficiently allocate resources and send important signals to people whose existence we have no idea, but with whom we can still cooperate and coordinate our wealth-creating efforts through a system of prices. This way of communication is going great until states start disrupting it when they want to "aid and protect" their citizens; most people - politicians included - do not know or understand this invaluable function of money, so they will not even see the consequences of its (partial) paralysis.

Urza is the author of the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism and more than a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media. He not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, ethics, education, the market, the economy and the role of the state in society for more than ten years, but also lectures (for example, as part of the series Anarchocapitalismus in Parallel Polis and in (de)Central, but also in schools and at many conferences), makes videos and accepts invitations to various programs or panel discussions where he defends the freedom of the individual.
Together with his wife Teresa, he forms the Free Harbor; heads the Czech and Slovak Institute of Ludwig von Mises, which he founded together with other anarcho-capitalists; creates the Freeport Studio, the Freeport Sewers, the Freeport Channel and the Urza.cz website; belongs to the board of the Freedom of Learning association; he actively cooperates with libertarian movements promoting personal and economic freedom and writes articles for various websites dealing with the functioning of society.

Four reasons why to make free market decisions about recycling!
It makes sense to recycle precisely when the resources needed for recycling are less scarce than the resources needed to obtain new raw materials and process old waste.
The rarity of goods on the free market is reflected in their prices. The variant that consumes less rare goods is thus also cheaper. Recycling is therefore more gentle in an undistorted free market precisely when it pays off economically.
Otherwise, recycling is nothing more than a waste of human or natural resources. Depending on the technology used, recycling may consume too much energy, etc.
Artificial state support for recycling leads to a distortion of the market, as a result of which it can be worthwhile to recycle even where it means waste instead of frugality.

Four reasons for free international trade!
When goods cannot cross the border, soldiers will. It is not so easy for governments to make an enemy out of someone you know and who is beneficial to you. 
Division of labor means prosperity. Artificial efforts at national self-sufficiency create barriers to trade, thereby limiting the division of labor; both at the level of the individual and at the level of entire states.
While tariffs may help domestic producers, they harm all consumers as they artificially make goods more expensive. If tariffs were really beneficial, there would be no reason to levy them only between states; we could easily introduce them between cities as well.
Import quotas reduce supply, thus raising prices similar to tariffs. Competition is desirable in the market, and any restriction of it harms customers. This applies to competition from abroad just as much as to domestic competition.

Four Reasons Why Central Planning Doesn't Work!
We live in a world of limited resources, where the fulfillment of one wish means that the wish of another cannot be fulfilled. Four reasons for separating money from the state!
Money is one of the most amazing inventions of mankind; prices are used to transmit information about the rarity of goods between sellers and buyers around the world. Any artificial intervention in this system distorts information and sends false signals to all market participants, causing a waste of resources.
Interventions by central banks in the economy cause business cycles. Before the existence of central banking, economic crises used to have specific causes - for example, natural disasters, lack of crops and the like; due to interventions by central banks in interest rates, crises occur even without external causes.
Artificial inflation causes injustice because it takes away the value of savings, which is shared between banks and people with access to cheap credit. It makes it impossible to save money effectively and forces even those who do not want to undertake the investment risk.
If the state has power over money, it can at any time decide to devalue everyone's savings for its own benefit; this is how governments typically finance, for example, arming for wars, paying off excessive debts or other large expenditures.

Four reasons why the state helps the rich at the expense of the poor!
Big companies can influence politicians and thus legislation. State regulations then effectively eliminate competition from smaller companies that do not have the means to meet often unnecessary standards and legal norms. 
Even a law adopted in good faith without corruption will rather be prepared with regard to processes in large companies, which are known to politicians and officials. In addition, corporations have entire departments of lawyers, accountants, and other personnel who can deal with regulations; in a small company, everyone is dedicated to the business itself.
Labor market regulations – such as the minimum wage – harm the least qualified, who then become unemployable, as the value of their work may not exceed the state-enforced minimum cost of their employment. Such people go into the gray area and live on social benefits. 
All state requirements for the minimum quality of services or goods make it impossible to sell products that are low-quality but extremely cheap. This makes life easier for the rich who wouldn't buy them anyway; however, the state deprives the poor of the opportunity to satisfy their needs at least somehow.

Four reasons for separating education from the state!
Education is monopolized by the state. He also decides on the conditions for the establishment and operation of private schools. Educating children in a way not approved by the Ministry is not legal even if it is the world's long-term successful learning methods. Parents with a different view on education are threatened with having their children taken away and imprisoned.
Like any monopoly, the state also provides expensive and low-quality services in education. Tabled teacher salaries discourage the able and attract the less able. The education provided by the state does not reflect the real needs of children - many important things are missing and a lot of unnecessary things remain. 
Even before reading, writing and arithmetic, a child learns to obey the authority assigned to him at school. It is difficult for him to start establishing equal relationships when he spends the entire educational process in a subordinate role. The logical consequence is a society full of conforming individuals always ready to submit to dictates and pressure from the outside.
Centralized education is used by states to indoctrinate young children. Each generation learns from a young age about the advantages of the regime it lives in and the disadvantages of other regimes. This effectively prevents critical thinking and constructive debate about the social order.

Four reasons to remember opportunity cost!
We live in a world of limited resources. So anything we do carries with it what is called an opportunity cost—that is, whatever we gave up in favor of what we did. It cost us at least time, but often something extra.
If we go to the movies instead of the gym, we sacrifice the opportunity to improve our fitness for the opportunity to watch a movie. And in exactly the same way, even nobler goals - for example, protecting the environment - are always realized at the expense of something - for example, treating the sick.
Every law, every regulation, every regulation, every investment, simply any state intervention has a price – not only money paid in taxes, but also unproduced goods, unprovided services, unrealized projects, jobs that will not be created, our time and the possibility of choice.
Opportunity costs must always be taken into account, i.e. when evaluating any state agenda - new or existing. The benefit of people spending their own money according to their preferences cannot be replaced by any state agenda.

Four Reasons Why We Need Market Prices!
Prices are a brilliant and irreplaceable tool to convey information. If something is in short supply, the price rises, which informs and motivates all market participants. The one who directs resources to the production of scarce goods or invents a substitute for them will earn. In the event of a surplus, the price falls again and resources are shifted elsewhere.
Prices also determine consumer behavior. Higher prices motivate consumers to save on scarce goods, or to replace them with something else - cheaper and therefore less rare. This saves not only human labor but also natural resources.
We influence the money in the market what we are really interested in. This leads to a better allocation of resources than when the state decides based on the will of the voters. Through elections, everyone tries to assert their abstract preferences at the expense of others, and thus projects are created that people would not spend their own money on.
In a truly free and free market undistorted by the state, those who can best satisfy the needs of the people who willingly pay for it will become the richest. Not those who are fine with politicians and officials making decisions about other people's money.

Although most people imagine something under the term "monopoly" - and even suspect that it is something harmful; however, few distinguish between a true monopoly and a dominant market player, but what's worse - the biggest, most harmful, most violent and most widespread monopoly is completely neglected and ignored. Adam Růžička's lecture for the "Free Harbor Conference 2020: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow" was entitled "Creeping social tyranny and the importance of freedom of speech".

Under the term tyranny, we usually imagine the violent dictate of a powerful individual or group that oppresses the rest. However, thinkers have long pointed out that tyranny can also manifest itself on a social level, in ways that are harder to define, but all the more insidious, because they are not clearly visible, but often have a comparable influence on the lives of individuals as despotic governments. This threat to free societies was described by John Stuart Mill in his famous essay On Freedom, and Václav Havel also touched on it in The Power of the Powerless when he spoke of social "self-totality". The lecture will present the basic theses of the issue of social freedom and connect them with recent psychological research in the context of the current challenges of democratic societies (e.g. social media, opinion bubbles, the phenomenon of divided societies, etc.).

After studying psychology at Masaryk University, Adam Růžička, MSc. MRes. at University College London, where he worked for several years as a researcher in the field of cognitive neuroscience and researched the brain with a focus on human speech. He currently works as the director of the H21 Institute in Prague, which focuses on collective decision-making, electoral systems, civic participation and the issue of a divided society.

The next speaker at the "Freeport Conference 2020: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Jan Zugar with his lecture "North Korea - a country much more open than we perceive it".

There is perhaps no country more emotionally closed to the outside world than the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. In 1950-53, a war took place here, during which the country was divided into southern and northern parts due to the efforts of the north, which sought, with the support of China and the Soviet Union, to unite the entire country under the red flag. This failed thanks to the intervention of UN troops, and so after a three-year conflict, Korea was divided into these two parts by the 38th parallel. While South Korea is a developing country that is moving in the same direction as comparable eastern states, North Korea is closed, an information embargo is imposed on the media of the surrounding countries, access to the Internet, which is also internal only to the DPRK, is almost impossible and the harsh dictatorship of the Communist Party and the Kim clan rules here. It is very rare to get to this country as part of diplomatic trips or a study stay, which Jan Zugar was able to do.

Jan Zugar is a graduate of BUT in Brno, a member of the Young Christian Democrats and an opponent of communism.

The second speaker of the "2020 Freeport Conference: Totality Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "The Different Faces of Evil or Recognize Totality".

Although everyone can probably agree that they don't want to live in totalitarianism, for some reason totalitarian regimes are an inherent part of our history; and not only long past, but also quite recent, in short, they keep coming again and again. You don't know what? Why, Czech Flag Day, of course! I consider statism to be the greatest and most dangerous global religion of both present and past; like most religions, it has various denominations (in the form of individual states); these have their sacred symbols (flags, coats of arms), places (palaces, memorials), texts (constitutional documents, founding declarations), and songs (marches, anthems), holidays (celebrations of victory or founding), festivals (processions, military parades), relics (standards, crown jewels), officials (politicians, bureaucrats), symbolic gestures (salutes, laying wreaths), saints (decorated statesmen, national heroes), and rituals (elections, coronations). Many states celebrate their flags on various days significant to them (coronations, deaths, battles, flag enactments, etc.); in the Czech Republic, it could have landed on March 30, which is the date of the passage of the 106-year-old Act 252/1920.
In 2020, the Czech Vexillological Society proposed this, which interested almost no one at the time; six years later, Babiš apparently needed to look like a patriot, so he proposed it in an amendment to Act 245/2000. So do we have it? Czech Flag Day codified into law? Nope. Not even a week before the big day, the Senate rejected and returned it. Could it be that they didn't want to clutter legislation with such nonsense? Not at all! Supposedly, this would overshadow the other six state symbols (the greater and lesser coat of arms, the tricolor, the standard, the state seal, and the national anthem – ever since my
appearance that ended at the police station
, I know them by heart); instead, they prefer to rename the St. Wenceslas Day holiday to Czech Statehood and State Symbols Day. Parliament will debate the proposal again... Hundreds of (well-paid) man-hours (funded by taxpayers) are spent telling us which day we are supposed to wave a little flag. How can anyone take this seriously?

Early anarchists typically did not understand economics very well, while proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This realization and full understanding of it changed my life considerably; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

I recently listened to a years-old recording of a debate with Petr Gazdík; in it, citing his past, "life story, and background," he explained why he would never accept a bribe. Let us assume for a moment that he was telling the truth and is truly an upright, incorruptible person; immediately afterwards, with evident pride in his voice, he declared that the gambling lobby would never break him and that he would fight against gambling his whole life, otherwise he couldn't look in the mirror. That man very likely doesn't even realize that he is promoting the
violent persecution of a group of people and trampling on their property rights
; and do you know what is worse than a politician initiating aggression against you? Well, far worse is a politician initiating aggression against you who cannot even be bribed to stop. Even if parliament were filled exclusively with people who "mean well" (and we are far from that), the state would not begin working in our favor; on the contrary, it could easily be even worse.

To answer the question of whether damaging a reputation violates
property rights
(and thus constitutes an attack that the victim may use force to defend against), one must first determine whether a reputation can be owned. My reputation is essentially people's opinions of me; reputation is what others think. And can I own the thoughts and opinions of others? Certainly not. How then could I own my reputation? It is not possible; what others think of me is neither my property nor my decision. Therefore, when someone slanders me, it is appropriate to respond, refute the slander, or ignore the whole thing (that is up to each of us to decide); however, it is not legitimate to use physical force and restrict the slanderer's freedom of speech and property rights, because he did not attack my property, given that I do not own my reputation (i.e., other people's opinions). He may have harmed me, but that in itself does not constitute a violation of property rights; if my partner leaves me for him, that can harm me too, yet it would be completely unacceptable to resolve the situation with violence.

On my wonderful journey through life, I encounter many opponents of anarchism or capitalism, most often of both. Anti-capitalists are typically bothered by greed, selfishness, the fact that some have little and others have much, inequality... These phenomena certainly do occur under capitalism; yet they do not vanish through regulation. Greedy, selfish individuals simply move into the service of the state, where they continue to grab (depending on the regime, they may focus on power, connections, and the like instead of money), only their self-interest is no longer harnessed to satisfy the needs of customers; and while inequality can indeed be curbed through state interventions, it comes at the cost of significantly reducing the wealth of society, because inequality arises through wealth creation – the market is not a zero-sum game (voluntary exchange increases the utility of both parties); inequality typically emerges when someone improves the lives of many people slightly, while their own well-being leaps forward dramatically. Anti-capitalists criticize things they dislike, but fail to see that these are not consequences of capitalism, but features of reality that socialism merely pretends to change while in truth transforming them into something far worse.

On my wonderful journey through life, I encounter many opponents of anarchism or capitalism, most often of both. Anti-anarchists typically take issue with the idea of a society without a central authority usurping a monopoly on violence. "Society cannot function without rules," they say; and they are right! But not even anarcho-capitalists seek a society functioning without any rules; they merely do not want those rules dictated from above by a central authority, but rather support their market-based emergence on a decentralized basis. Let everyone set their own rules on their own property, in their own enterprise – simply wherever they simultaneously bear responsibility. And if multiple people collaborate on something, let them freely agree on the terms of cooperation; and if they don't find them acceptable, they don't have to collaborate. If this proves too complex for people, there is nothing wrong with them voluntarily adopting uniform standards; but let them not force those who do not wish to do so, even if they are in the minority. Anarchy is not the absence of order; merely the absence of a central authority.

We often hear the phrase "freedom and democracy"; in reality, "freedom or democracy" is closer to the truth.
Democracy is often the nemesis of freedom
. What is democracy? Setting aside grandiose rhetoric, it is the coercive rule of the majority; yes, coercive, because against people who do not submit to laws dictated by the majority,
the state routinely uses violence
. If the majority decides to disarm the minority, it will happen. If the majority decides to raise taxes on the minority, it will happen. If the majority decides to restrict freedom of speech, it will happen. If the majority decides we must solve the Jewish question, it will happen. Are current authoritarian regimes typically far less free? Of course; however, that changes nothing about the above – just as the existence of the extremely deadly death cap mushroom doesn't turn the poisonous fly agaric into an edible mushroom.

Today marks thirty-one years since the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism," Murray Newton Rothbard, passed away just shy of his 69th birthday; his life's work consisted of taking two traditions to their consistent and logical conclusions – traditions that had seemingly little in common: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Earlier anarchists typically had little grasp of economics, and proponents of the Austrian school did not apply their (otherwise sound) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and arrived at a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This insight and its full understanding profoundly changed my life; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
Murray Newton Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926; that means he would have turned 100 this year. In honor of that, the Free Port is organizing its
seventh conference
on freedom, held on the first Saturday after his hundredth birthday.

I don't make any New Year's resolutions; when I want to change, I see no reason to wait for the turn of the year. Yet I have a wish; I would like to finish and publish the book, continue with #ne_poslušnosti (and not end up behind bars), the Free Port, Ježek bez klece, and relationships, and connect a bit more with my body, rest, and live healthier – I'm working on everything, some things are going better, others worse (the body part). It's all part of my journey toward freedom (and love); I want to live in a freer society, but it's clear to me that I can only change it by changing myself.
What about you? What are your wishes? What do you want from yourself? And what from others?

I recently heard a remarkable argument in a discussion: "The state is too weak, which is why it cannot defend itself against oligarchies and corporate influence." Hmm... that's quite an idiosyncratic interpretation. So what should we do about it? How do we "strengthen the state"? More bureaucrats, more money, more surveillance, more laws? Why that makes no sense and leads nowhere,
I have explained many times already
; here, however, it is even internally contradictory with the speaker's own belief. If one believes that the state is controlled by oligarchs and large corporations (which is certainly true to a great extent), how could any "strengthening" of that state (controlled by oligarchs and corporations) possibly occur without them controlling it anymore? After all, those same entities will intervene in that entire process too; and there is no reason to believe they would have any less influence there than anywhere else. Want to get rid of them? Then let's get rid of the state! It makes no sense to claim that they control the state while simultaneously calling for its expansion; that's like upgrading weapons for your enemy.

In the past, families were quite solid units; parents cared for their children, on whom they later relied in old age, which of course still happens today, though to a lesser degree. Why? Modern socialist states came along with their
welfare policies and state pensions
, thereby reducing families' incentives to maintain good relationships. Does that sound cynical? Is it much more complex? Surely relationships don't just depend on money? Can't buy love? Yes, of course! That is all true. I am not saying that if parents and children were more economically interdependent, paradise on earth would ensue – far from it; it's simply that a parent's incentive to maintain good relations with their offspring is higher when the parent knows they will one day depend on them, and conversely, the child's incentive to care for their parent is lower when they know the state will do it anyway – and especially when they know this is considered a fundamental duty of the state, as is constantly drilled into us (
from childhood on
); plus, the person already pays for that state through taxes anyway (leaving them with fewer resources).

Today I will venture a little beyond the boundaries of libertarian thought (with which this article is only very loosely connected); I would like to examine the concept of revenge, which people often perceive as an act of justice. I do not share this view (though at some point in the past I probably thought that way, but I don't remember precisely anymore); revenge makes no sense to me whatsoever, with the sole exception of attempting to deter the perpetrator – or others – from harming a person. But it is not at all clear to me where wishes come from, for example, that a deceased murderer (say, a terrorist) end up "in hell" after death or "may his soul be damned" (setting aside what anyone believes; while atheism is common in the Czech Republic, in the US, for instance, nearly everyone believes in an afterlife); I wish salvation even to Stalin and Hitler, may their souls rest in peace. Because why not? It won't harm anyone and will benefit them; why not wish even evil people good things in cases where it harms no one and has no (anti-)educational effect?

We all know from experience with socialism that the state is incapable of providing even trivial necessities like toilet paper or menstrual pads – things whose demand can be easily estimated and calculated; the reasons are explained by the Austrian school of economics, but let's set theory aside for a moment. Hardly anyone disputes that when the state attempts to supply consumer goods, it fails – unlike the market. But why do so many people, despite the state's utter inability to provide trivial goods, still trust its ability to provide things that are orders of magnitude more complex (education, healthcare, judiciary, security...)? Especially when they witness day in and day out how the state fails at them; heaven forbid we give the free market a chance, because "that surely wouldn't work" (though nothing points to that). So why do people still believe it? Well, there is one thing the state doesn't do half bad –
indoctrination through propaganda has always been its forte; and no wonder, when the target audience is little children
.

Every now and then, I hear complaints about our "modern consumerist, hyper-technological society" and its detachment from "nature" (as if we weren't part of nature ourselves); supposedly it's wrong that people live in cities, use technology, and lack contact with the wilderness. I don't really understand this lament; I don't understand why someone lives a life they themselves criticize. Why complain about "society" instead of renouncing technology themselves and spending time in the countryside rather than the city? Well, the countryside lacks many modern conveniences, the same opportunities for social life, as many jobs, and so forth; yes, that is all true – welcome to the "idyllic" life of our ancestors (or rather, a mere "sample" of it; in reality it was much harsher)! I don't see the "sickness" of our age in cities or in "man's detachment from nature"; rather, I consider the true "sickness" of our age to be how often we want something yet are unwilling to pay the price it costs, while complaining that others who don't need it are living wrong.

What happens to slot machine or roulette addicts when the state taxes gambling (even more heavily)? Let's start with what definitely won't happen: these people will certainly not calculate that with the higher tax burden it's no longer worth playing, and stop. How do I know? Well, if they were capable of that, they would have calculated it and stopped playing already, because it wasn't worth it for them before either; given enough plays, they are going to lose everything they shove into the machines anyway – and because they are addicts, they will play enough games. The rate of tax the state levies on gambling merely determines the ratio in which the addicts' money is split between casino operators and the crooks in government; it does nothing to help the addicts. Taxing cigarettes or alcohol can indeed lower consumption, because it makes a difference whether a smoker spends three or five thousand crowns a month on their habit; a gambling addict, however, will spend every penny they can on their habit (that is the very essence of addiction), so the tax will not help.

For a very long time, postal services were something various states claimed a monopoly over; and people universally believed it was truly necessary – everyone dutifully "knew" that under a free market "it couldn't work" (just as everyone today "knows" the same about many other fields). Today it's obvious how things stand: a state monopoly on parcel delivery is completely off the table in the vast majority of countries. Abolishing the state post office may not yet enjoy broad public support, but here and there voices are raised, and above all, the counterarguments have already shifted from "only the state can do this" to "in most cases, the private sector is more efficient." It is wonderful to observe an industry where public opinion has moved from "the state must have a monopoly" through "OK, let it face competition" all the way to "we could probably do without the state somehow (even if we don't want to just yet)." So when do you think Česká pošta will be abolished (or rather, fully privatized)? Will we live to see it? And when will the death knell begin tolling for Czech Television as well?

Mocking Christians – and creationists in particular – is fairly common in the atheist Czech Republic (and as a Christian myself – albeit one who accepts evolution – I sometimes laugh heartily at such jokes); such quips are sometimes witty, sometimes less so, but what would you say to the following remark: "Christians (creationists) are completely clueless because they believe Darwin, whose theories make no sense." Isn't that absurd? It certainly is; and perhaps that is why I have never heard that sentence uttered. But I have heard another – no less absurd: "Austrian economics is completely clueless because it assumes perfect competition, perfect information, and perfect people pursuing their economic self-interest." That is no less nonsense than the Darwin remark; the Austrian school of economics not only uses no models of "homo economicus in ideal conditions," it actually criticizes them fiercely – which nonetheless does not stop many people from attributing these very things to Austrian economics.

What would people do without state subsidies for science and research? First and foremost, they would retain more of their own resources (money), which they could decide how to allocate themselves. Then basically two scenarios can occur: Either the individual who kept the money in their pocket, rather than having it confiscated by the state, decides to fund some research with it (whether directly or indirectly by buying products from a company conducting research – for profit or other reasons), in which case the state is completely unnecessary; or the individual would choose to spend that money (or part of it) on something else entirely – but what does that signify? That according to their own subjective scale of values, whatever they spent their money on brings them more utility than the research the state wanted to force them to finance. One might argue that the person cannot properly foresee all consequences, but nobody can do that; and if someone believes another person is making poor choices, let them educate them, but
do not force them through violence
!

I participated in a debate on whether the state should force restaurant owners to mandate allergen lists for diners; the defense of
state coercion
rested on two arguments: First, that "nobody gets hurt by writing down allergens"; second, that it saves the lives of people with severe allergies. If "it won't hurt anyone" were a valid argument for violating property rights, then thieves who steal just a few crowns from thousands of people (through rounding "errors") wouldn't be doing anything wrong either, because "nobody was hurt." And saving allergy sufferers? Don't make me laugh! Anyone with an allergy so severe that they risk fatal anaphylactic shock must take far greater care (inquire about ingredients, question staff, dine only at trusted places); relying on lists that restaurant owners threw together haphazardly just because some inspector harassed them is nothing but another fruit of the state's efforts to turn us into irresponsible ignoramuses – and that cannot end well.

If children lack legal capacity, so that parents or the state must make decisions on their behalf until a certain age, how can they be bound from the moment of their birth by a so-called "social contract" that cannot be terminated and binds them to unconditional obedience to the state until death?

Earlier anarchists typically had little grasp of economics, and proponents of the Austrian school did not apply their (otherwise sound) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and arrived at a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Would you believe that the Sewers is celebrating its tenth Christmas? It feels somewhat unbelievable that it's been ten years since I started it; so much has happened and changed over that time, yet my approach to Christmas remains the same – I love it because in my eyes it symbolizes Christian spirituality, capitalist materiality, anarchist enjoyment of life, and the divine music that I share every year. last year's

I believe it's similar with love and freedom; searching for their intersections has become my new life passion, which I gladly share with you on an ongoing basis – and I intend to continue doing so. MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

Today marks exactly twenty-nine years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses – Murray Newton Rothbard, the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" – passed away just shy of his 69th birthday; his life's work consisted of taking two traditions to their consistent and logical conclusions – traditions that had seemingly little in common: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists often erred in economics, and proponents of the Austrian school did not apply their (sound) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and arrived at a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This insight and its full understanding profoundly changed my life; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

From time to time we may hear from some people that we have a "right to water" as a "basic human right"; such a belief most likely stems from the fact that we biologically need water to survive. Yet even that does not entitle anyone to force another by violence to provide something. While a negatively defined right to water means that no one may take water away from another, a positively defined "right to water" says that everyone must be guaranteed water; however, the dark side of a positive "right" is that someone must be forced by violence to provide that water, which is not ethically acceptable. In connection with this, one often encounters fears that someone will hold a monopoly on water and rule everyone; that makes no sense, however, because (ground)water is everywhere – it only depends on how deep you dig. If the price of water rises above a certain threshold, it will begin paying off for people to drill wells; by no means does everyone need their own – they can join forces, share the water, and the monopolist is out of luck.

On Friday, a minarchist-leaning text was published; and I respect it (which is partly why I published it). However, I would also like to offer an anarchist perspective. For over ten years I have been told not to be so radical, not to say this or that because it will scare people away, and not to use the word anarcho-capitalism. All along, I recognized the drawbacks of such an approach; yet I still did what felt right to me. Over time, I also discovered indisputable benefits: people remember it better this way, they are more likely to notice it, react to it, register it (even if it often infuriates them). I don't want to judge which approach is superior; however, I am convinced that you get the furthest by remaining true to yourself. Are you comfortable with subtle nuance? Paraphrase the idea and smooth out the edges. Do you feel better in vigorous dialogue? Boldly embrace anarchy. Both have their pros and cons; but nothing can replace authenticity. Not to mention that the more varied ways we present our ideas, the more people we will reach.

Someone recently asked me if I support legalizing cannabis for its medicinal effects; and guess what? I am not in favor of legalizing cannabis for its medicinal effects; I am a proponent of the full legalization (or decriminalization – depending on terminology, as everyone means something different by it) of all drugs (including marijuana) regardless of their effects. Whether weed heals is not relevant to me. I know ointments are made from it; I also know some stoners – they don't use it as medicine, even if they occasionally pretend that getting high isn't harmful, but that's their business. While I understand the health-based reasoning, it actually bothers me at the same time; it somewhat implies that if weed weren't healthy, it would actually be okay to ban it. But a free person should not have to beg anyone for permission to put whatever they deem fit into their body, even if it were cyanide. People love to talk about freedom, but when push comes to shove, "after all, we need some regulation."

All around us we hear about a crisis of values, a crisis of elites, a crisis in politics, a crisis of civilization, and a crisis of everything. I am convinced that we would have heard such talk in every era (historical records indicate as much), occasionally accompanied by crises in the supply of goods, food production, construction, and industry – depending on whatever the state had taken charge of. Wherever socialism flourishes, there is crisis; in the Czech Republic before 1989, practically everywhere; since 1989, in education, the welfare system, healthcare (in other words, state-run sectors), and logically also in values, elites, politics... Not that our "civilization" (as a whole) is in a "crisis of values" (although some like to claim so); ordinary people are still the same and the problem is not in them. Politicians are the ones in a "crisis of values"; and rather than a "crisis," it is a permanent condition; and an inherent one at that, not a failure of individual politicians; and as long as we have a state, the problem will not go away.

It is widely believed that in a free-market society people would pay too little for collective defense (an army) against an external enemy; but how much is "little"? The only way to find out what is "too little" is to lose the war (and even that does not prove with certainty that it was "too little," as there might not have been any chance of overturning the outcome anyway); conversely, maintaining an army when there is no threat can be "too much." All of this can only be determined ex post; ex ante, we know nothing. Therefore, if people in a free-market society pay less for collective defense (an army) than in a state, it does not necessarily mean it is "wrong"; because it is not clear how much is "right." The Czech Republic's military budget is (even proportionally to the national budget) many times smaller than that of the US military; is that wrong? The answers will surely differ and varied opinions with diverse rationales will emerge; why then is it "obvious to everyone" that in a stateless society it would be a disaster (even if people happened to pay less)?

I have already devoted plenty of time, text, and words to explaining how the free market deals with monopolies; but even if someone came to the conclusion that they need "protection" from monopolies, the intriguing question is what they are actually calling for. An antimonopoly office? But that office itself is a monopoly on resolving monopoly problems; do you sense the paradox? How is the state supposed to help such a person? A state that itself usurps a monopoly on violence in a given territory; is this goat-turned-gardener supposed to protect the garden? What internal logic is there in instituting the most brutal monopoly to protect us from supposed monopolies? Most likely none at all; the state indoctrinates us all with its propaganda from childhood in school, where we were told (without any reasoning, discussion, data, or examples) that monopolies are bad because they are bad, whereas the state is good because it is good, and without the state there would be monopolies, which is bad. Has anyone found any deeper logic behind this?

"Sweatshop" is a (derogatory) term for factories where people work in dismal conditions for low wages; they are typically in developing countries where poor people have no better means of earning a living. In the wealthy part of the world (where we live), some people find this terrible (even though our own ancestors had to work like that so that we could be well-off today) and protest by refusing to buy sweatshop products; where they shop is naturally their own business, but I feel they are missing something: If someone wants to help the poor, they should buy goods from companies where the poor are employed under better conditions; if that is not possible (or if the desire to help is not strong enough for the benefactor to overcome obstacles), buying sweatshop goods is at least something. Buying from competitors (such as local ones) is, in the end, even worse for those poor people in the third world; so when someone who actually helps criticizes those who buy sweatshop goods, that makes sense, but it is absurd when someone who doesn't even do that starts criticizing.

Supermarkets compete with small mom-and-pop shops, which sometimes go bankrupt because of it; does this harm society? In and of itself, definitely not; competition is desirable. A separate issue is state harassment, which burdens small businesses harder than large corporations that can more easily absorb it into overhead costs (formerly EET electronic sales reporting, VAT control statements, assorted regulations, and mountains of useless red tape; the mandatory holiday closure of large retail stores is rather an exception that penalizes the big ones). However, market forces ensure that customers get what they desire: a supermarket can offer a wide variety of goods and lower prices, while a small shop can offer a more personal approach or premium quality in specific niches; it is impossible to say objectively which is better, since human preferences are purely subjective. Everyone therefore shops wherever brings them greater utility; some shops survive, others do not, which is not bad – quite the contrary: consumers have signaled that something else provides them with greater value.

Public administration is notorious for dealing with "problems" where someone wins a (typically construction) contract by bidding lowest, only to make a fortune on cost overruns and extra billings; winning a tender with a bid that does not even cover costs is an absolute classic. And for years and years (I remember this from when I was a kid), people have been "solving" what to do about it; I cannot help asking: How about tendering these contracts as fixed time, fixed price? The risk and responsibility would fall on the contractor; sure, bureaucrats would have a harder time lining their pockets, and the room for corruption would shrink, but why doesn't anyone else call for such a solution? I wouldn't worry about finding contractors – especially if tender conditions were adjusted so that it stopped being a perpetual closed game for the five big firms. Most people would reply that while that would be wonderful, "there is no political will"; and they are right – it is lacking and always will be. As long as the state is the contracting authority, no reforms (no matter how well-intentioned) will likely produce the desired effect.

Drugs and weapons have quite a bit in common; however, I will focus on one aspect that is not mentioned as often: For both, there exists an abundance of sound statistical data showing quite clearly that current regulations inflict enormous harm; even from a purely utilitarian standpoint, the best course would be to deregulate both drugs and weapons (leaving freedom and the moral dimension aside for now). The existence of many people who simply ignore this data does not surprise me; what does baffle me, however, is how many of them can completely disregard arguments on one of these topics that are practically identical to the ones they use to defend their stances on the other. Indeed, Republican (right-wing conservative) doctrine dictates that drugs are bad and guns are not, while Democratic (left-liberal) doctrine says the exact opposite; it is sad to see how many people value doctrine over truth and treat data merely as a club to beat opponents over the head, rather than as a tool for critical reasoning.

In 1949, post-war devastated (and recovering) Germany was divided into two states: the FRG (West Germany) and the GDR (East Germany); in the former, a form of social-market economy was established (a relatively mild version of socialism), while in the latter, hardline socialism was imposed. While this state of affairs was grim for East Germans, from our vantage point there is at least one positive aspect: The partition of Germany was practically a textbook laboratory experiment on the subject of socialism. Both countries started from the same baseline – wealth distribution, culture, history, and the population's mindset were all comparable on both sides of that artificial line. What followed was a social experiment spanning four decades; and the outcome was stark and devastating, confirming Austrian economic theory to the letter: socialism simply does not work. The chilling question that remains, however, is: "How many more such experiments will have to take place before socialists learn their lesson?"

In discussions with various greens, I come across bizarre examples of "market failure": A house made of wood is more expensive today than a house made of some "industrial synthetic crap"; a plot of land with natural wealth of "incalculable value" is deemed worthwhile to buy for an office building. To them, such phenomena represent a "market failure" that must be addressed by the state; this stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of the pricing mechanism. The fact that building something in a given spot makes commercial sense indicates that people desire it more than the alternative that isn't worth building there; when building with a particular material pays off, it is evidently more efficient than building with a costlier one. Self-centeredness and a lack of humility prevent some people from accepting that when others desire something different, that desire is not "inferior" to their own; instead, they demand that their own preferences be enforced by violence, justifying it with catchphrases about "incalculable value" (which demonstrably isn't true even from their own perspective; if something were truly of infinite value to them, they would sell everything they own to save it).

Today marks exactly twenty-eight years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses – Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" – departed this world just shy of his 69th birthday. His life's work was taking two traditions that seemed loosely related to their consistent and logical conclusions: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often economically illiterate, while proponents of the Austrian school failed to apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard rectified both and arrived at the brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This realization and its full comprehension profoundly changed my life; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

Christmas is here again; my inner Christian enjoys its spiritual side, my inner capitalist enjoys the material side, and my inner anarchist delights in organizing it all my own way, as every year – so that I actually enjoy it, not because I am obligated to do what is traditionally expected at Christmas – which I warmly recommend to everyone. Most people dislike the holiday rush, yet every year they rush around anyway; in reality, they don't have to – there is no law requiring everything to be cleaned, baked, cooked, and decorated. Some people dislike Christmas commercialism; no one is forced to participate in that either. We are the masters and creators of our own lives – all of us, each of us; even though some unfortunately fail to realize this because of how they were raised (the good news is that there is another way).
As in the past seven years, this year I want to share some music; I love it even more than Christmas. Every year I remember Freddie Mercury. "Carol of the Bells" is one of my two favorite carols, so every year I share a version of it – this time by Pentatonix (unbelievable as it sounds, it's purely a cappella); and since they also recorded my second favorite, I'll share that one too. But I don't want to limit myself solely to carols; this year once again, The Glitch Mob were closest to my heart, and during numerous nighttime drives on the D1 highway, it was most often the track "Our Demons". Also holding very special meaning for me this year is "Comfortably Numb" by the legendary Pink Floyd.
To everyone for Christmas (and beyond), I wish above all two "things" (in no particular order): love and freedom. When I speak of love, I don't mean merely interpersonal love, but above all love as a guiding principle; "universal" love that we can feel within ourselves and that can express itself in creation, love for others and oneself, in all our actions, in daily life... And by freedom, I mean not only external freedom, about which I speak and write so much; I also consider inner freedom to be crucial, something I've pondered for many years and am now beginning to explore with my students and colleagues at Ježek bez klece, which will hopefully yield some concrete output in time.
And finally, once again without typos:
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, many people feel the need to define themselves against Russians; in a certain context that may make sense, but in other contexts far less so. The water pipes burst in the basement of an apartment building that my close friend partly manages; so she called a repair service to arrange a fix. Everything was going smoothly until she mentioned that the property owner is of Russian nationality; whereupon the repairman replied that he refused to do the job. He didn't care that the owner lives neither in Russia nor in that building. Naturally, I support everyone's right to choose their customers by whatever criteria they wish; nevertheless, I do not consider this urge to ostracize individuals solely by nationality to be wise. What I find especially ironic about the whole situation is that two Ukrainian families who fled the war are currently living in that building (one of whom we support financially); and it was they who ended up without running water, not the landlord.

The text "Marriage for All" triggered heated reactions on the Sewers, on social media, and in my inbox. What intrigued me most was the argument that marriage shouldn't be state-controlled (agreed that far), so extending it to more groups of people allegedly increases state power. Yet by that same logic, we could claim that amending building regulations so that more people can build increases state power, which makes no sense whatsoever; or we could argue that the state has no business issuing trade licenses (and anyone should be allowed to run a trade without a permit), but as long as it does issue them, the fewer people who obtain them, the better – which makes equally little sense. If the state regulates, say, firearm ownership, entrepreneurship, alcohol production, or anything else, it certainly isn't true that the more permits it issues, the less freedom there is; it is precisely the opposite. And I find it hard to believe this isn't obvious to everyone; rather, it seems to me that the thought of gay sex somewhat clouds some people's logic.

In debates over regulation, opponents often cite seat belts as an example of sound regulation; if they happen not to know I'm an anarcho-capitalist, they often seize upon it, attempting to pass off the seat belt argument as common ground we can both agree on. Why are mandatory seat belts treated as such a sacred mantra? After all, it is up to each individual whether the risk is worth a bit of discomfort; and that cannot be universally decided, because the risk is not uniform and the discomfort is purely subjective. How then can violent repression against those who choose not to buckle up be defended? Some argue that the rest of society pays for their eventual medical treatment; that is a fantastic argument against socialist healthcare, not for mandatory seat belts. Others argue that someone could be ejected from a car and injure others; even setting aside how improbable that scenario is, it would justify strapping down everything inside a car, not just humans. So why seat belts specifically? I believe the status quo is simply an iron habit.

When a foreign country slaps tariffs on our products, we must do the same; that follows a logic similar to claiming that if someone jumps out of a window, we have to jump too. By slapping a tariff on a good, we restrict competition for domestic producers, thereby harming domestic consumers (when the tariff prevents them from buying a foreign product they would otherwise prefer, we strip away their best option and force them to settle for an inferior one); this happens entirely regardless of whether the other side levies tariffs too. Why tariffs make no sense is explained in thorough detail by Austrian economics, and even by its forerunner Claude Frédéric Bastiat in his essay "That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen"; I lack the space here for a full explanation, but I would like to offer the reader food for thought: What if a single household imposed tariffs on everyone else? What if an entire street did so? A neighborhood? A whole city? Would they benefit? No? Then why would a nation-state benefit, especially when some states have smaller populations than certain cities?

Freedom is not given, freedom is taken. Polish students who understood this are holding a strike today for the abolition of (state) coercion in education; the goal is to open public debate on voluntary education and change unfree legislation. Their lucidly formulated demands resonate remarkably with me (perhaps except for the reference to the constitution); almost as if we wrote them at Freedom of Learning (Svoboda učení) – but we didn't – judge for yourself: "We, the children, want to decide our own learning. We demand constitutional protection of children's rights to educational freedom. We want free choice of schools, subjects, exams, and teachers. We want free choice of goals, materials, methods, scope, place, and pace of learning. We want to decide our own destiny. We must end schooling slavery." You can find more information on the English or Polish version of their website. Let's help them by raising awareness of their effort; share this text, or ideally write your own!

Is the US central banking system (the Fed) private or state-run? De jure it is complicated – it is a non-profit, supposed to be politically independent (haha), and its shares are held by member banks, which theoretically makes it a private corporation; de facto (though formally held by banks) its leadership is appointed by the state (so much for political independence). It resembles the "private" enterprises of the Third Reich, which were formally owned by straw men, yet the state dictated what and when they had to produce, at what price they had to sell, and how much they had to pay their employees. And that is precisely why we must distinguish between "private" and "free-market"; when something is private on paper but state-run in reality, it can inflict more damage than the state alone. So whenever you hear socialists claim that the Fed is evil because it is a private company, ask how much it is actually controlled by those private "owners" and how much by state legislation; the only meaningful solution is abolishing the Fed, and above all, separating money from the state.

The events in Ukraine affect me deeply; partly because I have people there whom I care about – together with Students for Liberty, we are helping them (and others) escape. However, I have already written plenty about the conflict itself; and I would like to address something else. More and more often I encounter people trying to "help" by ostracizing ordinary Russians here in the Czech Republic (for instance, a university lecturer who stopped supervising his Russian students' theses). I understand that war stirs up intense negative emotions; but please, let's not vent them on those who have done nothing wrong. Putin and his state constitute an aggressive war machine; not Russian citizens living in the Czech Republic who had the misfortune of being born on the wrong side of a border. It is politicians and their states that commit evil! Please, let us not play their game in which every Russian supposedly backs Putin's actions; in reality, they do not. Let us judge each individual on their own merits and actions; let us not assist evil by judging individuals according to their nationality.

I am happy because Christmas is here again! The Christian in me celebrates spiritually; the capitalist in me materially; and my inner anarchist completely non-violently, as I refuse to do anything stressful out of duty simply because it is expected of me, which I highly recommend to you as well (Zrzka and I even dedicated an episode of our podcast to this). The great thing about Christmas is that it shows us (libertarians) a PR masterpiece that we (Christians) pulled off two thousand years ago: The original pagan holiday of Saturnalia was transformed into Christmas. What do you think – will we (anarchists) ever manage to turn, say, Czech Statehood Day into Decentralization Day? xD
I enjoy music even more than Christmas; so, as every year, I will leave a few links here. Of course Freddie Mercury! "Carol of the Bells" is also slowly becoming a tradition; but each time I share a different version – this year it will be Metallica. On the other hand, AC/DC haven't been featured here yet. And how about dubstep Deck the Halls xD. And Pentatonix singing a carol in a church I view as a celebration of the journey our society has traveled since the days when the church murdered homosexuals; some might see that as the decay of traditional values, but I personally see in it God's love for every single one (!) of us.
I am immensely grateful (not only) to God that I can be here this Christmas. When I crashed my paraglider in the summer, the previous Christmas came close to being my last; fortunately, I survived, though I'll be in a wheelchair for a while yet, rehabilitation will take months to years, and no one knows to what degree I will ever be able to walk again. However it turns out, I am extraordinarily happy and grateful to remain in this world and enjoy life (or simply to still have legs, even if not fully functional). Furthermore, from the accident, the proximity of death, the pain, and many weeks in the hospital, I gained a wealth of insights and experiences that I am convinced greatly aid my self-discovery, personal growth, and overarching pursuit of being a better person. So thank you!
To every reader (and indeed every human being), I wish happiness, joy of living, love, living in truth... and of course freedom. None of this can I bestow upon anyone, however; happiness and joy are states of mind – and they stem from within, not from without; living in truth is a matter of personal courage; love is the result of all that... and freedom is not given, freedom is taken. Sometimes it requires courage; an example can be found in the soldiers who managed it under far grimmer conditions (and coincidentally also at Christmas) – they defied orders and were, at least for a while, free. Let us follow in their footsteps – peacefully, lovingly, non-violently, but steadfastly, every single day.
And finally, once again without typos:
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

Very often I hear from someone (especially from various "right-wingers") that they aren't proposing state intervention to achieve equality of outcome, but "only" for equality of opportunity; but what does that mean? How do you "equalize opportunities"? Considering how diverse human beings are, nothing like "equality of opportunity" can even exist in principle; indeed, how would you "equalize" the opportunities of a genius and a fool? How do you ensure that attractive and unattractive people enjoy the exact same opportunities? And how do you compensate abused and psychologically scarred children for their suffering so that they have the same "starting line" as everyone else? It sounds nice in conversation, but it simply isn't feasible; and all attempts to approximate it are absurd, because out of the vast, colorful spectrum of human life, only a handful of arbitrary metrics can ever be leveled. Nor is that effort remotely cost-free; on the contrary, we pay dearly for such interventions, and among those bearing the brunt are the severely disadvantaged themselves. You want to give people "equal opportunities"? Be my guest, as far as I'm concerned... but pay for it out of your own pocket!

"The problem isn't democracy; the problem is the people!" Unfortunately, I have heard this sentence – meant in all seriousness – more than once in my life; can anyone truly mean that? Defending democracy – as a system of government by the people – by claiming it is fine, but fails because the people are the problem, is like saying that a potion made of deadly nightshade is magnificent, and the only problem is that people die from drinking it. With communism, this is often cited mockingly (it's a great system, just not for human beings), and occasionally one hears similar critiques leveled against anarchy; how then can it be deployed as a defense in the case of democracy (especially by the very same person who criticized anarchy on those grounds)? Well, it's simple – democracy is our idol, cult, religion, our imposed deity... We are conditioned to believe that democracy cannot be flawed, that criticizing it is socially unacceptable, and that if it produces abysmal results, the fault must surely lie in something else – perhaps in the people.

I feel the need to respond to one of our contributors who came up with a "better name for ancap." Many people have been trying to convince me for years that I should call anarcho-capitalism something else. About half of them think anarchism sounds cool, but capitalism repels people; whereas the other half views those two words in precisely the opposite way – depending on their social bubble. The fact is that at least one of those words will rub almost anyone the wrong way. Furthermore, there already is a widely used and peaceful term that can describe anarcho-capitalism – "voluntaryism" (which is, in my opinion, far more fitting than the "multiarchy" proposed by the previous writer). Why, then, do I continue to call this philosophy anarcho-capitalism?
First, because it feels natural to me to call things by their most precise names (I dislike pretending, and authenticity is very dear to me), plus I don't want to retreat from unpopular terms (I prefer to redeem them); but above all, the word "anarcho-capitalism" makes me stand out and captures listeners' attention (even if often negatively). Countless times I have heard anarcho-capitalists talk about freedom in such a manner that listeners didn't really object, but completely failed to grasp that the speaker wasn't talking about the state and "reformed" democracy with minor tweaks. I have nothing against such an approach; on the contrary, I appreciate that some have taken that path – it is beneficial to reach multiple target audiences simultaneously. But for me, it wouldn't feel right; it comes more naturally to me to call anarcho-capitalism anarcho-capitalism (which the listener will remember better anyway) and then find the words that best explain what it is truly about.

On the one hand, there is broad consensus (among economists, throughout society, and perhaps even among politicians) that voluntary exchange and the division of labor lead to prosperity and well-being; virtually everyone understands that cooperation is the path to prosperity. From this it follows logically that anything restricting exchange and the division of labor produces the exact opposite: poverty and decline; the extent naturally varies with the scale of the restrictions. Whenever someone advocates protectionism – that is, restricting foreign trade in the name of "protecting" domestic businesses – they are logically undermining societal welfare; and why, really? For what reason do I need to "protect" a business owner simply because they happen to share the same side of an artificial national border with me? If someone argues by exclaiming, "Nothing but the nation!", I consider it foolish, but not necessarily inconsistent; but don't let anyone tell me that protectionism "helps the economy."

State interventions are often justified by the presence of imperfect information in the free market; yet perfect information is absent not only in the market, but also within the state. However, the state requires an enormous volume of information to plan its interventions – not only far more than individuals need (who seek to manage "only" their own lives), but so much (since the state attempts to direct the lives of vast numbers of individuals) that it is realistically impossible for it to ever obtain it all. And here comes the intriguing paradox: The better the decision the state is expected to make, the more information it requires; this information is not free, as subjects must supply it at their own expense, costs that escalate the better-informed the state must be. Paradoxically, the better the state could potentially become in terms of decision-making, the worse it must become in terms of expropriating people's resources. And what is the optimal balance? In principle, that cannot be discovered, because doing so would require that very information; changes in the observed entity thus alter the methodology of observation.
