The typical planning horizon of an average democratic politician is roughly one election cycle, so these parasites rule in an "après moi, le déluge" fashion; green eco-terrorists are not all that different from them in this regard, yet as part of their media narrative, they pretend to have significantly lower time preferences when explaining to us that we ought to sacrifice various goods today in order to help ourselves (or our descendants) in the distant future. Many people believe that the further ahead one plans, the better; but is that really the case? It is not, and for two main reasons. The first reason is that time preferences are a purely individual matter—some people prefer to be better off now and pay for it later, while others prefer the reverse; both of these approaches have their pros and cons, the appraisal of which rests with each of us, and one cannot objectively decide which approach is "better."
The second reason, easily comprehensible to those not intimately familiar with the principles of the Austrian School of Economics, is the impossibility of predicting the future (especially the distant future). Consequently, it cannot be ruled out (and is in fact often quite likely) that we might adopt costly measures dictated to us by environmentalists today, only for it to turn out in the end to have been completely pointless; for instance, we might curtail the production of slowly biodegradable materials, only to discover in a few decades that thanks to technological progress, we can not only break them down easily, but even extract value in doing so. Of course, nothing of the sort may end up happening, but nobody can know; all of us (even the most educated among us) are left in the realm of guesswork. Everyone should therefore decide for themselves, without anyone (least of all the government) using force to compel them to comply with the visions of eco-terrorists.

Over the past many decades, and especially in recent years, the "fight against inequality"—typically meaning wealth inequality—has become wildly popular. Let us set aside for a moment how such a fight typically unfolds: the state forcibly robs one group in order to give a fraction of the loot to someone else, embezzles a little, and simply squanders a large portion of the resources. Instead, let us focus on what this crusade actually stems from—a universally (and quite thoughtlessly) accepted premise that inequality is bad and must be eradicated. The first question is why "inequality" is always somewhat automatically understood as wealth inequality; people are unequal in terms of mental and physical attributes, talents, gifts, character traits, charisma—in fact, inequality prevails in absolutely everything. Why, then, make an artificial attempt to bring about some dubious equality specifically in the aspect of wealth? Is it acceptable to rob a rich fool for the benefit of an intelligent pauper? Isn't the latter already at an advantage?
Far more serious, however, is the question of why inequality is bad in the first place; almost everyone takes it as a given fact not worth debating, which I refuse to accept. Take, for example, the complaints that employees in certain professions are poor devils who have to toil long hours every day for little money; these laments arise solely from the fact that other professions exist where this is not the case, while completely ignoring that a few decades or centuries ago, the majority of people worked under even harsher conditions. That was considered acceptable back then because many people were equally badly off, whereas today it has become unacceptable simply because it is no longer the norm and there is a kind of demand for equality. But can anyone logically explain to me why a certain level of hardship should be considered unacceptable not based on its absolute degree, but based on how well off the majority of people happen to be at a given time?

Someone recently asked me in a discussion how I, as a libertarian, would address the market failure of manufacturers of various goods driving prices down at the expense of quality, because customers respond to low prices more than to anything else; my response, naturally, was that I wouldn't address it at all, because it is not a market failure, but rather market efficiency. If people prefer buying cheap, lower-quality products, it means they prefer them over expensive, higher-quality ones; there can be numerous reasons for this: financial hardship, planning an upgrade (people used to buy washing machines or refrigerators to last twenty years; today they don't, but on the other hand, newer products offer new features, designs, and the like), the joy of more frequent shopping and product turnover, a preference for a larger quantity of low-quality items over a smaller quantity of higher-quality ones, but also a lack of information (a customer might prefer the cheaper item because they don't know the more expensive one lasts much longer).
First, note that the market always responds to consumer desires regardless of their underlying reasons; this is entirely for the best, because it is precisely through market mechanisms that shifts in consumer preferences are revealed—shifts that a central planner could hardly ever anticipate, given that people themselves often cannot articulate them (quite the contrary: how often do we hear griping about short product lifespans, and how seldom praise for the benefits resulting from it!). Second—and this is very interesting—not even a shift in preferences resulting from a lack of information constitutes a market failure; quite the opposite! Acquiring information also carries a cost (at the very least, time); and until we have the information, we typically cannot know for certain whether it will have been useful to us, yet we must decide whether or not to sacrifice the time to acquire it. Whoever buys uninformed is indeed in a worse position regarding that specific purchase, but has saved time that could be put to other uses. Is it worth it? Depends on the person; so let everyone decide for themselves.

You have surely heard the phrase in the title countless times; not necessarily phrased in these exact words, but it essentially lurks behind the justification for most regulations and laws. For a moment, however, let us set aside that providing such protection through the state is
immoral
and
effectively impossible
; let us suppose instead that we had a tool capable of genuinely delivering that protection. What would happen? The cost that people have to pay for making poor decisions would decrease; as a result, the motivation to make good decisions would also decline (making sound choices takes time, effort, and sometimes education, which in turn requires time and effort; and above all, it often requires personal responsibility). People would quite logically grow complacent and become less responsible, as well as duller (intelligence also needs to be cultivated and trained; an untrained brain atrophies just like an untrained muscle). Fair enough, but they would be protected, so wouldn't it be worth it after all, you ask?
Well, let us look at the further consequences: a society with more irresponsible and foolish people will require even more protection. And what happens when they get it? Naturally, they will grow even more complacent, lose more of their sense of responsibility and sharpness, which will once again create a need to mitigate the fallout of poor choices. But what is even worse? There will be more children raised by irresponsible parents, causing society to degenerate to the point where each successive generation will require an even greater degree of protection from itself. And where will all this lead? To an utterly stupid, uneducated, and irresponsible herd of dim-witted masses who cannot even wipe their own behinds. And mind you, we are still discussing conditions where a magical way exists to protect these people from themselves at zero cost to them. In the real world, no such thing exists, unfortunately... or perhaps fortunately?

Buddhism? Judaism? Christianity? Islam? Although people around the world have committed all sorts of atrocities in the name of many beliefs, none of the commonly known religions even comes close in brutality and fanaticism to the most dangerous religion of all. It is the religion responsible for unequivocally the most deaths, as well as the greatest number of sheep and fanatics; their
indoctrination goes on constantly and in all sorts of venues
, and it is extremely insidious also because it is typically not even recognized as a religion, even though it displays all the hallmarks of one—yes, you guessed it, statism. Like other religions, this one has its dogmas ("we need the state, otherwise we would slaughter each other"), which are virtually never questioned and, above all, never subjected to critical thought; sacred symbols (the flag, the anthem); priests (politicians); ceremonies (elections); and more holy wars have been fought—and are still being fought—in its name than in the name of anything else.
Statism, however, has one more peculiarity: it is the only religion that truly possesses the characteristic (so often attributed to Islam of late) of being inherently aggressive and, as a matter of principle, requiring violent propagation. Why is that? Well, in all other religions, branches can (and do) arise that continue to acknowledge faith in God or certain holy men, yet do not demand the forceful imposition of that faith on others (we can debate how much of a departure this is from this or that sacred text, but in practice, it is an achievable and achieved state). Statism, however, in the absence of that element of coercion, simply ceases to be statism altogether—whoever demands that the state hold power only over those who voluntarily consent essentially ceases to be a statist and becomes a libertarian (that is, in fact, the exact opposite of a statist, since the latter is de facto defined by imposing virtually anything on others through the state).

Everyone has surely heard some smart aleck hold forth on the wonderful idea of "running the state like a business"; and many even assume libertarians must be thrilled by the notion. How did this idea come about in the first place? Well, the state struggles with inefficiency, private companies are often efficient, so why not give it a shot? First and foremost, because it's impossible—businesses possess no magical efficiency dust; tons of them are hopelessly inefficient. The entire "magic" lies in the fact that those that perform poorly cannot sustain themselves, so they go bankrupt; ergo, only the efficient ones remain afloat in the long run (and the moment they slack off, others replace them in the free market). There is no single way of "running it like a business," because there are countless ways to manage a firm; and nobody knows today which approaches will still be competitive tomorrow, yet the market mercilessly weeds them out—something entirely out of the question for the state. Why?
Since the state extracts the resources for its operation through violence and provides services irrespective of performance,
there is no meaningful metric for the state's efficiency
; and if someone "runs it like a business," that might mean a thriving business, but far more likely a failing one (which, however, will never go bankrupt because taxpayers will foot the bill). Which of these outcomes has occurred remains up in the air, as it cannot be ascertained even ex post (though it can be guessed). For an entrepreneur, things are clear—as long as his company thrives on the free market, he is managing it efficiently; as soon as it ceases to thrive, it means the opposite. But what about the state? A politician starts "running it like a business," but how can you tell whether it helped, and what good it did compared to the previous state of affairs? You can take a look and take a shot in the dark, or commission a bunch of various statistics and look very scientific... but how do you evaluate utility? After all, it doesn't even have units...

I have noticed that many people consider inconsistent the stance of almost all anarcho-capitalists who, on the one hand, fiercely reject collective guilt, yet on the other hand have no qualms about declaring that cops are pigs. Why is this inconsistency only apparent? Because collective guilt means blaming someone for what other members of the group to which that person belongs have committed; for instance, excusing Hiroshima and Nagasaki by what happened earlier at Pearl Harbor is a quintessential example of collective guilt, because the specific individuals who attacked Pearl Harbor were overwhelmingly not the same people massacred by the atomic bombs a few years later—they merely belonged to the same nation. Nation, of course, does not have to be the only criterion; it can be religious affiliation, skin color, or other attributes; regardless of whether someone was born with them or acquired them in life, they bear no responsibility for acts committed by someone else.
Does an exception apply, then, to uniformed monkeys? No. We judge them solely by their deeds as well; however, in order to be a cop, a person must commit immoral acts (starting with enlisting in the service of the largest criminal syndicate in the territory as an enforcer of violence, and culminating in the fact that throughout his duty, he actively violates the Non-Aggression Principle every time he demands someone's ID, pulls someone over in a car, and the like). Similarly, when I pass judgment on murderers, robbers, thieves, or sexual predators, it is not for what other members of that group have committed, but for what every single one of them had to do in order to be categorized into such a group. It is essentially a group defined by a specific act or behavior—and if we condemn that very behavior, rejecting the entire group is not an application of collective guilt, since all its members are guilty of the very thing we condemn. And it is precisely on this principle that the blanket condemnation of cops as pigs operates.

The overwhelming majority of people would answer this question with a no, because we have a democracy; and given the propaganda the state pumps into us from our compulsory school years, such a naive answer is hardly surprising. First of all, let us clarify the difference between totalitarianism and dictatorship: one of those terms describes the scope of state power, while the other describes its concentration. Dictatorship means the concentration of power in the hands of an individual or a small political clique without the existence of an opposition or any other entity limiting that power; it does not matter how the rulers govern (usually cruelly and totalitarily, but that is not a requirement). Totalitarianism, on the other hand, describes a condition where the state intrudes significantly into virtually all aspects of its subjects' lives; power in a totalitarian regime, however, does not necessarily have to be held by a single person or a small clique. While totalitarianism often goes hand in hand with dictatorship, both regimes can also exist independently.
Democracy is indeed incompatible with dictatorship, because unlimited power can be held either by the people or by a monarch (or a select few)—both cannot happen at the same time. However, the existence of a democratic system by no means precludes totalitarianism, because even a democratic state can ruthlessly intrude into every sphere of its citizens' lives. Personally, I am furthermore convinced that the drift toward socialism (and consequently toward totalitarianism) is
an inevitable inherent feature of every democracy
in which the right to vote is not significantly restricted in some way; and the Czech Republic is a shining example—just take a look at the Civil Code or the Labor Code (and far from only those). Whether you come to the conclusion that we live under totalitarianism or not, remember that while dictatorship and democracy are mutually exclusive, the same does not hold true for totalitarianism.

Many people (including politicians) speak very negatively about "buying" votes and "bribing" voters; doing so openly and directly (giving someone money to vote for me) is even illegal, so it is done through doughnuts and sausages instead. Yet if politicians truly wanted to eliminate this phenomenon from society, it would be remarkably easy; and as a side effect, only those who are genuinely interested in the political situation and care about it would vote: let the state stop paying political parties subsidies for the votes they receive (thereby depriving them of part of the funds used to bribe voters) and use this money differently—let every citizen at the ballot box have the choice either to cast a vote or to take the cash. Bribing voters under such conditions with a doughnut or a sausage would be virtually impossible, because anyone voting merely for that would rather take the cash for abstaining (or both, after all, voting is anonymous).
Politicians, however, will never pass anything of the sort, partly because they care about the dough from elections, but above all because it might also turn out that for most people who still vote (and voter turnout isn't exactly breathtaking even today), their vote isn't even worth a few crowns. How low would voter turnout drop in that case? Not that I consider the whole thing a particularly great idea—it wouldn't salvage the misery of democracy anyway—but the problem of "buying" voters would be solved once and for all. Why doesn't anyone put something like this into practice, then? Well, simply because politicians mostly don't want to; they (and far from only they) will endlessly babble about it, but they will never risk voter turnout dropping from the current fifty percent or so down to perhaps a tenth, because then someone might start questioning their legitimacy. Thus, we are far more likely to see
Zeman's fines for not voting
.

Even setting aside falsified statistics and pseudoscientists who tap into state funding by manufacturing evidence and constructing doomsday scenarios based on unreliable
weather forecasts decades or centuries
in advance, I acknowledge the objective fact that over the last hundred or hundred and fifty years that we have been recording temperatures, it has warmed up slightly; however, we have no proof that human activity has had a non-negligible impact on this. Even if it did, it remains an open question whether this is a problem at all; and if so, it is unclear how severe. On the other hand, we know demonstrably that the Earth tends to cool down and warm up dramatically on its own—regardless of the existence of heavy industry, automobiles, or other modern technologies (even without them, there were ice ages, as well as green pastures in Greenland); the crucial question is how significant those few degrees or tenths of a degree of warming possibly caused by humans are compared to the dozens of degrees caused by nature.
Unfortunately, no one knows the answer; everything consists of more or less substantiated guesses. De facto, on the one hand, no one can say what effect human activity has on the global climate, but above all, it is not at all clear what the truly long-term (meaning not decades or centuries, but millennia and more) temperature trend is, nor what greenhouse gases and other technological side effects are actually doing: are we adding to an already ongoing warming phase? Or are we postponing the next ice age? I fear that at our current level of knowledge, nobody simply knows. How should we approach this, then? Simply let everyone make their own choices; until there is proof that atmospheric warming is genuinely harming someone (or will realistically harm someone in the future), initiating violence against anyone who contributes to emissions is unacceptable merely on the basis of someone's conjecture that it might someday cause some harm.

Almost everyone has encountered the popular scare that machines and technology in general take people's jobs; and many have bought into this economically unfounded claim. Let us therefore demonstrate why this is not true; it can be explained simply as follows: human needs are practically infinite (once we have food and drink, we want shelter; once we have shelter, we want a car; after a car, entertainment; then more leisure time, even more entertainment, and so forth—this is merely an example, of course). Thus, when machines take care of a portion of those needs, it does not result in unemployment, but rather in demand for other goods, which in turn creates jobs. Most proponents of theories about "technology taking our jobs" will concede this, but immediately counter that while jobs may exist, there won't be any for unskilled labor. Yet even this makes no sense; why?
Well, suppose machines push all unskilled workers out of the market and they become unemployed; what then? These people will still have needs that must be met (food, drink, clothing, a roof over their heads, and the like). The wealthy with technology could provide these, but the unskilled workers have nothing to offer them (their labor is not demanded by the machine owners). Thus, basically two possibilities can arise: either the wealthy provide them with goods for free (which is not very likely, but if it were to happen, unemployment ceases to be a problem anyway), or the group of unskilled unemployed will start demanding and supplying labor among themselves. They will be poorer, certainly, but not unemployed, because in the worst-case scenario, they will essentially create a parallel economy, which will naturally develop (not least thanks to the know-how of the mechanized segment of society). So when it comes to machines, you can sleep soundly.

We often hear it said around us that capitalism is failing; current problems facing our society (typically caused by the state and its regulations, which may not always be obvious at first glance, but often are) are presented as proof. Why is this argument entirely flawed? Well, primarily because we simply do not live under capitalism, but rather in a mix of capitalism and socialism, with problems arising mainly in those sectors that the state regulates the most (education, healthcare, and the like), whereas sectors in which the state interferes little (such as IT) function smoothly.
Capitalism is a system in which the means of production are privately owned and their owners can dispose of them as they see fit; socialism, on the other hand, means that the means of production are owned or controlled by the state. Nowadays, while most means of production are still formally owned by private individuals, disposing of them is severely constrained; through its regulations, the state restricts owners in how they may and may not use their means of production. Moreover, a fairly telltale clue is that we surrender most of the money we earn to the state and its central planning, keeping only a minority for ourselves to spend on the market—surely that isn't capitalism, is it?
Not to mention that our society—in defiance of the state and socialism—continues to prosper. Yes, of course, problems exist, but just look at what even relatively poor people can afford today: a roof over their heads, plenty of food, hot water, entertainment, information and education, leisure time, accessible and cheap transportation, a wide variety of clothing. Who had access to such things a century ago? Only the wealthiest; and it is solely thanks to capitalism that this prosperity has spread to the broad masses, who now so often rail against it (even though virtually none among them would forego the fruits of capitalism).
After all, what is capitalism based on? On the free market and voluntary exchange! And the beauty of voluntary exchange lies in the fact that it increases the utility of both participating parties; were that not the case, and had the utility of at least one party decreased as a result of the trade, that party would never have entered into it voluntarily. Despite all the ambitions of central planners and regulators, each of whom believes they know best how the world ought to run, the best and simplest way to achieve prosperity is simply to let people act, voluntarily exchange goods, and decide for themselves; and this system is called capitalism.

Welcome to the Sewers in 2019!
2018 was a wild ride—and quite possibly the best year of my life.
You can read a recap of it here!
The ranks of libertarians continue to grow; and many of you are beginning to get active and create things. Please keep at it! If you don't have the time but still want to help,
you can do so here
.
Above all, let's not forget that kindness and love when dealing with people are exceedingly important for what we do; and also that what comes out of us reflects what is inside. So let us work on our own happiness, as a result of which we will see the world as beautiful and make it even more beautiful—that is my wish for the New Year.

Money
, income, debt, and financial transactions in general represent a sensitive topic for many people; why is that? Well, I have observed two reasons: the first, which I completely understand, lies in protecting private information, which can easily be used against each of us (especially by the state). Often, however, I see another reason that doesn't stem merely from keeping information private: money is frequently perceived as something inherently bad. You have surely all heard the disparaging remark that someone does something "only for the money"; but what is wrong with that, provided the activity itself harms no one? Female and male prostitutes, porn actors and actresses, clinical trial subjects, and sometimes even merchants are all
looked down upon simply because
they do their work "only for the money"; similarly, people who are "too money-minded" face condemnation. Not to mention socialist myths claiming that money is the root of all evil.
Remarkably, despite this rather negative view of money, people consider labor—which can be
very easily exchanged for money to mutual benefit
(and this takes place on a massive scale day in, day out, among billions of individuals worldwide)—to be something very virtuous; yet money is the very thing most people work for. Not to mention that its far more crucial function (beyond providing motivation) is transmitting information about the real world, which in my view makes money
one of mankind's greatest inventions
. That is why it is a shame that so often (and from early childhood, see fairy tales), we steer young children toward a negative attitude toward it. I am not suggesting we should raise them to be misers, but I certainly do not believe it is healthy to fall into the opposite extreme; money is an immensely vital part of human society, its usefulness should not be overlooked, and the desire to acquire it (through honest means) should by no means be condemned—quite the contrary.

I've finally lived to see it: Christmas is here again! Perhaps no other holiday so wonderfully combines the spiritual, the material, and the opportunity not to conform to what "one ought to do," but to arrange things in one's own, better way; thus the Christian, the capitalist, and the anarchist within me all rejoice. At the same time, Christmas showcases for us (libertarians) a PR masterpiece that we (Christians) pulled off thousands of years ago: the established pagan holiday of Saturnalia was transformed into Christmas. That is rather like turning Czech Statehood Day into a celebration of anarchy; I think we still have quite a bit of work ahead of us in that regard. So let's get to it!
As every year, I will make room for music; carols belong to Christmas, so I'll start right off with
the very best
, because Freddie will never die... I also cannot help sharing
this
and pointing out that our society has progressed from a state where the church murdered homosexuals to a state where they can sing in church; feel free to write to me about the downfall of traditional values, but I care little about those, as I believe God truly loves us all (!!) and Pentatonix singing in church pleases Him (unlike the hateful outbursts against homosexuals from many of my brothers and sisters in Christ). And because love, life, and music are more intertwined than I have ever felt before (thanks to R.), I won't limit myself to carols; if you have a moment, give
this
a listen, or look back on the past year to the sound of
this beauty
. If I didn't match your taste, my apologies; hopefully next time will be better.
Please, let's not be unkind to one another, let's respect each other's property rights, love our neighbor, refrain from initiating aggressive violence, do no harm, avoid regulating the free market, practice voluntary solidarity without forcing those who don't want to participate, and avoid looking down on others; all these things are deeply connected. Let us strive to find common ground with others, spread the ideas of liberty, think critically about them, and shed dogmas; violence breeds violence, malice breeds malice, hatred breeds hatred, but banning it and restricting expression will always bring even more evil. Whenever we vent anger (even toward collectivists), the world becomes a slightly nastier place; whenever kindness flows from us, we make the world a little better. Let us therefore do no harm even to our enemies unless strictly necessary; if they are aggrieved and frustrated, so much the worse for them, but also for us and our loved ones. Life is not a zero-sum game; and relationships certainly aren't.
In closing, allow me to
remind you of this
and quote one of the wisest human beings: "Love one another."
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!
(Who's going to write to me again this year saying it's a typo? xD)

As a result of state propaganda, the vast majority of people adore democracy; many even take it as
good by definition
. But what are its quantitative limits? Evidently, it does not hold that whenever a majority within an arbitrary group agrees, the minority ought to submit; or are there advocates for letting any gang of thugs together with their victim vote on who walks away with the cash? Is a larger number of individuals required, then, in order to minimize the risk of error? Why, in that case, don't people across the globe vote on global wealth redistribution, for instance? How many European enthusiasts of democracy would voluntarily invite billions of bushmen from the poorer parts of the world to vote on the forcible redistribution of wealth? And what arguments would they offer against it? Would something be said about primitives incapable of understanding our situation? Yet how many primitive voters in the Czech Republic influence matters they don't understand in the slightest, purely because they received a sausage or a doughnut?
This raises the question: why should a system for determining the legitimacy of human action that yields absurd outcomes on both a micro and a global scale be considered the ideal specifically for nation-states? Why should it be right at this precise granularity when it fails at every other? Of course, one cannot dismiss out of hand the possibility that although democracy leads to misery in most groupings, it happens to work well at the level of nation-states; on the other hand, I see no reason why this should be so, when states often represent quite artificial political constructs (for example, Masaryk wheedled Czechoslovakia out of other great powers). Isn't it perhaps rather that democracy is inherently amoral and unjust at every scale—with borderline cases exposing this at first glance, while in our day-to-day reality, a sober assessment of all the misery is prevented by the state indoctrination we have been subjected to since childhood?

Although Czech firearms legislation is among the less strict compared to other European countries, it is hard to speak of freedom as such, because a person cannot simply go out and legally buy a gun or ammunition just like that—one needs a permit from the state (which cannot even be obtained for many weapons); not to mention that politicians and the media constantly try to stigmatize gun owners, paint them as extremists, and frequently declare publicly that gun ownership is a privilege rather than a right, with hardly a single politician on the political scene welcoming and supporting an armed society.
The libertarian rationale I encounter most often is typically that the government fears an armed society because in such a society, the military or police as a whole are not stronger than the civilian population, so in the event of a civil war, whoever controls the state's armed forces might not prevail. They are right about that, of course, but I don't believe that is the primary reason, as I doubt Czech politicians seriously contemplate a civil war—nothing of the sort is even remotely on the horizon (and if there is such a thing as a "national character," the Czech one is quite at odds with that).
Personally, I think it is first and foremost about dependence, secondly about responsibility, and thirdly about confidence; only in fourth place do other reasons (including civil war) come in.
Dependence—unarmed citizens are dependent on the police; armed citizens can defend themselves and subsequently see even more clearly how useless (and harmful) the uniformed monkeys are.
Responsibility—an armed citizen takes on a certain responsibility that he didn't have before, which can make him more responsible; and that runs directly counter to the interests of most politicians.
Confidence—politicians want citizens to look up to them when trouble strikes; armed citizens can resolve part of their problems (security) themselves, ergo they don't look up to them, or do so less.
An armed society means a freer society, because people take on a portion of the responsibility that the state assumed for them in an unarmed society; let us therefore strive to make the boomstick a completely standard part of life for as many people as possible. And let us not forget that the moment a government begins disarming its citizens, it means those citizens will soon be needing their guns...

Nearly every one of us occasionally reads—or hears—something about how many people live "below the poverty line"; usually we learn about this in the context of some alarming report to the effect that the number of such people is growing, or at least not shrinking. Does this mean, then, that while our society grows ever richer, the poor have less and less, or at best the same? No! It doesn't! Can you guess why? Well, the so-called "poverty line" is nothing more than a bureaucratic construct continuously redefined to split the population into rich and poor in whatever proportion currently suits the powers that be. Yes, it's that simple—if we were to keep the definition of "poverty" constant (and there's no need for any libertarian definition; simply taking the bureaucratic benchmarks of the past is more than enough), we would find that the number of poor people is steadily decreasing.

"If everyone took care of themselves, everyone would ultimately be taken care of."
In my view, this sentence perfectly captures the essence of most problems in today's world: everyone feels the urge to manage everyone else's life, social engineers know best what is good for whom, socialists yearn to centrally plan absolutely everything. The idea of someone taking care of themselves is treated by the current establishment as blasphemy against the biggest, most widespread, and most dangerous religion of our time—statism.
Just look around at the newspapers, politicians, and various bloggers, and read their articles: they mostly tackle mass problems on a grand scale and, as part of their solutions, dictate to others what they should and shouldn't do. Yet it would be more than enough if everyone simply minded their own business and stopped dreaming up nonsense: if you come up with something for yourself and find out you were mistaken and suffer the consequences, you simply reconsider your choice, because you feel its fallout firsthand. But when someone decides on behalf of others in this way, then even when their error is laid bare, they often cling to it out of sheer vanity, because someone else bears the consequences and someone else bleeds for it.
The typical objection, of course, is that some people cannot take care of themselves; their loved ones or family can take responsibility for such people (which is perfectly fine), but even then, a certain (small) percentage will remain of those who are incapable themselves and have no one else. Well, those can then be looked after by all the people who dislike the principle described above (and some others too; I personally donate a portion of my income to help people who I believe need it). Nothing, however, entitles anyone to approach someone and forcibly rob them of resources they do not wish to surrender.
Yes, I concede that the result will be that here and there someone ends up badly off; on the other hand, that happens now and always will. The difference is primarily that we currently pay an absurdly high price to the state for this—and by that, I don't just mean most of our income, but also the liberty the state robs us of through its laws. We have reached the point where the view that everyone should take care of themselves and not interfere in the lives of others (unless both parties consent) is branded as extremism; please, let us not be manipulated by this—what is right is for people to decide for themselves.

An acquaintance of mine is very fond of South America, where he spends a month or two every year; he occasionally tells me about conditions there, and it's always fascinating. Recently he told me that although official unemployment is quite high there, the gaze of the authorities doesn't reach that far; as a result, even the officially unemployed can make a decent living. For instance, he met a woman there who earned her living by cooking a large pot of food every morning, loading it onto a cart, and wheeling it into the streets to sell, so that by late afternoon or evening she would return home with enough money to live comfortably.
How simple it is to make a living when unemployed, when there is no state and bureaucracy to tie everyone down! Who couldn't cook up a pot of goulash, buy fresh bread, and sell it from a stall? And when that stops being lucrative? Simply switch products, sell or make anything else, start virtually from scratch on a small scale, without the need for major capital investments; and it doesn't even have to be about cooking—anyone with a garden can buy chickens and sell eggs, anyone can learn basket-weaving, or thousands of other things. How many people would try this if not for bureaucratic legal terror?
Yet under the current dictates of the state, which regulates absolutely everything by law, such a person must obtain a permit, at least a trade license, an additional hygiene certificate for handling food, study all regulations and comply with them, track income, pay taxes, issue receipts, and nowadays also run EET [electronic sales reporting]. How much bureaucratic runaround must they endure before finding out whether their idea is even profitable and can sustain them? At that point, they'd rather just give up on the whole thing, especially when the welfare system and benefits are available—after all, socialist cakes come even (or rather, primarily) without working.
Of course, for politicians, it is best when the unemployed do not fend for themselves; they can then pretend to be active, create an impression of their own indispensability, and in doing so
make people dependent on the state
. After all, as some cow from ANO lectured us in connection with the introduction of EET, business only makes sense if the person pays taxes on it; if someone who doesn't report their income goes bankrupt, it is supposedly no loss, because such a business was worthless anyway. And as long as we keep electing representatives who hold a similar view of business, nothing at all will change in this regard—or if it does, only for the worse.

Over the course of my life, I have had the privilege of debating many restrictors of liberty and prohibitionists whose motivations varied widely: some were merely afraid of something, while others I would describe as chronic ban-enthusiasts who need absolutely everything regulated by law. Because they arrived at their conclusions in very different ways, it long seemed to me that these were entirely disparate lines of reasoning that merely happened to arrive at the same conclusion. Quite recently, however, I realized that there is indeed one logical fallacy in their thinking that is shared by almost all restrictors and regulators (apart from the downright actively malicious ones who are fully conscious of the consequences of their actions—though those, in my opinion, represent a negligible minority). What kind of fallacy is it, then?
Well, it is a rather widespread notion: when something is banned, people very often imagine that the thing simply vanishes; the foundation of all their reasoning rests on the simple belief that when the state bans something, it is essentially the same as if the thing disappeared from the face of the earth and ceased to exist the moment it was banned. What at most a slightly more enlightened prohibitionist can occasionally see is the inefficiency of regulations; they typically grasp that the disappearance won't be total, but only partial, since not everyone obeys laws. Yet practically every prohibitionist ignores enforcement costs, negative side effects, and least of all the restriction of liberty or market distortions; calls for bans are then the logical outcome of such thinking.
It is certainly revealing to present these objections to a prohibitionist: he typically either trivializes them, ridicules them (for example, many people respond to the objection that a typical ban entails the use of aggressive violence against the innocent by declaring such a claim absurd), or simply ignores them. From most reactions, however, it is evident that the person never even attempted to weigh the costs of regulation against its benefits (not that this is truly possible—we run into the interpersonal incomparability of utility here, but for a prohibitionist even to grasp that, he would first have to attempt a comparison). He simply sees something he dislikes, so he automatically wants to ban it (gambling, drugs, Islam, prostitution, and so on).
I know not all of them are like that; some are outright villains who understand the consequences of their actions (and ban things for personal gain). However, I firmly believe that most prohibitionists act from the motives described above (believing that a ban will solve a problem). For that reason, everyone who supports bans on anything must be constantly reminded of the cost of such measures. And the cost is truly high, for it is far from just a matter of regulatory enforcers being able to do something productive instead of their "job" (and their time isn't free), but above all about the consequences: curtailment of freedom, violence against innocents, increased corruption potential, and the potential emergence of mafias (prohibition). Please, let us continuously emphasize these costs to all prohibitionists; let us repeat again and again that almost every state ban in practice entails the use of aggressive violence against the innocent, however little people want to hear it!

Classical civilization is often spoken of as a paragon of virtue, a magnificent society from which we could learn a great deal, and for example, the famous anti-Islam crusader Bill Warner contrasts it with the barbaric Islamic world, which has enslaved people since its inception; to bring up slavery in that context seems rather absurd, considering that all of classical antiquity rested on slaves (free people were a minority in that society). Equally detached from reality is the romantic notion of battles between heroic Romans and the "barbarians" of the north: what was that actually about? Well, Roman legions were simply conquering more territory, whose native inhabitants were subjugated, butchered, enslaved, and tortured in the process; in their cruelty, the conquering practices of Roman legionaries were not matched even by the Nazis, who surpassed them in scale only due to population growth and technological advancement.
Ancient Greece, in turn, is frequently hailed as the cradle of democracy; and in a certain limited sense it truly was, yet it certainly was not a democracy that meant "rule by (all) the people," as real democracy took place among a handful of privileged individuals (free citizens), while the majority (slaves) had no part in the decision-making process. Paradoxically, that was the reason why those early democracies exhibited
greater stability than modern ones
(not that both kinds weren't vile, albeit each in a slightly different way). While it is true, of course, that our civilization gradually evolved from that one, it was under no circumstances a society we should take as a model: we as humanity have come a long way, learned from many mistakes, and should not lose sight of the fact that idealizing the past can be quite dangerous in many respects.

Today, it is taken for granted by almost everyone that we carry documents like national ID cards to identify ourselves, that the state maintains a central citizen registry and gathers vast troves of personal data about them. It is fascinating how many people react with extreme outrage when private entities do something similar (and doing so on a mere whim is even prohibited by law), yet when it comes to the state, the very same individuals remain completely indifferent. The existence of such measures is presented to us as a "necessity" without which society could not function reasonably; through this propaganda, we easily overlook that just a century ago, ID cards were not mandatory (which, by the way, was instituted by a certain Adolf, who found it helpful for his "final solution"), two hundred years ago they did not exist at all, and if we go back another hundred or two hundred years, we find a complete absence of entries in parish registries—people simply weren't registered in any way, yet no doom ensued.
One could argue, of course, that in times when people traveled far less and everyone lived in an environment where everyone knew them, identification wasn't necessary, whereas in today's globalized world, requirements are higher; and that is certainly true. On the other hand, in today's world we possess cryptographic tools unknown to our ancestors with which the problem can be resolved entirely;
an exhaustive (and in my view underappreciated) article
on this was written by OC—one of the smartest and most educated anarcho-capitalists I know. You might ask: why doesn't it work that way if it's so good? Well, simply because the state already does it in a different (albeit worse, more expensive, more exploitable, and scummy) way, so there is no interest in expending additional resources on an alternative system when the state one exists anyway and we have to pay for it regardless. If the state system ceased to exist, however, market solutions would replace it virtually overnight.

The purpose of this text is not so much to convey a message as to spark a discussion on a topic that has been on my mind lately; I would like to hear what other libertarians think about it. Model situation: Someone close to me finds themselves in a critical situation where an immediate tracheotomy is required for their survival, but I lack the skill and the tools to perform it; the only doctor in the vicinity has the equipment and the know-how (other help will not arrive in time). The doctor agrees to perform it, but demands all my property in exchange. All of us (libertarians) would probably agree that he has the right to do so; my question, however, is: is it a dirty trick? At first glance, I would say yes, but...
To keep the discussion on track, let me explicitly emphasize once again that I am not addressing the
NAP
here; from the standpoint of the Non-Aggression Principle, the doctor's conduct is perfectly legitimate: he is allowed to do it, violates no one's rights, and I have no right to force him into the procedure at gunpoint (whether putting a gun to his head or first promising him the property, but then doing nothing for him and forcibly resisting his attempts to claim what is rightfully his). Naturally, however, even things compatible with the NAP can be scummy; for instance, cheating on a partner, betraying a friendship, turning your back on someone who has helped you over the long run, hurting someone's feelings for fun, and many other similar acts can be done in full compliance with the NAP.
At first glance, I would place the doctor's conduct into that same category. On the other hand, a discussion took place some time ago in the Sewers in which someone said something to the effect that the doctor ought to charge the market price; and at that moment it struck me: what actually is the market price in that situation? It naturally varies by time and place (the price of water in a desert is different from by a reservoir); ergo, I wonder: isn't "all my property" genuinely the market price? Given the circumstances, I'd almost say yes. And if the doctor has no personal relationship with me, why should he provide me with a service below market price? From this perspective, it seems fairly obvious that his conduct is not "scummy."
On the other hand, I would certainly brand it "scummy" if a doctor in a similar situation—where my loved one was present, but not me (and no one from whom he could collect payment)—left the injured person lying on the ground, stepped over them, and walked away (even though he naturally has the right to do so); failing to render first aid (when one knows how and it poses no risk to oneself) strikes me as revolting behavior. But charging the market price for it (and perhaps negotiating it on the fly, so that if the victim's loved one says they won't give up all their property, but "only" a million, he performs the procedure) can hardly be evil, can it? As demonstrated by the familiar example of selling "overpriced" gasoline in disaster-stricken areas where only a single intact gas station remains, such behavior is not only fine, but actually desirable and "socially beneficial." Is there anything fundamentally different here?

Have you ever wondered what happens if you don't pay taxes? Well, it depends: if it's a pile of money and you also lied to the state about your income, you will be legally kidnapped and thrown straight into a cell; if you simply do nothing, the state will send notices, then dispatch bailiffs, and if you defend your property against them, sadistic uniformed monkeys will show up—and if you resist them, they will either shoot you down like a dog or lock you in a cell for even longer than in the first case. In practice, this is no different from a mafia collecting protection money; the only difference lies in the legality of one and the illegality of the other—in other words, in what a bunch of crooks in parliament voted into law.
Occasionally, however, one encounters this statist argument: "But I pay taxes voluntarily."
We may question, of course, whether that is truly so, and whether the person would pay taxes in the amount demanded by the state even without the threat of force; but even if that were true, taxes cannot be justified on that basis.
Why? Well, if this justification held up, any violent act could be excused as long as there is at least one victim who doesn't mind being a victim and essentially wants it that way.
For instance, we could say that roaming through parks at night raping women is acceptable because there are some who would sleep with the attacker even without a knife to their throat.
Unfortunately, state propaganda is strikingly visible on the issue of taxes: not only is an act where someone merely refuses to hand their money over to an aggressor routinely branded as "theft," but on top of that, many people think of arguing that because they pay taxes voluntarily, everything is fine. Just imagine how absurd that would sound in any other context: you tell someone how you were mugged, only to have the listener tell you that nothing really happened, because when he was last mugged, he didn't mind it all that much, so what are you complaining about? But different standards apply to the state, of course, as our schoolteacher taught us...

You know those pictures of heaps of food being thrown away while African children starve? They are often accompanied by some deeply moralistic message about our selfishness and how we should be ashamed of throwing away something that is in short supply elsewhere; I have two fundamental objections to these superficial messages, by which I intend to refute them completely:
1/ Food here and food in Africa are two entirely different goods; the cost of transportation is astronomical compared to the cost of that discarded food, and in many cases it would be cheaper to grow new food locally.
2/ Given how much food our society consumes, it can be considered a (free-market) miracle that surpluses are so small; hitting consumption exactly to the millimeter is simply impossible—so would you rather have surpluses, or starvation?
Besides, who wants to return to the previous regime's meat queues? And even back then, surpluses existed.
Not to mention that there were times when even in Europe people starved; but then came the Industrial Revolution and raw capitalism, which solved this problem. Let us be glad for that and wish the same for Africans; but let us not feel guilty about having those surpluses—on the contrary, let us be grateful for them—it harms no one, and it is a natural consequence of the prosperity in which we live.

I was just listening to a debate on drugs in which a cop from the narcotics squad was "refuting" the thesis that
drugs are varied
, people are too, and thus the effects of substance use differ, ergo it isn't fair to ban everything across the board; the person used an analogy that alcohol behind the wheel also affects different people differently, yet the law applies equally to all and no one even thinks of questioning or debating it. Well, not only has that occurred to me many times, I have even engaged in such debates before, though I haven't written about it until now; and the fact that this cop took the correctness of such a law as a given prompted me to realize that a short text on the subject wouldn't hurt.
Not only does alcohol affect different people differently, but above all, it doesn't automatically make everyone a bad driver; only past a certain threshold (which is highly individual) does it impair an intoxicated person's capabilities. And there are unquestionably people on the roads who, even with a blood alcohol level of 0.2% (two per mille), will be better drivers than youngsters fresh out of driving school; not to mention that some people begin stumbling after a few drinks, while others with the same amount are only just warming up, with their motor skills and reaction times virtually intact. Alcohol thus not only impairs driving ability differently in different people, but does so from entirely different baseline abilities (some being vastly better drivers than others).
From this perspective, it truly seems absurd to punish people based on their blood alcohol level, since many a completely sober driver is far more dangerous on the road than an intoxicated professional with millions of kilometers under his belt. What is the solution, then? Laissez-faire, I say! Only the free market can deliver an answer. Perhaps private insurers and road owners would ban alcohol behind the wheel entirely; perhaps they would allow a flat threshold, or base permissible intoxication on accident-free mileage, or only factor it in upon an accident, or not at all; and what I consider most likely is that they would come up with something I haven't even conceived of here.
Not to mention that it isn't even clear that the optimum lies where alcohol causes the fewest accidents: we cannot ignore the possibility that road users would willingly accept a slight increase in accident risk in exchange for the utility derived from other things (convenience, enjoying an evening, and so on). Such a possibility is by no means far-fetched, because everyone who leaves home to visit a pub for a beer (even on foot) demonstrates a preference for taking on certain risks to satisfy certain needs; it is therefore hardly unrealistic that people would think similarly regarding driving. The problem, of course, is that
without a free market, we will never find a solution to the problem, because it is simply impossible
.

It is remarkable how often one hears calls to buy "domestic" products, especially food, even though it has been nearly two hundred years since Frédéric Bastiat explained with crystal clarity what nonsense that is; anyone unfamiliar with his work is warmly urged to read "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen" (good news for those who dislike lengthy texts: this one is short and very readable). Patriotism, however, is potent, emotional, and state-subsidized; not to mention that whether someone gets publicity, has influence, and can persuade others has, unfortunately, almost nothing to do with whether they are right or preaching falsehoods.
Supermarkets are even mandated by some new law to flag foods with national flags so that consumers can see which goods they are buying, since the conviction that it is "right" to support "domestic" goods enjoys significant popularity; people are falsely led to believe that they are somehow helping themselves by buying "domestic" goods, as if the prosperity of "their" state translated into personal benefits. Not that this isn't true to a certain (very negligible) extent, but those benefits are utterly dwarfed by the drawbacks resulting from market distortions.
There are many ways to dismantle these fallacies, but I will choose the one that strikes me as simplest: what is the essence of the market? The best producers and suppliers of certain goods make the most money because people voluntarily pay them for those goods; the worst go bankrupt. And it is this very mechanism that is most advantageous to consumers, because it ensures they receive precisely the goods they desire; if we prioritize "domestic" goods over foreign ones instead of looking at other factors, we may well end up giving business to a producer or supplier who, while Czech, isn't as good as their foreign competitor.
I am certainly not saying we should deliberately avoid buying Czech goods; merely that if we choose solely on the basis of quality and price while ignoring country of origin, we will support the best producers and suppliers regardless of where they are from. If, however, we factor country of origin into our criteria, next time we may end up with an inferior Czech product or service instead of a superior foreign one. Personally, when given the choice between Czech and foreign goods of otherwise identical specifications, I pick the foreign ones to counterbalance the patriotic whims of my fellow citizens xD

The goal is a free market, a stateless society—anarcho-capitalism... how do we get there? Privatization? If so, how? Auction off state property? Give it away? To whom, and by what method? All at once? And what about opting out of state "services"? Which ones? In what sequence? Creating parallel structures? I would be keenly interested in your thoughts—and as detailed and well-reasoned as possible, including alternatives you considered and dismissed (and why). Please share them in the comments! For I believe there is no single "right" path; in my eyes, there are only more and less flawed ones. While I am convinced some are better than others, my goal right now is not to persuade, but rather to learn.
If someone is not an anarchist and their aim is a minarchist state (or at least one smaller than the current one), that's perfectly fine; describe the path you would take from the status quo to your ideal system.

"People don't know what they want, they're manipulated by advertising, we must regulate it to help them!" Such is the common refrain against consumer market society; and I never cease to be fascinated by the thought processes of those who advance it: "I am educated, conscious, unmanipulated, and wise; corporate ads don't work on me; I have seen through what millions of people haven't. So now I will be the savior and help them... even against their will, through violent state intervention." Sometimes, if particularly arrogant, such a person throws in an analogy to parents raising children; then washes down the thought with a sip of latte from their favorite hipster café (marketing has no sway over him, you see—he's a hipster because he chose to be). He lacks humility, respect for people and their wishes, tolerance for different lifestyle choices, and the realization that he is no better than anyone else—and the more deeply rooted these virtues are in a person, the more that person champions
the free market
.

Traffic jams seem to be a necessity of our time; and it is quite logical that when there are too many cars, the roads simply clog up and traffic comes to a halt. How to solve this? I have no idea; nobody else knows either, so it is presumably a necessity. There have been plenty of such "necessities" throughout history: for instance, there was a time when traveling around the world in eighty days seemed nearly miraculous, just as it was once considered obvious that heavier-than-air objects cannot fly, that speaking with someone halfway across the globe is impossible, and that a human traveling faster than sixty kilometers per hour would perish. Yet resourceful individuals driven to achieve great things have always managed, through the thorny path of trial and error, to find solutions; and compared to challenges like those, a mere traffic jam looks like child's play. But none of those in a position to solve it have any incentive to risk anything, because they hold cushy positions and everyone has already accepted traffic jams as an inevitability; so why make an effort and risk losing voter favor?

Cars of certain colors are more visible on the road, while others are less so; imagine—purely hypothetically—a regulation banning "dangerous" car colors: red and yellow are clearly visible, but away with grey. For some time now, I've been probing opinions on such a regulation among supporters of (other) regulations with whom I debate; and guess what? Almost all of them are opposed—even staunch supporters of mandatory seat belts. I find myself wondering why that is: this is a textbook regulation consisting of banning something "pointless and vain" (which nobody strictly "needs," being a mere "whim") in the name of safety (accompanied by the popular argument of endangering not just oneself, but others as well); ergo, opinions on it ought to mirror those on drunk driving or using a phone behind the wheel, yet they don't. Where lies the difference, then? Personally, I think it comes down purely to media barrage and what happens to be "fashionable" to ban nowadays. Do you have a better explanation?

As many readers know, I am involved with
Svoboda učení [Freedom of Learning]
; and because its members and supporters frequently put their principles into practice (with wonderful results, by the way), their children often do not attend school. This is not pure unschooling—current legislation does not allow for that, as children are required to undergo periodic examinations; and that is precisely where something fascinating occurs. These children simply fail to comprehend why they should have to undergo such a process: they ask whether the examiner doesn't know the answer to what they are asking, offering to help and explain it (which would make sense), but when they discover it is a "test," they cannot grasp the point of the whole exercise. Why should they prove what they know to a stranger from whom they want nothing? You'd be hard-pressed to find such a mindset in an ordinary schoolchild: they have been conditioned to do things simply because they are ordered to—and testing is seen as normal. Yet the question "Why should anyone be testing me?" is a prime example of critical thinking; and that (despite claims to the contrary) is hardly welcome.

One possible—if somewhat morbid—way to measure the well-being of a population is to track suicide rates; this naturally has its limitations (it only measures the most dissatisfied segment and is influenced by a host of other factors), but also advantages (the "survey" cannot be skewed by dishonesty). And what does this metric say about the claim, popular in some quarters, that we were better off "under communism"? Well, under the previous regime, an average of 24 people per hundred thousand took their own lives each year (in the five years following 1968, as many as 28); since the Velvet Revolution, we average 16 suicides for the same population size. People committed suicide "under communism" fifty percent more often than today! Naturally, I am not claiming that a person who would otherwise be happy commits suicide solely because of who is in government (I personally don't believe that explanation even in the case of Jan Palach); I am convinced, however, that the political system affects people's lives enough to provide reasons for suicide in some (though not all) cases.

Neoliberalism. The new liberalism. What does it actually mean? On Wikipedia, one can find the original definition along with many newer ones, as well as an account of how often its meaning has shifted. Today, the term is used almost exclusively by proud leftists, mostly as an insult. Yet when one asks them for a definition, their answers are either nonexistent or extremely vague (even the panel discussion on "Diagnosis: Neoliberalism," which drew me to visit Klinika, began with an explicit declaration that they would not define the term—a promise they kept). Consequently, when they do manage to articulate something, it is usually a claim that it refers to deregulation, the "free-marketization" of society, and the privatization of state assets; but that directly contradicts their frequent habit of using "neoliberalism" to describe current reality, where the trends are precisely the opposite. So I ask—especially of proud leftists, if they happen to read this: is the word "neoliberalism" anything more than a slur and a cliché?

Some people are horrified by the ingenuity of drug manufacturers, who periodically introduce new narcotics whose destructive effects are often worse than those of the drugs previously on the market; in recent years, one example is the substance krokodil, named because it inflicts damage on users akin to crocodile bites (flesh literally rots off their bodies—hardly surprising given the ingredients). Where does the demand for such drugs come from? Well, they typically emerge as substitutes for more expensive ones (for instance, some turned to meth to substitute for cocaine, or to krokodil for heroin). And what drives the price so high when the production cost of drugs is negligible? The state and its regulations, of course; this entire nightmare was spawned by the
war on drugs
, without which no desperate soul would ever inject compounds of gasoline, paint thinner, and hydrochloric acid into their veins.

Virtually all libertarians agree that the state should not interfere in marriage at all (whether heterosexual or homosexual); people should simply arrange their affairs as they see fit. The reality today, unfortunately, is that the state usurps decision-making in this realm (as in almost everything); and the rulers have decreed that only two people of different sexes may marry (two people of the same sex may register their partnership, while other combinations are barred). Some libertarians take the stance that since the state shouldn't be marrying people at all, we certainly shouldn't support same-sex marriage either, as having fewer recognized marriages is closer to "no state marriages." Yet that makes little sense so long as the state disadvantages unmarried couples relative to married ones in numerous ways. From a purely practical standpoint, marriage currently offers relief from certain state regulations; and as long as those regulations exist, we should not deny anyone the option to marry—regardless of gender or the number of individuals involved.

One of my readers posed a question to me: when someone steals Bitcoin, does that violate the
Non-Aggression Principle (NAP)
? The "theft" in and of itself (namely, broadcasting a signed transaction that transfers BTC from one address to another) does not, in my view, constitute a violation of the NAP. Nobody can own a private key (it is a sequence of bits, which in principle cannot be owned—only known and kept secret) or prevent others from signing transactions (doing so would itself violate the NAP); ergo, handling "someone else's" BTC is not a violation of the NAP. The real question, however, is how the "thief" acquired the key: in that step, a violation of the NAP almost certainly did occur (even if he didn't break in physically, but hacked a device, that still violates the NAP, as it involves tampering with someone else's property—the device—against the owner's will), though theoretically it might not have (for example, if the "thief" simply saw the key and memorized it).
You can watch the recording of my lecture on this topic from the "Bitcoin is Retro" conference on the Free Port Channel.

They say that in a blind taste test, wine tastes better to people when they believe it was expensive; well, cheers! In the 1980s, the U.S. military bought a toilet seat for what would amount to forty-five thousand crowns adjusted for inflation, and a hammer for thirty thousand; had they told the soldiers, maybe they would have shit and hammered better. When news of this broke, taxpayers could have lost their shit; however, they had to do so on toilet seats two orders of magnitude (!) cheaper. Some time ago, I
compared the budget of anarchist Wikipedia with that of state-run Czech Television here
; how do you think it turned out? Everyone understands why you shouldn't spend thirty grand on a hammer—because we know the market price of a hammer. Yet there were times when manufacturing a hammer consumed far more resources even on a free market than it does today; toilet seats didn't even exist back then. In light of this, I ask: How do we know that spending on state education, healthcare, the judiciary, and the police aren't just more thirty-grand hammers?
How much are they "supposed" to cost?

Social engineers have a problem; and as is typical in a state-run society, we have it along with them. The Czech Republic has a low birth rate, the population is aging, the nation is dying out, the apocalypse is nigh; not that there would be any problem at all if the comrades in government hadn't long ago devised an infinitely moronic pension system that presupposes this won't happen (and not that anyone would even notice the whole thing were it not for the Czech Statistical Office and state registries recording every single fart). However, it happened; the state made a mistake (once again); and instead of correcting it by gradually abolishing the pension system, it is trying to salvage the situation with further blunders.
Child benefits, birth grants, child tax deductions, and now possibly even reduced social security contributions for having more children—these are all measures intended to stimulate the subjects to procreate more intensively; much like when a farmer owns livestock and needs more heads of cattle for economic reasons, that is pretty much how our overlords look upon us. They concocted a pension system based on assumptions that held true once upon a time; and as if the plebs were allowed to disrupt their plans now—no such thing, you will pop out babies whether you like it or not!
By the way, what kind of people do you think will actually be swayed by the state's incentive methods? Do you want to increase the birth rate by handing out financial perks to people with children, dear social engineers? Good grief! In the best-case scenario, it simply won't have any effect; in the worst-case scenario, it will mean people start having children because they received state subsidies for it. Surely those will be well-off people overflowing with love, capable of passing on the best to their offspring and raising them into decent human beings. The result will be yet another generation even more dependent on the state than the previous one; and worse still, I highly doubt this is some diabolical master plan—it is merely the normal cycle of things, where moronic state solutions naturally generate and nurture mindless statists.
Another question, of course, is: what is the "correct" number of people in the Czech Republic? Ten million? Eleven? Nine? A hundred? A single million? Although our society would look vastly different with ten times or one-tenth of its current population, living conditions would change, but who really knows how exactly? There is no one who can convincingly justify why ten million people in the Czech Republic is a more "correct" state of affairs than nine million; the only argument for striving for those ten million (or more) is that poorly designed pension system. But why use social engineering to mitigate the consequences of a bad decision when the right solution is to
change that decision
?

Every now and then, Romani activist Ivan Veselý enters my radar, commenting from time to time on various events in society; I recall his statements about Germans, whom he distrusts and dislikes because of the Holocaust ("they killed our elites"—meaning Romani elites), as well as about Muslims, whom he would have impaled on stakes if he had to fight them. Let us grant that his second statement might have applied only to those Muslims with whom he would be at war; nevertheless, he distrusts Germans across the board (even without a war) because of what their—long-dead—compatriots did. Isn't that ironic? His lifelong cause is urging people not to judge all Gypsies based on bad experiences with certain individuals, yet he publicly applies the exact same approach himself (albeit toward a different group). Unfortunately, like so many others, he fails to realize that the solution is not to "go to bat" for one's own group against others, but to rid oneself of collective guilt once and for all and lead by example.

Leading British market research agency Ipsos MORI revealed a phenomenon that caught my eye in their 2013 study "The Perils of Perception"; they asked people about the severity of various issues (crime, unemployment, drug addiction, vandalism, immigration, litter on the streets, and others), both as perceived in their own neighborhood and nationwide. The results were truly remarkable: respondents perceived every single problem (without exception) as more severe on a national scale than in their local area; in other words: "These problems don't really happen around me, but other people have them." Do you know what that reminded me of? "
I can take care of myself, but others need the state because they are too stupid.
" Just as almost nobody sees crime, junkies, vandals, and immigrants around themselves, yet everybody knows that "out there in the world" there are tons of them, hardly anyone considers themselves an ignorant fool, yet naturally they know that the vast majority of everyone else is.

Lately we occasionally hear talk about restrictions and eventually the complete abolition of cash; what would that achieve? Well, the state would gain absolute control over every single monetary transaction that takes place; whenever you pay anyone for anything, an electronic trail remains for the uniformed apes to follow whenever they see fit. In that case, even EET [electronic records of sales] would basically be redundant, because the state would see vastly more. Of course, it won't happen overnight—people would grumble—yet step by step we are heading in that direction (large cash transactions are already restricted by law); and once some "advanced Western nation" abolishes cash, our politicians will start holding it up as an example worthy of following, because "an honest person has nothing to fear, right?" It is truly enough to make one weep, but what can we do about it? Fortunately, we still have cryptocurrencies; the abolition of cash could open up enormous room for them to thrive.

Paradoxically, a frequent argument in favor of the EU is the free market; thanks to our EU membership, we are supposedly able to reap the benefits of open borders and a free market, for which we allegedly "must" pay through the bureaucracy that regulates those markets (which is quite a paradox—regulating your way to a free market). It is claimed that without regulation, states could not protect "their" businesses against subsidized and privileged competition; I argue, however, that nothing of the sort is necessary. If other countries subsidize their producers while the Czech Republic does not, Czech producers may indeed become less competitive, yet Czech consumers will be able to buy cheaper (subsidized from abroad) goods; and if someone follows this line of thought further and concludes that all Czech entrepreneurs will go bankrupt, their employees will lose their jobs, and no one will have money for anything, I suggest not stopping the thought experiment there, but thinking one step further (thinking it through thoroughly will explain why even that catastrophic scenario could never materialize).
