; since D-Day has arrived, I am reminding you of the invitation once more. And if you have someone in your circle who might not be an anarcho-capitalist or libertarian, but whom you think might find it interesting to hear why the state is a bad servant and a cruel master, bring them along.
Tonight's lecture is titled "The State Is Immoral"; it will be about the ethical aspects of the state's existence.
And I also warmly invite everyone to the next lecture in two weeks (December 14 at 20:00), where we will examine how anarchy relates to the Austrian school of economics.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 20:00 at
Paralelní Polis
.

In November 2015, terrorists attacked in Paris
; the French government declared a "state of emergency" back then, which translates to a (theoretically temporary) police state. We had a chance to see the effectiveness of this measure for ourselves
in July in Nice
; the cops failed; an armed populace would likely have stopped the maniac in the truck, but weapons are bad (and therefore regulated), riiiight. While the "state of emergency" keeps being repeatedly extended (always by several months), French Prime Minister Manuel Valls announced that in January 2017 it will be extended again by several months, because (quote): "It is difficult to end the state of emergency now. Especially in a presidential campaign with meetings and public gatherings. We must protect our democracy. The state of emergency allows arrests and searches, which is effective. Therefore, without a doubt, we will live with this state of affairs for several more months." And thus freedom dies; who remembers what Benjamin Franklin said about trading liberty for security?

About a week before launching the first wave of the EET, Babiš proposed unexpected changes: he wants to exempt online shops and small sole proprietors (natural persons with a lump-sum expense deduction and annual revenue up to a quarter of a million) from the obligation to record sales; as far as I'm concerned, the more people are exempted, the better, but an interesting question arises: why is he doing this? Officially, he supposedly listened to feedback and blah blah blah; no, surely nobody is naive enough to believe that. So why? Does he want those exempted to feel relief and like him? If so, why would he announce it only after they had already procured the software? Or is he anticipating that his coalition partners will reject it, allowing him to shift the blame onto them ("I wanted to exempt online shops, but Sobotka blocked it")? Or does Babiš have inside info that the system technically cannot handle the load and is trying to reduce the volume so it doesn't crash? I don't know myself; and I look forward to reading every opinion in the comments, as that is the primary purpose of this post, so please share your thoughts!

Two cops from Pilsen, and I will name those bastards – Jan Pergl and Lukáš Zahradník, were dispatched in October 2012 to handle a grave situation: a homeless man was tapping on the window of a dormitory hostel. When they arrived, he wasn't tapping anymore, but the guardians of the law tracked him down and beat him to death; and what did the courts do? The district court acquitted them, the regional court slapped them with eight years, the high court lowered it to four, and finally the supreme court gave them six and a half years.
For many reasons
, I consider punishment by incarceration pointless, counterproductive, unjust (especially toward those who foot the bill), and foolish; but even setting that aside, look at the severity of the sentence and compare it to other murderers... heck, not just murderers, even Smetka got double that for the H-System fraud! Well, either a homeless man is a subhuman in the eyes of the courts, or a uniformed monkey is a superhuman, or perhaps both. Incidentally, if a
private arbitrator
judged a murder committed by his own employee, everyone would call it a farce; why then is it completely fine when done by the state?

The director of the Dvůr Králové Zoo, Přemysl Rabas, has a penchant for multi-million bonfires; in 2014 he organized a ritual burning of horns in Dvůr Králové, and this year the boys (accompanied by Jan Stejskal, head of international projects) flew to Vietnam to fool around in the exact same manner. Too bad they haven't read (or understood)
my article that I published on this topic back then
; then they might know that by burning tusks and horns, this commodity becomes scarcer, hence more expensive, ergo poachers' incentive to hunt elephants and rhinos increases. Furthermore... if they sold them, besides reducing scarcity (and thus the price, and consequently poachers' incentives), they would raise plenty of funds to protect those animals (the Dvůr Králové bonfire cost a hundred million back then); not to mention that poaching problems are best resolved by permitting
private breeding farms (without which bison, for instance, would have gone extinct long ago)
, which is likewise forbidden for protected species. Unfortunately, mindless activism is far more popular than thinking.

The EET needs no introduction; we all know this Babiš system designed to make state robbery more efficient. As part of my job, however, I've had the chance to get to know it in detail, since I am implementing the interface into our clients' software through which they will submit receipts. Aside from the technical aspect of EET virtually screaming that it is a state project, it also has loopholes; which ones? First of all, it does not restrict transactions "without a receipt" in any way; where a receipt is issued, falsifying it isn't advisable because the EET features a snitching system where anyone can verify a receipt and subsequently report the merchant. Yes, that's precisely how Babiš envisions "justice": people ratting each other out; but what else could one expect from Agent Bureš 007... and to top it off, massive propaganda naturally fosters fertile ground for informants so they can excuse the inexcusable by telling themselves they are doing a good deed (because whoever refuses to be robbed is actually stealing... and so on).
What is equally interesting, however? An EET transaction is defined by: Tax ID, business premises ID*, cash register ID*, receipt ID*, amount, and timestamp (items marked with an asterisk are generated by the merchant themselves); and now imagine that in some hypothetical pub or hotel, it just so happens that multiple items are sold for the exact same price (lunch menu, hotel room...), or items are divided across receipts such that, by coincidence, multiple receipts for the same amount are generated around the same time, and as luck would have it, a regrettable error occurs where multiple guests receive a receipt with identical identifiers... they have no way of knowing, and even if they verify the receipt in the snitch system, it will tell everyone that it's OK. Wouldn't that be a disaster? In conclusion, let me emphasize that I am merely warning entrepreneurs about this potential mistake so they can be aware of it and avoid it (if anyone doesn't understand, reach out, I'll be glad to explain); this is definitely not a public incitement to break the law!

The state regulates gambling, which entrepreneurs in the field evade in various ways—such as officially turning their gaming parlors into private clubs and the like. The Ministry of Finance, however, is on them like a hawk; recently, it obtained a court order shutting down a Pilsen-Prague network of gaming rooms ironically called "Gaming Against Stress" with the official status of a private club. Many might think that eliminating gambling is beneficial, but this involves two catches, one moral and one practical (as usual): the moral one is that it constitutes aggressive violence by the state against free individuals; and on a practical level, as usual, it doesn't work—additional taxation is ultimately paid by the customer, and restricting the number of venues merely distorts the competitive landscape, which also penalizes the gambler without curing their addiction; it only makes them blow through their money faster. Gambling addiction is foolish and harmful, but the state certainly isn't helping.

For many years (actually, it will soon be eight years) I wrote a lot and didn't personally visit fellow libertarians that often; times are changing, however, and I accepted an invitation from
Paralelní Polis
, where every other Wednesday (beginning November 30, exactly two weeks from now) starting at 20:00 I will talk (and subsequently discuss with attendees) about
anarcho-capitalism
. I would be thrilled to see you all there; especially, of course, those who more or less sharply disagree with my views, so you can challenge me (or at least quietly disagree and reflect, if you don't feel like speaking up). If you have someone around you who might not be a libertarian, but whom this topic could interest, don't hesitate to bring them along; the more diverse the palette of opinions among the discussants, the better.
I look forward to seeing you on November 30 at 20:00 at Paralelní Polis!

More than a year ago, I
wrote in the Sewers about a place in Lety
where a concentration camp once stood and where they have a pig farm today; personally, I am satisfied with the situation, because—unlike concentration camps—I really like pig products. However, there are people who mind the pig farm being there for commemorative reasons; I don't exactly share this view, but fine, everyone has their priorities, and I don't strictly need the pig farm to be right there for my pork schnitzels—in fact, I don't care at all. The shareholders who own the pig farm have a similar view; they also wouldn't mind raising pigs elsewhere. Such a situation clearly provides room for
voluntary exchange
: Let the people who are bothered by the pig farm in Lety buy it from the shareholders and build a memorial there, for example; a great solution, but... but for that, they would have to sacrifice something of their own, which they naturally don't want to do. So the government approved a proposal to force all of us by violence (including, for instance, me, who is perfectly fine with the pig farm being there) to pay for it.
Why is this wrong? Simply because the resources required to relocate the pig farm would bring greater utility to people if they were spent differently. How do I know? Well, very simply—it follows from the very fact that people did not voluntarily pool their money to buy out the pig farm; by not doing so, they
demonstrated their preferences
to use the necessary resources differently, for something that brings them more utility. There is no way to "measure" whether it is better to have a memorial in Lety or to spend that money on something else, because the benefit of both is subjective; however, it can be ascertained quite easily by letting free people act: If they voluntarily spend enough resources on a memorial, then it means it is more beneficial to them; otherwise, it is not, and the pig farm should stay there. This choice has already been made, and people clearly demonstrated their preference not to spend money on relocating the pig farm; then the government came along and
forced them to waste resources
and do it anyway.

Mithra is a very old god—so old, in fact, that he was a celebrity nearly two thousand years ago; back then, people worshipped him and built temples for him out of their scarce resources (not always voluntarily). Now, history is essentially repeating itself: the European Union subsidized the study of this god with the generous sum of twenty-seven million crowns; once again, these are resources collected involuntarily (through taxation) under the threat of violence. And how were these scarce resources handled? What was the project's output? What benefits did we get for our money? Tereza Fojtová, spokesperson for Masaryk University, which received the grant, stated: "The greatest success was a publication in the prestigious journal Nature about why people feared the gods." And judge for yourself—could something better have been acquired for that money? Well, nobody bleeds when spending other people's money; and if someone spends money that doesn't belong to them, they don't have to think very carefully about it... so why not try to restore past glory to a long-forgotten god?

DJ Trump won
the great CvsD showdown
, and the USA has a new president; it is horrifying, of course, but we can console ourselves with the thought that Hillary wouldn't have been much better. What will happen next? Once the shitstorm dies down and DJ Trump assumes office, we will see which of his campaign promises he actually took seriously; I fear we will witness him failing to live up to his commitments on issues like tax cuts, while reveling in his promised protectionism. Time will also tell what his supporters were really after—the ones who glorified him before the election and made him out to be a hero who would bring freedom, hope, and "finally a change for the better"; it is more than obvious that DJ Trump will deliver none of that... the question remains whether he will then be a disappointment to his fans or not; I hope so, because the opposite would mean they didn't care that much about freedom after all, but mainly about protectionism, which is likely the only thing their candidate will be able to push through.
Also worth noting are all the articles praising DJ Trump as a savior, redeemer, change, and fighter against the establishment, which sound utterly absurd—so when one points this out and brings some counter-arguments, their authors or promoters suddenly switch from the "divine Trump" tune (which I criticized) to "the lesser evil" (which I disagree with, but understand). Another bombshell of logic is the voices now celebrating the victory of a man of the people and an outsider—because a billionaire with political connections and the money for a massive campaign is, boy oh boy, the typical underdog with no chance, who won only thanks to divine providence and the sharp vigilance of the American people (who elected Obama four years ago, which often drove these very same people mad), something like Babiš over here (many point to similarities with Zeman, but notice that Babiš is a much better fit). Well, let us hope DJ Trump impacts us as little as possible.

Americans have a big day today—the presidential election; unlike the Czech presidential election, where there was nothing to choose from at all, in the US there is at least one candidate I can imagine voting for, and that is Gary Johnson. However, he has no chance, and the real "cunt vs. dick" showdown will take place between a disgusting socialist and a totalitarian populist; and where exactly is the lesser evil? Hillary is a classic statist, DJ Trump is something like an American Babiš; in my view, both possess the remarkable quality that in the event of their election (and unfortunately, one of them will be elected), the United States will have the worst president of all time (not that it was much better with Obama). What is my take? I'd probably mind a Hillary victory slightly less; DJ Trump disgusts me far more on a human level (not because of his boorishness, but because of his vicious totalitarianism); I fully understand the opposite view, but what really turns my stomach are the articles glorifying either one of the candidates.

Some time ago, we could
read bad news in the Sewers
about how the bastards at the Prague City Hall were crushing Uber drivers; now I bring good news—the municipality lost its court case against the first Uber driver. Their aim was to shake down the driver for fifteen thousand crowns for operating an illegal taxi service; however, the Municipal Court in Prague overturned the fine, ruling that Uber is not a taxi service, but paid ridesharing (reasoning that, under the law, a taxi service is open to anyone, whereas Uber only provides services to a narrow circle of people who have installed the mobile application). I congratulate the driver and welcome the court's decision; what is worse, however, is that in the reasoning of the judgment, one can read, among other things, that using the Uber mobile app was not prohibited by any legal regulation—let's hope nobody takes this as an invitation. For now, however, the municipality got its knuckles rapped; I hope (even if I don't really believe it) that this marks the end of the harassment of Uber drivers.

There is a harassing law of sorts that mandates a forty-five-hour break for truck drivers every week; in Belgium, they have upgraded this harassment to the point where they fine drivers if they decide to spend this time in their truck. And to top it off, the French and Belgian governments agreed on a joint initiative trying to push through an EU regulation under which drivers wouldn't even be allowed to spend this break in a hotel; the goal is clearly to send them "home." This is textbook protectionism, the absurdity of which
Claude Frédéric Bastiat wrote about nearly two centuries ago
; but who would bother reading when they have the force of the state on their side in the form of an armed police fist? In light of such measures, talk of how we need the European Union for the sake of an open market sounds paradoxical and absurd, when its own bureaucracy only shackles the market and does everything to distort it.

Yesterday was All Souls' Day, and two days earlier was Halloween; and the Internet is once again teeming with pseudo-patriotic articles and musings about "our All Souls' Day" and "that American holiday of Halloween," which we supposedly shouldn't allow to "crowd out" All Souls'. A typical response to this is the objection that Halloween is actually a Celtic holiday, and All Souls' Day isn't entirely "ours" by origin either; however, as is usually the case, defenders of traditions are very often those who don't really bother learning anything about them—the main thing is defending something "ours." Personally, I couldn't care less about All Souls' Day, and the same would go for Halloween, but I really like those smiling pumpkins, so I'm a fan of that Celtic holiday; on the other hand, I fully understand that someone else prefers All Souls' Day (and yet another likes both for a change, or neither). But I don't understand the endless talk about "our traditions" and how we must not let them be displaced by others... why not?
I fully understand that someone prefers All Souls' Day, perhaps because they like visiting relatives' graves, or simply because they don't like Halloween (such as those awesome pumpkins); what lies completely beyond my comprehension, however, is the stance that we should somehow "protect" All Souls' Day simply because it is "ours." In what way is "our" tradition better than a "foreign" tradition? Personally, I don't think it matters; there are some customs I enjoy, others I don't care about, but I certainly don't give a damn about their roots or whether they are sufficiently traditional here. I always judge the thing itself, not its origin; anything Czech is not (merely by virtue of its origin) any better than anything (say) Slovak or German. Only patriots feel the constant urge to push "their own" everywhere, and above all to define themselves against "the foreign"; I consider the "Halloween versus All Souls' Day" dispute nonsensical and its
patriotic
dimension absurd.

I'm just browsing the Internet when suddenly an ad from the European People's Party in the European Parliament pops up: "Does it bother you too that different brands of mobile phones use different chargers? Thanks to EU regulation, phone manufacturers selling in the EU will have to offer customers universal chargers usable across all smartphone brands starting in 2017. No more annoying hunts for your charger and less electronic waste!" I don't want to get into why this is once again an absolute outrage—everyone probably understands that—but what is the point of it now (!), when manufacturers have finally, through market mechanisms, basically standardized on USB chargers? Besides, I can easily imagine how our reality will be presented once it becomes history: Every type of phone had a different charger until the EU came along and finally unified them; who cares that chargers first unified through the market, only for the EU to come in afterwards and issue a pointless bureaucratic regulation.

You might have already heard Babiš yelling that during his time in government, the national debt fell for the first time and that we are borrowing less than before; I admit that, technically speaking, this time (exceptionally) he isn't lying. But when we look at the budget deficit, we find that the sums are still astronomical; how is that possible, you ask? Can Babiš do magic? Well, here is a clue: in 2012, for example, the national debt rose by (very roughly) two hundred billion crowns, while the deficit was "only" about a hundred; yes, Babiš is such a financial wizard—he can leave borrowed money sitting in an account for a few years, then spend it and show off that he isn't going into debt—now tell me, who among us can pull that off? On top of that, we have cash pooling—by law, the state granted itself the power to simply tap into the funds of certain (even non-state) institutions (such as health insurance companies), which it does have to pay back eventually, but they don't count toward the national debt. So what do we say to Babiš's bullshit about reducing debt? "Like hell!"

Today, October 28, the state declared a public holiday in honor of the founding day of the independent Czechoslovak state; and how shall we celebrate the founding of the state—that is, an organization based on violent coercion and robbery? In style, of course—with more violence, how else! Politicians recently passed a law forcing large retail stores to close on public holidays. The Chamber of Commerce is protesting... hmm, against what? Could it be against threats of violence from the state against anyone who doesn't close and refuses to pay fines for it? No; the complaint is directed at the fact that large stores must close while small ones do not—meaning, if there's going to be terror, let it be for everyone! And people find it completely normal to debate this, or they even think it's right to comply; why is it that if I walked up to a shopkeeper and told him that he must either close his shop today, pay me a fat fine, or I will physically attack his property, everyone would condemn that behavior—yet when parliament does the exact same thing, it's just fine? How could it be?

While I am being paid handsomely to program connections to EET [electronic sales registration] servers into various information systems (an interface that, by the way, is technically speaking also... how should I put it... of state quality), Babiš is touring the Czech Republic explaining to people how EET won't cost business owners almost anything; the promotional tour is going great, after all, according to his own words: "In Mikulov they even wanted to beat me up, elsewhere people shout at me. I try to explain it all to them; in some places they listen to reason, elsewhere they don't want to talk at all." Despite this "explaining," I would like to set the record straight:
The state works by
taking most of the fruits of people's labor under threat of violence, of which Babiš pockets a cut, among others; and he not only brazenly calls thieves those who refuse to let themselves be robbed by the state, but on top of that he introduces EET, which is neither free nor cheap, and only makes those state robberies (called taxes) even easier... no wonder this is hard to "explain."

Back in August, we could
read in the Sewers about Pelikán's bluster
, which spawned a bill that has already passed its first reading in the Chamber of Deputies—under it, terrorism, its planning, financing, material support, cooperation with terrorists, and offenses facilitating a terrorist attack will be penalized more severely; so far, so good... but it wouldn't be Pelikán and his melody boys from ANO if they didn't shove an extra outrage in as a bonus: in this case, up to twelve years in prison for anyone who publicly endorses a terrorist attack (even if they have nothing whatsoever to do with it), on social media for instance—you simply post a status along the lines of Osama being a badass who did the right thing (either because you're an idiot, or maybe you're just joking), and off to the slammer you go; long live freedom of speech. All that's left is to hope that the Senate will throw it right back in their faces...

Minister of the Interior Milan Chovanec decided to become the Minister of Truth as well; he had a survey conducted (with our money) which showed that a quarter of people trust "alternative media" more than state media, and furthermore, half of us hold "bad" (meaning different from Chovanec's) views on certain armed conflicts around the world. And what to do about it? Well, when you don't have to pay for propaganda out of your own pocket, plenty of options exist; so Chovanec is creating the SJJP (Special Unit of the Sole Truth; not an official name, just what I dubbed it) within his ministry, tasked with preventing the spread of "false or misleading" information and propaganda (that is, propaganda other than the most massive kind—the state's), because allegedly: "We must set the rules so that people have the opportunity to find truthful information within minutes or a few hours."
And how does he intend to achieve this? The SJJP will have around twenty people (after all, we don't employ enough bureaucrats yet), some of whom will be professional, paid internet trolls tasked with debunking "bad" opinions on social media and across comment sections everywhere; the job of others will be to train civil servants in the "correct" truths, while the majority will spend their time scouring the Internet and snitching (to cops, secret services, and other state agencies) about whatever they find that displeases them; after all, which state thug would care about
freedom of speech
when his own propaganda is under threat? Incidentally, the entire SJJP is part of the new Center Against Terrorism; remember this if you are ever tempted to applaud when the state fights against terrorism, immigrants, Islam, and whatever else—with the money it plunders from us, it will turn around and launch censorship and paid trolling against us.

The Bundesrat (the German Federal Council) is asking the European Union for a regulation that would ban internal combustion engines across the board starting in 2030; German politicians are already trying hard to push electric cars through financial incentives for the companies manufacturing them, yet we can see the result of this squandering of money for ourselves—how many alternatively powered vehicles are driving on the roads around us? And what can't be done the hard way will be done the even harder way; when emissions regulations and nonsensical subsidies aren't enough, an outright ban steps in. I don't think they'll manage to push it through within fourteen years, but we can see where the will of the socialists is heading; by then, I'll hopefully register
my beloved Elise
as a historic vehicle so I won't have to worry about it. Finally, I'll add one more note for all the environmentalists thrilled by the idea because electric cars produce virtually zero emissions—while that is true, someone somewhere has to generate that electricity... and solar panels and wind turbines won't cover that.

The French government pushed through yet another law: all retailers and businesses will have to gradually phase out and, by 2020, completely stop selling, giving away, and using plastic bags and plastic tableware (cups, cutlery, plates, etc.), unless made from biodegradable materials—which is naturally much more expensive. Everyone will therefore be forced to pay extra (not only) for beer in a plastic cup and many other items; instead of people deciding for themselves what their priority is—whether to save money or to avoid leaving non-degradable traces behind—the government ordered them to do so, because politicians naturally know best (after all, they have the money for it, plundered from taxpayers' pockets, and nobody bleeds when spending other people's money). Also remarkable is the fact pointed out by the secretary of Pack2Go (an association representing packaging manufacturers): there is zero evidence that biodegradable materials are any better for the environment.

In response to the low voter turnout in the recent elections, voices calling for electronic voting have resurfaced, arguing that it would get people who don't feel like going to the ballot boxes to vote; the most common objection I've noted is the potential for manipulation in such elections, where one cannot go behind the voting booth alone, and so forth. In my view, this isn't that much of a problem, because situations where someone coerces someone else to vote would occur only minimally (not to mention that the entire state apparatus is built on coercion, so this isn't really contrary to the spirit of the state xD). That turnout would increase is likely true, which, as an anarcho-capitalist, I consider (ceteris paribus) a bad thing, even though it isn't entirely clear how large the increase would actually be; available data suggests more young people would vote, which is generally viewed as an advantage, though personally I see no reason why a young voter would be in any way better than an older one.
Most advocates of electronic voting operate on the assumption that the higher the turnout, the better; in my opinion, this assumption is nonsensical not only from an anarchist perspective, but even from the perspective of most of those people themselves, if only they thought about it a little more. Democratic outcomes do not depend on the quantity of the electorate, but on its quality (which is not to deny that democracy is a dirty business either way, but even dirty business can take various forms and degrees); and what do you suppose happens to quality when we introduce electronic voting? To make an informed decision on whom to vote for (or not to vote for), a person who doesn't follow politics needs dozens or hundreds of hours; those who don't vote simply because they don't want to spend ten minutes walking to the ballot box (which is completely fine) certainly won't spend oceans of time acquiring information either (which is also fine)—but do we really want these people voting, just casting a ballot for whoever was on the last billboard they saw?

Yesterday I vented my anger here over
the Prague City Hall's crackdown on Uber drivers
; however, thanks to the popularity of the Internet, there are many other similar services, such as Airbnb, where people can rent apartments to one another, or Doginni, where dog owners can have their dogs walked or people can earn extra cash by walking them. These are all services that nobody forces anyone to use, and for those who do, they are clearly beneficial (otherwise they wouldn't use them); yet the state cannot resist sticking its greedy claws into it, demanding protection money, and harassing decent people. Aside from trying to collect taxes, officials are even demanding trade licenses for walking dogs (another stroke of bureaucratic genius xD); and the result? Well, Doginni is considering moving abroad, where parasites hopefully won't harass them as much. Great job, bureaucrats: destroy the service, which is surely the best way to serve the people you feed off of.

Just about every libertarian and plenty of other people know Uber; it's a smartphone app that lets you either offer someone a ride for money or book that service. Practically anyone can easily become a driver without unnecessary paperwork (and taxation xD), and Uber also offers passengers various advantages over standard taxi services, so its popularity is growing. Naturally, this pisses off all kinds of dickhead state regulators and other parasites to no end, because it's difficult for them to extract protection money from it. So a couple of thugs from the Prague City Hall decided to pass the time by hailing Uber drivers, having them drive to Podolská Street, where fucking uniformed monkeys were already lying in wait; everyone caught in the trap now faces fines at the very least, and some face even harsher penalties, since none of them had a taxi license.
Now seriously... how can anyone defend these mafia practices!? One person wants to drive people for cash, another wants a ride for money, and someone else writes an app for them; everyone is satisfied, no one is forced to use these services, so what the fuck is the problem!? A few uniformed monkeys and bastards from City Hall—disgusting freeloaders living off protection money called taxes—simply decided during their "working" hours to harm decent people who voluntarily exchange services with one another. They justify this with some shitty consumer protection that makes you want to puke—after all, anyone interested in such protection doesn't have to use Uber in the first place! And on top of that, there's the damn lobby of traditional taxi drivers trying to ban it by any means necessary; damn it, if you can't compete with it, start running it yourselves and stop forcing people to use services they themselves consider worse (if they didn't, you'd be able to compete).

4,882,098 people (more than 65%) did not show up for the regional elections; this means that Babiš, the election winner who garnered twenty-one percent of the votes cast, was actually elected by a mere seven percent of all eligible voters. And what about the rest? The media (especially online) talk about them rather pejoratively; I've heard more than once that they "didn't bother" to turn out and are basically thought of as ignorant (especially certain anti-Islam parties that constantly claimed to speak for ordinary people and, unable to accept their error and defeat, resort to insulting non-voters). Of course, it is more convenient for politicians to claim that only ignorant people don't vote than to admit that many non-voters are expressing their dissent; while it's hard to estimate how many there are in total, in my social circle this accounts for the overwhelming majority of non-voters (granted, I am surrounded by libertarians xD).
Personally, I always vote—not because I believe one can vote one's way to freedom, on that point I completely agree with the critics, but if an aggressor gives me an opportunity to marginally improve my conditions, I take advantage of it (I elaborated on this
in more detail on Mises.cz
); furthermore, I know of a political party that can be used as a platform for spreading libertarian ideas to the public, so the more visibility, the better. I also vote because the following stance doesn't seem reasonable to me: "I don't vote in order to express my disapproval." Why? Well, if I want to communicate something, I should do so in a way that ensures my message is understood; and non-voters are seen by the majority as ignorant, not as informed dissenters. Once a significant portion of the population understands this message, I will stop voting as well; for now, however, I am merely laying the groundwork for it—for instance, with this very article.

During her time in office, Minister Marksová has become a celebrity in the Sewers; not because of her name, but because of her
unbelievably
dense
or
dangerous
legislative
proposals
... and the latest one is a real treat too. In order to make the pension system "fairer," Marksová believes that childless people should pay higher social insurance contributions than people with children; at first glance it sounds quite logical, if somewhat grotesque—whoever raises future taxpayers should pay less. Such reasoning might make some sense if social insurance possessed at least some characteristics of actual insurance (aside from the name) and weren't simply (yet another involuntary) tax; the amount paid in social "insurance" does not depend on risks or coverage amounts, but on the income of the payer, which makes zero sense from the standpoint of any theoretical "fairness" (especially since higher-income earners statistically require "payouts" from this state "insurance" less often).
Leaving aside the moral aspect entirely—namely that social insurance as a whole is legalized robbery—and assuming for a moment that it is a legitimate system (which it isn't by any stretch, but let's assume it), then while it is true that people with children "produce" future contributors and thus might seem to "deserve" perks, under this same logic where we look at merits rather than needs, it would make just as much sense to grant perks to people with significantly above-average incomes, because they personally (not hypothetically their children one day) pay far more money into the system than most others. Trying to ensure "fairness" in such an inherently unfair system by penalizing the childless is like ensuring "fairness" for bullied schoolchildren by padding the classroom walls. So why is Marksová doing this? Well, either she really is that dim, or she doesn't give a damn about fairness and is just trying to score political points; I would almost find the second option more palatable.

Karel Schwarzenberg proclaimed that our survival is only possible within the EU, without which we would (quote) "starve to death," and countries like the Czech Republic or Austria (quote again) "shouldn't run their mouths" against the EU; the old man is dropping gems and likely suffers from delusions where European bureaucrats and politicians supposedly feed entrepreneurs and their employees, who would perish from hunger without them, while totally ignoring who actually produces real value and who is a parasite on it. That politicians' audacity knows no bounds is hardly surprising; the sad thing (though for me, unfortunately, less and less surprising) is that it doesn't even click for most people commenting on his statement—sure, they often curse the EU and Schwarzenberg over migrants, but no storm erupted similar to the one when Mládek labeled sole proprietors as parasites, even though what Schwarzenberg said boils down to basically the exact same thing, merely sugarcoated with statist rhetoric.

Patheticism, thy name is Pavel Kočiš (hereinafter referred to as Whacko)! At seventeen, he wallpapered his room with eight hundred and ninety photographs and pictures of Václav Klaus, then president; now, at twenty-two, he has decorated his room with over five thousand photos and pictures of Miloš Zeman for a change (and complains that he is slowly running out of space). But that's not all; Whacko sends various gifts to his favorite presidents (boxes of chocolates, pickled gherkins, hand-painted pictures, and the like) and, like a proper stalker, tries to get a job at Prague Castle (unsuccessfully) and bombards his idols with letters. So far, he has earned the attention of Zeman's spokesman Ovčáček, who visits him to indulge his psychosis a bit and get a bite to eat; so the next time you hear talk about a secular state, remember that the most hardcore religion is statism—and whoever falls for it especially hard gets a visit and praise from the priests of the President's Office.

Actor Stropnický, currently Minister of Defense, must enjoy watching military-themed porn, because he came up with the idea of an all-female special forces unit; the first thing that crossed my mind when I read it was: "Dude, why!?" Apart from the porn angle, that is. Not that I'm opposed on principle to women in the military—let everyone do as they please (even though I'd prefer not paying for it, but the same goes for the men)—yet why assemble a unit exclusively out of women? What is the point? And I find it particularly bizarre at a time when the state spends considerable money pushing gender correctness; why is a private company forbidden by law from discriminating on the basis of sex, while the Minister of Defense can construct special forces modeled after Charlie's Angels without having—apart from his masturbatory fantasies, presumably—any relevant reason for it?
Another brainchild similar to Stropnický's Angels is the minister's desire to have a woman hold the rank of general; he shared his plan with the media in these words: "I believe that in the foreseeable future, we will have our female general. [...] I'd like to make it happen before next year's elections." Seriously? Well... seriously, of course; he's a politician, so that is naturally how he thinks. But to have the gall to brag about it in the media, and nobody finds it odd? Stropnický would "like to make it happen before the elections"? The army currently has four female colonels, which basically means the goal is to promote one of them within a year, so congratulations in advance to the future female general on her new rank, for which she qualified primarily by virtue of having a vagina—and she didn't even have to use it. What makes me shake my head most of all is that most people don't even see anything strange about this in light of how obsessively opposed the state is to gender-based discrimination, while intending to practice it itself on an enormous scale.

Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro Moros has unleashed hardcore socialism in his country; the results did not take long to appear. Although Venezuela boasts rich oil reserves, poverty reigns everywhere, as no one there is able to properly extract it anymore; the situation is so dire that the local population has been thirsty and starving for a long time. Whenever the market comes up with a solution, Maduro doesn't hesitate to shut it down; about a year ago, he capped the price of bottled water by law—and what a shock, a shortage immediately followed. Now people queue outside supermarkets all night long; but even that has now been made illegal. State enforcers patrol the country, arresting thousands upon thousands of people in droves; for what? For instance, if someone is caught with food for which they have no receipt, or if someone sells groceries, or simply stands in line overnight to get their turn; because, naturally, scalpers and middlemen are to blame for everything and need to be cracked down on. Sounds familiar?

Once upon a time, about a year ago, some guy in Germany was trying to figure out whether he was the biological father of his child; there wouldn't be anything too strange about that (although I personally believe blood ties are overrated xD), but the guy handled it like an absolute moron in court... and so, at German taxpayers' expense, this monumentally important case made it all the way to the Constitutional Court, which ruled that no law currently obliges a mother to disclose the names of her lovers—the potential fathers—though it added that it would welcome such a law. Minister of Justice Heiko Maas jumped on this remark right away, proved his "usefulness," and rushed in with a bill; if it passes parliament (and so far it looks like it might), another uncharted territory opens up for the state to stick its nose into on taxpayers' dime—a public matter: Who fucked whom!?

Babiš's Pelikán of Justice wants to liquidate companies that do not submit their financial statements to the Collection of Documents of the Public Register in time; according to Pelikán's bluster, such a company should simply be dissolved, struck off the commercial register, and that's that. Even now, a fine of up to one hundred thousand crowns can be imposed for this, but our righteous Minister of Justice finds that punishment too soft; it's better to simply eliminate those companies (and people) outright. And freedom of enterprise? Well, sure, suuure, but only up to a point; simply put, freedom of enterprise ends where a politician's whim begins. The state can simply do whatever it wants, now including shutting down companies for not handing over potentially sensitive information; how would people react if a private entity acted that way? There would be an uproar; when it's the whim of some corporate suit in the private sector, it's terrible, but when it comes from a suit in the service of the state, well, that's completely different.

Prague city councilors banned overly large trucks (that is, longer than twelve meters) from entering Prague starting in early 2017; Minister of Transport Ťok justified this by claiming that trucks don't belong in Prague, which, by the way, is a sentence that every cheering socialist or green idiot will enthusiastically applaud. Why? Well, mainly because they don't think... for instance, about the fact that those trucks aren't joyriding there, but transporting goods; and hardly anyone sends a thirteen-meter truck to deliver a single loaf of bread. So what will people do who need to get so much cargo into Prague that they currently load it onto such big trucks? Most likely, they'll send more smaller ones, which will end up being more expensive (and get passed on in consumer prices), produce more smog and noise, and worsen the traffic situation; but otherwise, bravo comrades, great job—with this ban, the world will be a slightly better place to live.

The Slovak government has thrown
yet another
wrench in the gears of local entrepreneurs; anyone who wants to print (promotional) flyers, brochures, business cards (!), or catalogs intended for customers becomes a "manufacturer of non-packaged goods" and must register with the Ministry of the Environment (sure, this registration consumes some paper for letters, envelopes, and official forms, but what wouldn't we do for nature?). Unfortunately, it doesn't end there: when the printing actually happens, the person must also pay protection money to a waste recycling company; not just any company, of course, but one of the few certified with a stamp from the ministry. So waste disposal will effectively be paid for twice—first by the person who throws it away, and second by the person who produced it. I wonder when Czech politicians will come up with something like this; someone like Babiš could surely run one of those certified waste recycling companies.

Partly as a result of the ever-increasing frequency of online shopping, the price of low-grade paper (cardboard boxes and the like) is rising, leading scrap collection centers to increase their buyback prices; demand for paper is higher, so people's incentive to recycle is growing, the world keeps turning, and
the market works great...
Yet there are also petty thieves scavenging paper from recycling bins to sell it, which displeases municipalities as they lose out on sales profits. And the solution? A typically political one: the Union of Towns and Municipalities of the Czech Republic (a sort of mayors' club) is pressuring the state to ban the purchase of scrap paper (much like the purchase of scrap metal was already restricted); fortunately, the Ministry of the Environment rejected it. Still, the fact that anyone could seriously propose this in the first place is fascinating; it is roughly equivalent to someone stealing my watch, and me demanding that the state ban people (who have nothing to do with it) from selling watches.
The way the rising price of paper motivates people to recycle demonstrates another interesting point, by the way: recycling as such isn't automatically "right" (as some try to tell us; nor is it "bad"); it simply carries certain benefits, but also entails costs (time, convenience, space...). But how do we determine whether the benefits outweigh the costs? Everyone must decide that for themselves (no higher authority knows better), while the incentive for doing so is dialed up by the market depending on how urgently it's needed: higher paper consumption leads to higher prices, which in turn leads to greater motivation for people to sort and recycle. This issue naturally encompasses a wide range of aspects—economic, environmental, social, logistical, and so forth; one cannot unequivocally state which of these is actually more important, but we can let people act and
leave the market unregulated
, as it is the only mechanism capable of providing acting individuals with the necessary inputs for their decisions.

Fico pushed through an utterly insane law in Slovakia: Any entrepreneur whose supplier provides a service performed by an undeclared worker will face a fine ranging from roughly 55,000 to 5.5 million Czech crowns. Yes, you read that correctly—it does not matter at all whether the client knew about it, because they become automatically guilty simply for failing to spy on their contractor enough. A rather interesting question is whether Slovak bureaucrats will enforce this law across the board, or only in cases of selected individuals who need to be eliminated for some reason; not that the outcome wouldn't be horrible in either case. If we consider that employing someone under the table simply means refusing to pay protection money to the state, we arrive at the reality that not even the mafia has the audacity to punish someone for purchasing services from someone who failed to pay them; Fico, however, is a blazing hammer of people's democratic justice that happily crushes any entrepreneur.

France's most famous Islam-basher, Marine Le Pen, was seized by a fit of consistency in which she proclaimed that if Muslims are banned from wearing headscarves and burkinis, logically yarmulkes should be banned too; however, she didn't follow her logic to its ultimate conclusion, because then she would also have to ban Christians from wearing crosses, Buddhists from wearing dharmachakras, and statists from flying flags (the paradox of the whole thing lies, among other things, in the fact that Le Pen herself belongs to the most brutal religion of modern times—one that has succeeded so thoroughly with propaganda that it isn't even called a religion anymore, despite exhibiting all of its traits). Banning Islamic symbols naturally solves nothing, and their underlying motivation could be summarized roughly as: "We have to stick it to those mud-people." Stupid and primitive, yet understandable. But saying "People are bitching that we only ban Muslims, so let's ban something else too" requires a truly remarkable dose of stupidity or malice.

Today marks exactly one year since
the opening of the Sewers
; back then, I let my libertarian acquaintances know about it, and 152 of them (unique IP addresses) dropped by, only for a mere few dozen to keep returning over the following days. It took about a month or two before at least a hundred people visited the Sewers per day; currently, traffic hovers in the high hundreds of unique IP addresses daily, occasionally exceeding a thousand, and almost never falling below five hundred. While these numbers don't make the Sewers a wildly popular website, I am very glad that hundreds of people read what I write every day; and I am equally pleased that others have taken advantage of this opportunity alongside me, so that we now have twenty-one authors in the Sewers.
My thanks go to all of these authors; I will welcome every single piece you write. Thanks also to the commenters whose ideas inspire further writing, and last but not least to the readers, especially those who spread libertarian ideas further into the world. Share xD
The purpose of the Sewers is to spark discussions on libertarian topics under short, easily digestible texts, which may even be inaccurate or incomplete for the sake of brevity and easy readability; in a way, it is a "libertarian tabloid"—the aim is not theoretical and academic analyses of given topics, since those can emerge in the comments or in an article inspired by them. The Sewers are thus heading roughly in the direction I intended; there is only one thing I am unhappy with, however: although—as creator of most of the content—I am a very positive person in life, the articles here are too often excessively negative, dealing with politicians, socialism, curbs on freedom, and other gloomy topics; in light of this, I would like to ask all current and future authors not to hesitate to bring forward positive topics, such as freedom, the market, capitalism, and good news xD

A few days ago, I had the opportunity to debate a socialist who defended redistribution with a sentence that made me realize what lies at the root of most egalitarian ideas: "When you take such a small portion of wealth from a truly wealthy person that it has almost no impact on him, and give it to a poor person, it helps him far more than it hurt the rich man." Anyone familiar with the Austrian School of Economics sees at a glance that in light of the interpersonal incomparability of utility, this claim makes no sense; we could close the debate right there, but since by no means everyone has read (or will ever read) Mises, I present an argument understandable to anyone (though not completely generalized and universally valid in every time and place, for twenty-first-century Europe it will suffice).
If you claim that an extraordinarily wealthy person should be forced to give property to the poor
because it will help them more than it will hurt him, but at the same time you own designer clothes, a smartphone, perhaps a computer or a car, or maybe even a house,
you are hypocrites
! If you truly believed what you claim, you would have sold your belongings long ago and given the proceeds to starving poor people in Africa or Asia,
because compared to them you are extraordinarily wealthy people
—the personal property of most readers of this text could save many lives; or are you perhaps unwilling to sacrifice your comfort to save someone else's life!? Fine, neither am I. But I don't want to hear another word about redistribution for the sake of greater utility for the recipient. Ever! And no buts!
Because either it is true—in which case donate everything except one set of clothes to charity and haul yourselves to a homeless shelter—or it isn't true
, in which case whoever made that claim should shut up, keep their head down, and take great care not to preach similar socialist bullshit next time.

President of the Agrarian Chamber Miroslav Toman declared that he would like to see more protectionism—arguing that eighty percent of goods in Czech stores should consist of Czech products; Sobotka reacted as well, suggesting that more Czech goods on shelves could be enforced through stricter inspections. Good grief. What does supporting Czech products mean for the consumer? It means that instead of "the best" winning open competition based on market mechanics (according to the customer's criteria, whether quality, price, or any other indicator), "the Czech one" is favored; in the end, this means that worse alternatives to the customer's top choice are artificially and forcibly favored over better ones (if this weren't the case, there would be no need to mandate anything and Czech goods would appear in supermarkets purely through the market).
Anyone interested in a more detailed justification of why artificially forced preferences for Czech (or any other) products ultimately harm consumers, I recommend the first parts of my
series on anarcho-capitalism
; for those who would prefer a great analogy, I offer this one: Imagine that you, as a resident of Pilsen for example, decided to buy goods solely from Pilsen to "help your city" (or imagine if Pilsen stores were legally required to carry eighty percent Pilsen products); suddenly it becomes obvious that your shopping options will be severely limited and you will end up worse off. The exact same holds for buying "Czech goods," only it doesn't manifest as drastically; the restrictions are smaller, yet far from zero. What should one do? Personally, whenever I choose between products where one is foreign and the other Czech, with all other parameters being equal for me, I buy the foreign one, because I try to counterbalance the purchases of patriots.

At primary and secondary schools, another school year starts today; first-graders are often excited, which is largely due to not knowing what awaits them, whereas older children already know, which tempers their enthusiasm; I would like to take this opportunity to once again point out something obvious that is often completely ignored: What is compulsory school attendance? We have all grown so accustomed to it that most of us have developed Stockholm syndrome, tending to ignore the obvious fact that it is a violent ultimatum from the state demanding that we either let our children be indoctrinated and taught as state bureaucrats see fit, or they will be abducted (by force if necessary) and indoctrinated by the state anyway; does this claim seem too harsh and exaggerated? Well, on a factual level, it is a simple description of the status quo; on an emotional level, it may seem absurd... why? Precisely because you too went through that indoctrination.
The schooling system serves not only to brainwash even the youngest children and spread state propaganda (every one of us is taught from an early age that we need the state and that it is necessary, that the police are good, and that democracy is synonymous with goodness, without any discussion—just imagine the uproar if such massive advertising were forcibly imposed on children by a private entity), but also to instill conformity in our children and suppress their individuality (the school system was even originally designed with this goal in mind for the Prussian army; and we still use it, only pretending now that this isn't the goal, with many actually believing it). Although this topic is very close to my heart, there is unfortunately not enough room in the Sewers for a detailed analysis; I therefore take the liberty of recommending to the reader
another text I wrote about education
, or directing you to the
website of the 'Svoboda učení' [Freedom of Learning] initiative
. To students, I wish the best of luck; and don't let yourselves be molded too much.

The star of the Sewers, my favorite Michaela Marksová,
whose
ideas
I
occasionally
dissect here
, comes forward with an amendment to the Labor Code in which, among clouds of other bullshit, my attention was caught by the protection of mothers returning from maternity leave (naturally protection against employers—how else); for example (among other things), they are to be legally entitled (!) to the exact same job duties they performed before. Let us put aside for now the impracticality and harassment potential of this law, and assume that it will actually achieve the desired effect; what happens then? Well, logically, employers' incentive to hire women will drop even further, because their 'post-maternity protection' comes at a cost; the result will be another 'problem' for Marksová to solve—inequality between men and women in the labor market. She will then once again have the opportunity to be 'useful' and devise another regulation to 'fix' the situation; which will understandably also have negative repercussions, so hooray—yet another opportunity for a 'solution'!

The European Commission has come forward with another saving-grace proposal: messaging apps used for chatting (like Skype and similar) should newly be subject to the same rules (which in practice means regulations and restrictions) as telecom operators; this primarily means that their providers will be legally mandated to cooperate with the cops and surrender sensitive user data and chat histories upon request. Officially, of course, it's about the fight against terrorism, so every proper Islam-basher can applaud; unofficially, I wonder whether this is just another classic expansion of state power, or whether telecom operators lobbied for it to torment their competition a bit (the technical implementation of cooperating with the uniformed monkeys will cost something, especially for apps that don't store chat logs on their servers). In any case, the outcome will be the same—yet another step toward tyranny by the EU.

Some Muslim women have an issue with revealing too much skin in public, so they decided to swim in pajamas known as burkinis; and some idiots have an issue with them revealing too little skin in public, so they decided to ban them from swimming like that. Utter bullshit through and through; hence, a perfect political topic—in France they already have local ordinances for it, and uniformed monkeys are enthusiastically harassing insufficiently undressed women. Islam-bashers furiously applaud this because anything directed against Muslims supposedly serves the greater good—regardless of what an extraordinarily nonsensical piece of stupidity it is; politicians are having a field day because they can be "useful" once again—this time it isn't just Le Pen, but Valls and Sarkozy are also backing the burkini ban, because why not score points with the public when the victims being harassed are few, practically unable to defend themselves, and will find no sympathy in a democratic society.
I certainly don't claim there shouldn't be beaches where the owner bans burkinis, just as I have nothing against the existence of nudist beaches where the owner decides they don't want people in swimsuits; such bans are completely legitimate if decided by the lawful property owner—let everyone set the conditions on their own beach for who can and cannot visit, which, by the way, is the only sensible way to resolve the situation, or rather not to resolve it and avoid creating problems where none exist. Anything else constitutes an initiation of aggressive violence, and from a purely human standpoint is nothing more than venting frustration; various efforts to ban face coverings at least excuse themselves with some pseudo-security risk, whereas in the case of burkinis, there is literally nothing resembling any reason other than the good old urge to harass someone and poke one's nose into business that belongs to nobody else.

Politicians need to take a tough stance against terrorism, so the government has proposed an amendment under which endorsing a terrorist attack—even simply via a social media status—will now carry a prison sentence of three to twelve years; that is more, by the way, than what you can get for rape. That is certainly not to say that endorsing terrorism isn't idiotic, but on the other hand, I am staunchly against initiating violence against someone simply because they are an idiot; not to mention that locking people in cages is probably the dumbest form of punishment in itself. It is also remarkable how many people constantly swear by freedom of speech, yet when push comes to shove, don't hesitate to persecute people for their opinions in the name of hysteria; to say nothing of the fact that the actual benefit of such a measure in fighting terrorism is undoubtedly zero, and perhaps even slightly negative in the end.

The European Commission is coming (once again) to save the world—yet again, utterly predictably, via edicts, regulations, and harassing laws, this time concerning the minimum wage (though this time the promised paradise on earth is totally going to arrive with them); what is it about? Well, employees working abroad are now supposed to receive the minimum wage (and be subject to other collective bargaining agreements) of the country where they are currently performing their work, rather than the country where they are employed; in practice, this means drivers traveling through multiple countries will see their minimum wage and other working conditions change in mid-trip depending on what local trade unions have negotiated. Good luck with that. I can already see how this won't cause anyone any trouble or complications whatsoever, whether on the financial side—where companies from poorer countries will have to pay employees the minimum wage of richer nations—or the administrative nightmare of dealing with continuous shifts in labor conditions.
Fortunately, this entire stroke of genius is still only in the proposal stage, so there is a realistic chance it might not be implemented; either way, it is defended with textbook protectionism: protecting domestic workers so foreigners won't "steal their jobs." Claude Frédéric Bastiat showed more than two centuries ago that such an approach makes no sense, brings zero benefits, and is purely destructive: customers on the market will always choose the services that suit them best, so any state intervention that forces them to reconsider their choice means that instead of the optimal option, they are forced to settle for second best. Yet this blatant truth has been cleverly obscured by assorted socialists to the point where nobody pays attention to it anymore; it has been supplanted by inflammatory populist propaganda about protecting "our own" from "foreigners," completely ignoring that in the end, it is always the consumer who pays the price... "our own" consumer.

In Texas, someone had a bright idea... and lo and behold, people over the age of twenty-one are suddenly permitted to carry concealed firearms on university campuses; naturally, a chorus of professors and other leftist intellectuals grumbled against the law, predicting bloodbaths and student massacres. This change marks the second sensible adjustment to firearm regulations in Texas in recent times; you could
read about the first one in the Sewers back in June
. Now let us closely watch which direction crime trends take in this American state over the long run, how many people die in campus shootings in the coming years compared to the past, and what benefits these firearm deregulations bring to local residents; if it turns out (as I firmly believe it will) that the situation improves, let's hope this will lead—not only in Texas—to the further repeal of unnecessary laws, and not just gun laws.

Recently, the frequency of terrorist attacks in Europe has increased dramatically; most of them are quite undoubtedly Islamic radicals, and I find it ridiculous to argue that their motivation has nothing to do with the religion they practice. Most recent terrorists are Muslims, the proportion of terrorists among Muslims is higher than among followers of any other faith, and of course we have no reliable way of distinguishing someone who merely believes in Allah in private without bothering anyone from someone who intends to use their faith as a pretext for sadistic murder; what to do about it?
Before you answer that question, please consider the following: Since time immemorial, the incidence of rape has been high everywhere in the world, not just in Europe; the vast majority are quite undoubtedly committed by men, and I find it ridiculous to argue that the motivation for these acts has nothing to do with the perpetrators' sexuality. The percentage of male sex offenders is even higher than the percentage of Muslims among terrorists, the proportion of rapists among men is also higher than that of terrorists among Muslims, and we likewise have no reliable way to distinguish a man who only has sex with a woman's consent from one who doesn't care much about consent; what to do about it?
Just to be clear, the message of this article is certainly not: "Let's do nothing." Self-defense is of course entirely justified; the state should stop getting in citizens' way when they want to arm themselves (which, by the way, would help victims of both terrorism and rape), nor should laws stand in the way of private discrimination. On the other hand, global persecution of a certain group of people simply because they are statistically riskier is nothing other than an absolute outrage, and makes just as much sense in the case of Muslims as it does in the case of men.

Back in 2011, someone cleaned out Lukáš Kuzmiak's apartment, making off with his computer; however, he still had remote access to it and installed software allowing him to take screenshots and monitor the webcam. He took this to the uniformed monkeys, who told him to take a hike because that allegedly "isn't standard procedure" (quite an excuse, isn't it?); so he took matters into his own hands and eventually found the computer, though along the way he published photos of the people using it (albeit with black bars over their eyes). The result? The people photographed and published online are suing Lukáš Kuzmiak for emotional distress (the court of first instance ordered him to pay nearly two hundred thousand crowns, though both sides appealed), leaving him facing dragged-out court battles; and the moral of the story? Don't you dare do the cops' job better than they do: it isn't hard, but you'll have hell to pay.

The foreign police raided Prague 6, finding a company employing 44 workers, 38 of whom were foreigners, including 24 without permits; the owner faces six months in prison, the illegals are being deported, the uniformed monkeys boast about it, and nationalists applaud because "Bohemia for the Czechs." And what actually gives so many people reason to rejoice? Well, twenty-four people will have their lives made worse, their employer will likely do time and his company will shut down, harming its customers, including potential ones; and the supposed upside? The vacancy in the market might be filled by someone else—never mind that they are clearly less preferred by customers (otherwise it would have happened naturally through the market already), but above all, they'll be a thoroughbred Czech! Is destroying human lives and making customers worse off really something we should applaud?

The Association of Small and Medium Enterprises is begging the Ministry of Industry to ban handymen from performing more complex jobs, such as masonry, plumbing, painting, or carpentry; going forward, they would only be allowed to do minor chores like mowing lawns or cleaning carpets. Why? According to the chairman of the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises, handymen allegedly "steal jobs" from licensed tradesmen and often do shoddy work; and because customers are so monumentally stupid that they keep hiring them anyway, the state must now step in to legally protect them from the competition—and above all, from themselves—because heaven forbid a craftsman and a client agree on the terms under which work is done! And after all... what is wrong with someone "taking away a job" by offering a service that people voluntarily choose, thereby demonstrating that it is a better option for them?

Anyone who has ever gone canoeing or river boating can easily imagine how few boaters aren't constantly under at least some influence of alcohol; rum in the boat, beer at the riverside stands—it's practically tradition. This year, unfortunately, it dawned on the uniformed monkeys as well: they leafed through the law books and discovered that the same zero tolerance applies on boats as in cars; and in fact, it's even worse: on a canoe, not only the sternman and the bowman must not be drunk, but this even applies to anyone riding along in the middle like fragile porcelain. So the cops camped out along the Ohře river to harass boaters and collect fines; blood alcohol content on a boat can cost you up to a hundred thousand (!) crown fine. Yes, you read that right; I kid you not. With roadside harassment, at least one can make the excuse that a drunk driver poses a danger to others; but here? It's nothing more than shamelessly fleecing money from people who aren't harming anyone and whose drunkenness puts at most themselves at risk; no entity other than the state would ever get away with such disgusting behavior.

Anarcho-capitalism is often a target of mockery by statists, who claim it is mere theory that cannot be put into practice; if you start talking to them about private courts or something along the lines of police, they usually respond by pointing out that nowhere is law handled completely privately, because the state does it better and it "would never work" at all.
The typical responses from anarcho-capitalists then mostly consist of a theoretical (and usually entirely sound) explanation of why and how it could work; however, any such considerations are often dismissed simply by pointing out that nothing of the sort is currently implemented anywhere, resulting in a debate where the libertarian defends something while the statist scoffs, automatically assuming a far more advantageous position.
Given the way things actually stand, I consider this manner of debate completely absurd; why?
Well, in recent history we have seen what a centrally planned economy looks like—and it was appalling. We have also seen in various countries that whichever economic sector a state chose to relinquish to the market began functioning better than before; conversely, there has probably never been an instance where the state ceased managing something and that led to the realization of all those catastrophic statist predictions about market failure.
Imagine that you know two fundamentally different ways of solving problems: you first try to solve everything using the first method and the results are poor; then you start addressing individual issues using the second method and things improve every single time. Would you then strive to preserve the status quo at all costs, or would you pursue (further) improvement?
There are essentially two ways to manage affairs: either let free people act, or violently central-plan their lives through the power of the state. Central planning has consistently failed so far; and every time it was replaced by free-market principles, positive change followed.
So what actually works and what fails? Who should be questioning, and who should be defending? Upon whom should the burden of proof rest? What, then, is truly theory and what is practice?
The reality is that there is a vast array of fields where the state has failed across the board, whereas the private sector has succeeded; conversely, there is likely not a single sector that languished in private hands only to flourish thanks to the state.
On the basis of what empirical evidence, then, can anyone claim that we need the state for anything because on a free market "it wouldn't work"?
In a rational discussion unclouded by state propaganda, it should instead be the statist explaining to the anarchist why a given sector ought to be the rare exception that requires a central plan in order to function.

Croatian Finance Minister Boris Lalovac boasted about what a wonderful EET system they have over there: the state can see how much money entrepreneurs have, their sales figures, daily turnover, and even what they buy with their money. The tax office monitors all of it, searching for anomalies which it then eliminates; the Croatian Chief Snoop Minister even bragged that since they know absolutely everything about business owners (they reportedly even track the physical movements of cash registers, if they are moved), they can manage not only taxes, but even economic activity, and by extension the entire economy—all through information harvested by EET. Terrifying? How could it not be, considering we are getting this gem in the Czech Republic too; and what if ours doesn't transmit that much data to the tax office yet? Well, this is only version 1.0; in reality, in my view, the question is not whether the Czech EET will be upgraded to match the Croatian model, but rather when it will happen and under what pretexts.

Viktor Tolar, with thirty years of driving experience, lost his driver's license for over a year, after which he had to retake driving school just to get it back; why? Over the span of three years, he exceeded the speed limit three times in the Strahov Tunnel by less than twenty kilometers per hour, and four times drove under sixty in a fifty zone; add to this that "he felt it beneath him to haggle with the police" as well as the administrative consolidation of offenses for joint hearing—which effectively halts the expiration of penalty points—and there you have it: point suspension. I can vividly imagine all the comments about how foolishly he acted; and I grant that his approach was hardly the pinnacle of foresight, but on the other hand... is that really the point? Laws like this are always justified by talk of safety, but when they are used for bureaucratic harassment, it's often excused with the line that the victim didn't defend himself when he had the chance; but do we really want that to be necessary?
The most important question, in my view, is not what most people start debating in connection with this issue—namely whether revoking his license complied with the letter of the law in this specific case, whether an official or cop slipped up, or how unwisely the victim of state harassment acted—but rather whether it is right for someone to lose their driver's license for what he did; and this isn't just an anarchist stance: I am speaking of the spirit of the law and the supposed reasons it exists, which should carry weight even for statists. The question is: on the basis of someone with thirty years of driving experience exceeding the speed limit three times by less than 20 km/h and four times by less than 10 km/h over three years, can one conclude that this person is a danger to society as a driver and that a year without a license and driving school will fix the problem? If not, then it simply shouldn't happen—regardless of "the law is the law" and similar excuses.

The year was 1995, and twenty-four-year-old Jaroslava Jelínková went to the police with a fabricated rape accusation; the description of the culprit's car matched the vehicle of one Fehim Hanuš (dark-haired with an athletic build, although the perpetrator had been described as a stocky blond), originally from Yugoslavia, so the uniformed monkeys wasted no time and tasked the SWAT team with apprehending him. Never mind that a gynecologist soon determined (and notified the cops) that there were no signs of rape on the woman's body; the cops had probably already clocked out for the day, so word never reached the tactical unit, which launched its raid the following day. They brutally stormed Mr. Hanuš and his son at home, but both men (quite understandably) defended themselves, sparking a shootout in which the innocent Fehim Hanuš was literally riddled with bullets—eight shots to the abdomen, two to the head; miraculously, he survived! Unfortunately with lifelong disabilities, and before they put him back together in the hospital, his business went under.
What did the monkey Jiří Houba, who ordered the raid, have to say for himself? Naturally: "Were we supposed to wait until the perpetrator raped someone else?" And then? Twenty-one years of legal battles for an apology and compensation. Seriously: the uniformed monkeys refused, the Supreme Court remanded the case back to lower courts four times in a row, eventually even ordering that a different judge take it over; after twenty-one years, the court finally ruled that the Ministry of Justice must apologize and pay three hundred thousand crowns. And that, dear friends, is the price of breaking into someone's home, assaulting them, shooting them full of lead, crippling them, nearly killing them, and destroying their life... provided, of course, that you are wearing the right uniform, in which case the media barely bat an eye either; but can you imagine the outrage if this were a private operation? State propaganda is immensely powerful; lives destroyed by repressive state organs simply count differently than lives destroyed by private individuals.

With this title, I certainly do not intend to trivialize the tragedy that occurred in Nice on Thursday night, claiming the lives of dozens of people; I merely adhere to the life philosophy that there is nothing that should be exempt from humor, so I took inspiration from
several witty comments
