. What happened is likely well known to everyone: two sadistic thugs got into a truck and drove two kilometers through a crowd of people before being shot dead by uniformed monkeys. Unsurprisingly, the most popular talking point became the religious faith of the two mass murderers, as though consequences for other followers of their religion should follow from what they did (assuming it is Islam, which I consider likely); I shudder to think what will happen once someone realizes that the percentage of men among suicide bombers is even higher than that of Muslims... I suppose we'll deport men from Europe, safety first. What I want to pause over, however, is the method of execution.
A truck was used for the massacre, which demonstrates quite clearly that when people seriously decide to eliminate others, firearms are not necessary—there are countless other methods, and this one appears to be rather effective. A ban on trucks is not yet being seriously debated anywhere, which is nice; but what about bans and regulations on firearms? You object that firearms are unrelated? Well, it depends on how you look at it: the attackers managed to drive a full two kilometers through an unarmed crowd before being shot... how far would they have gotten and how many people would they have murdered if all their victims (including potential ones) had been packing heat? How many lives could have been saved? And why is it that every time someone uses a firearm in a massacre, this fact is endlessly hyped by the media, whereas when firearms could have saved lives, there is nothing but radio silence?

Do you remember what French President François Hollande looks like, particularly his hairstyle? Wondering why I'm talking about his hair when he doesn't sport a mohawk, just a boring politician haircut? Well, his personal barber receives over a quarter of a million a month for his work; I'm probably the last person to begrudge anyone earning money, but he gets that money from state coffers (and his salary, by the way, equals about two-thirds of the president's salary; few people would pay that much for a barber... but nobody bleeds when spending other people's money). The revelation of the barber's salary sparked outrage among the French and the conviction that Hollande is an idiot for squandering money; but how do they know it's wasteful? Well, from their perspective, the expenditure isn't worth what it brings them (and no wonder); the question remains, however, why the overwhelming majority of people then defend subsidizing everything under the sun, when the very fact that something requires subsidies indicates that
people don't find it worth paying for out of their own pockets
.

Minister for Regional Development (what a bogus post) Karla Šlechtová posted a heartbreaking tale on her Facebook profile about how she went to a Baroque concert commemorating Charles IV at a church, from which she was allegedly kicked out by the priest because she champions the taxation of church restitutions; she demands an explanation from the church as to why it discriminates against a minister of the Czech government, appealing to democracy in the process. Setting aside for now whether this is even true—since discrepancies in the date and location have surfaced, and whenever someone points them out, their comment mysteriously vanishes—let us assume for a moment that it really happened exactly as the minister describes. Even if that were so, is it truly something so dreadful and reprehensible on the church's part? What actually happened?
The state confiscated church property, which after long years was finally acknowledged as a wrong, leading to the decision to return the stolen estates; yet from this very transaction, the state now wants to violently extract a cut (taxation of restitutions), creatively justifying it by claiming it collects protection money from other transactions too—that is the first degree of this insolence. The second degree comes when the spokesperson for and champion of this robbery acts shocked that the robbery victim refuses to host a free musical performance for her on his own property; followed by whining about how the church discriminates and refuses to admit a minister of the Czech government to a concert in a democratic country, as if that were some kind of duty. The worst part of the whole affair is that the absurdity completely escapes her, because in her eyes, robbery isn't robbery if it is legislatively sanctioned, and whoever organizes a concert must not bar entry to anyone, because discrimination (is bad, yeesss) and also "one simply doesn't do that."

Ever since the outcome of the Brexit referendum became known, political bargaining dances have begun regarding who needs mutual trade more: the British or the rest of Europe; various declarations and speculations are flying around about what the EU will "allow" British citizens in terms of trade, tying into all kinds of pro-EU arguments about how wonderfully freely we can move goods and people thanks to the Union. Bullshit, I tell you! The reality is that one gang of thugs in national governments threw up completely nonsensical obstacles to free people trading, while another—transnational—gang tweaked them to make them somewhat more tolerable; all while we are forced to finance these bandit clans out of our own resources under threat of violence in the form of protection money called taxes.
So the next time you hear some thug in a tie whose salary you slave away for so he can play parasite babbling about how European officials "enable" us to trade and how we need bureaucrats and politicians to remove barriers to free trade, remember that naturally no such barriers exist in the first place—because when two people want to exchange goods, they would naturally just do so; the reason it ever becomes an issue is certainly not the people, but the politicians, who feel entitled to a cut of trade they contributed nothing to and only complicate, meaning the obvious solution is for them to simply stop fucking with it, not to set up yet another apparatus of the exact same leeches to soften the blow of what the first ones broke at the price of mountains of bureaucracy and additional regulations. The claim that these bureaucrats "enable" us to have free trade is, in my view, absolute chutzpah.

Some EU bigwigs have recently been spouting metaphysical bullshit on the subject of robotics and artificial beings, which they call "electronic persons"; robots are allegedly already at quite a high level of autonomy, so a legal framework needs to be devised and implemented for them. What else to expect from the EU? Regulating potentially future artificial autonomous beings before they are even built; of course that makes sense, we have to think ahead, right? But then it turned out that mindless regulation at all costs wasn't the only reason; it turned out that the primary goal is social insurance for robots. Seriously, this is no joke; it was discovered that social insurance contributes to people being replaced by machines, so the "logical" step according to the EU is taxing those machines. By debating this proposal, the European Parliament is demonstrating what has long been clear to every libertarian: Social insurance is simply a tax; it has very little to do with anything social or insurance-related.

After the avalanche of foolish ideas from Marksová paused for a moment, she probably decided to take inspiration from Brno; she now wants to legally compel municipalities to provide social housing to their poor and homeless because... well, simply because socialism. Rob everyone, squander the loot, waste it, embezzle it, hand out the rest to someone, report activity, buy votes, and maybe even feel good about yourself; that's probably how Marksová works, since she likely doesn't realize at all that in the end, handing out something "for free" harms not only part of those receiving it, but above all everyone else who faces the risk of ending up in such a situation. How so? Well, it reduces the benefits of responsible behavior and mitigates the natural bad consequences of irresponsible actions; and unfortunately, that is an inevitable consequence of all socialist measures—willy-nilly, they produce irresponsible people.

It is truly fascinating how many people automatically feel that those who rule are somehow professionally or expertly qualified to make decisions; the state deliberately cultivates this aura for them to convince citizens that decision-makers know better than they do what is best for them. Even setting aside that even with the seemingly qualified, the whole thing is nothing but a myth, a political game, and an illusion, sometimes someone gets appointed to a post so masterfully that it makes your head spin; for instance, the mayor of Brno currently has Matěj Hollan as his deputy for transport—a musician without a driver's license (who has never even had one). But what does it matter that transport in the second largest city of the Czech Republic will be decided by someone who has never even driven in it? What matters is political affiliation—the Žít Brno movement with the support of the Pirates; well, quite a socialist return to roots... before 1989, a personnel profile was also more important than expertise.

Summer holidays are starting, which affect quite a few of us in some way, whether schoolkids, their parents, college students, teachers, visitors of various festivals, and the like; traffic to websites with articles (even such Sewers non-articles) and comments is dropping, but my schedule will also be slightly affected by the holidays. For that reason, I am switching the Sewers to vacation mode for two months, which means:
1/ Texts might not be published here with the same regularity as before; I will try, but I don't know how well it will go.
2/ I ask libertarians who have more time to submit articles for the Sewers; please send them to me by email (or publish them yourselves; ideally with a future publication date so I can schedule them).
3/ Everyone who discusses things with me via email, please understand if replies are slower; I enjoy discussions, but I won't be at my computer as much.
4/ My participation in the Sewers discussions will be limited; when you post something here, don't count on me always reading it (though most likely I will).

The company Elektra PV ran the most popular e-shop of 2015; but that is over now. Why? Well, one of its 250 suppliers (or perhaps one of their suppliers) didn't pay VAT, which the tax office handled in its own way—before investigating the situation, it froze the assets and bank accounts of this company with a 25-year track record and a billion-crown turnover, without notifying anyone (the owner had to track down the reason himself and was only told the next day); Elektra PV was thus completely paralyzed out of nowhere, and with no way to pay suppliers or fulfill orders, it has no choice but to shut down operations, because such a large company cannot be kept alive under these conditions. One hundred and twenty people will lose their jobs, countless customers will have to wait for their orders, and suppliers will wait for their payments as well; great job, Financial Administration! Because without the state, who would liquidate e-shops?

Last week in the Sewers, you could read that while I supported Brexit, I didn't believe in it very strongly; and now I can only conclude that it was a pleasant mistake. And what can we observe around us now that just under 52% of voting Britons chose Brexit? Among the less interesting things is, for example, David Cameron's speech, which was surprisingly classy for a robber in a suit who lives on extorted money (which wouldn't be so strange; after all, he has people to write it for him), but mainly in that, as a Brexit opponent, he announced his resignation from office so that Britain could be led out of the EU by someone who agrees with it (what surprises me is the ability to accept defeat; but I tend not to trust politicians' words too much, so we'll see what happens); completely unsurprising, on the other hand, are the outbursts of Brexit opponents across the Internet, as well as their criticism from those who would have reacted the exact same way had the referendum gone the other way.
What I find more interesting, however, is the petition for calling a second referendum and other tricks or hints of a similar nature that we can witness; I wouldn't normally take such things seriously, but they worry me in the context of the rerun referendum on the Maastricht Treaty in Denmark in 1992, the adoption of the euro despite referendum results there in 2000, two rerun referendums on the Nice and Lisbon treaties in Ireland in 2001 and 2008, the planned adoption of the euro in Sweden after it was rejected by a referendum in 2003, two circumvented referendums on the European Constitution in the Netherlands and France in 2005, or that one on the bailout package in Greece in 2015. And even though in Britain it currently seems the referendum will be respected and talk about it being non-binding or petitions to repeat it are not taken seriously, I tend to believe that overall, though certainly not unconditionally. Do you think my skepticism is warranted?

The US Senate showed a flicker of common sense: it shot down a shitstorm of four consecutive bills restricting gun sales. That Democrats would try to exploit the Orlando massacre for their prohibitionist cravings probably surprises no one; this time, however, Republicans also stepped into the spotlight and proved they are the exact same bunch of prohibitionists—the highlight was John Cornyn's proposal demanding that gun sales to people suspected of terrorism be delayed by 72 hours... mind you, not convicted, suspected! The purpose of those 72 hours was supposedly to allow authorities to make an effort and beg a judge for a total ban on the purchase; the rationale of such a measure completely escapes me even within the bounds of statist logic and morality—if the court did not ban the suspect from gun ownership up to the moment he went to buy one, how can it reconsider this decision solely based on the fact that he is doing so? In other words: "You are allowed to buy a gun as long as you don't actually want to buy one." Fortunately, that was too much even for the senators (well, for about half of them).

Today, the UK holds a referendum on leaving the EU; the vast majority of the establishment (naturally and unsurprisingly led by socialist Cameron of the Conservatives) is of course losing its mind over this, frightening Britons that it will be a fatal and irreversible decision that will basically be a disaster for their lives, but fortunately (even within Cameron's party) opposite views exist as well. Initially, the official line was scoring points, then the tide turned and Brexit became the more popular option, but in the end the murder of Jo Cox was skillfully exploited for yet another shift in polling—merely hinting at a connection to Brexit supporters was enough, which I consider exceptionally retarded, since on the one hand it wouldn't have helped them, but above all, even if it did, how is the murder of a politician related to whether EU membership is beneficial for the British? Well, we'll see what the vote count ultimately brings; what do you think? Personally, I naturally support Brexit, but I don't believe in it very strongly.

Donald John Trump hardly needs an introduction, yet I find it bizarre how many libertarians harbor a certain sympathy for this totalitarian enthusiast—maybe Molyneux's rants are to blame, maybe just some repressed, base urges to hurt people; whatever the reason, I would like to reiterate here who DJ Trump really is: no "fighter against the system," but a statist yearning for a police state. After the Orlando massacre, he stated that Americans who don't snitch on their neighbors should go to prison; specifically regarding Omar Mateen's neighbors, he declared that because they noticed his weird behavior, receiving many packages within a short time, an increased amount of time spent in the garage, and didn't report any of it, they should face consequences, serious consequences, and do some time in jail. Frankly, I cannot fathom how a candidate with such a stance could be acceptable to any libertarian.
And not just to libertarians! The whole premise defies common sense as well; sure, it sounds dramatic when delivered in a DJ Trump speech, but it lacks even a shred of logic. How could something like that work in practice? Yes, Omar Mateen behaved strangely before the attack, spent time in the garage, and received lots of packages; but how many other people exhibit the exact same signs without ever committing anything? How is this snitching supposed to work? I have a weird neighbor, I report him to state authorities, and they do what? Open a file? Or go interrogate him to see how crazy he is? How many millions of people across America would need to be vetted if all citizens actually behaved as DJ Trump demands? And what would that mean in practice? Extreme restrictions on the freedom of virtually everyone, enormous financial expenditure, and practically zero tangible results; or does anyone genuinely believe that terrorists can be eliminated this way?

An unidentified thief stole an expensive bicycle, captured on security camera. The owner fully understood that uniformed monkeys are useless in such cases (and anyone who has ever reported a theft to them surely understands why), so he decided to distribute the footage among people on his own in hopes of identifying the scoundrel; but the state stepped in after all, doing a bit of "protecting and serving"—the Office for Personal Data Protection intervened in defense of the little thug, and the Supreme Court sided with it. The ruling states: "The purpose of operating camera systems in property protection is not (in short) making recordings for their future publication, but solely for potential handover to designated authorities for further action. Investigating and prosecuting criminal activity (which can also include misdemeanors) falls entirely within the jurisdiction of state authorities." Does anything else even need to be said? I don't think so.

"Gun licenses should only be issued in extraordinary situations. I don't think there is any reason why people should carry guns on them." Jiří Dienstbier, Minister of Nothing and Chief Purveyor of Nonsense, shone with this totalitarian statement some time ago; and after the Orlando massacre, the socialist in question naturally didn't miss the opportunity to push his own agenda, even though it is blatantly obvious that a lunatic setting out to shoot up a gay bar will certainly not be stopped by a gun ban (if only because a far more fundamental ban on killing people didn't stop him), whereas a few tough homosexuals packing heat would have eliminated him quite reliably, so he would only have had time to shoot a few, or—better yet—the mere fact that his victims would fight back and not give in easily would have deterred the piece of shit who only dared attack the unarmed.
Dienstbier commented on the massacre with the words: "I take every such attack as proof that weapons belong only in the hands of the state's security forces. They don't belong in the hands of any hypothetical militias, nor do they belong in the hands of a fearful public," while completely ignoring that precisely due to the lack of guns in the victims' hands, a single sadistic lunatic—who will always obtain a gun somehow—is enough to inflict such carnage, because the glorious state security forces simply cannot prevent it; even if they arrived everywhere within five minutes, that is plenty of time for a massive bloodbath if the victims cannot effectively defend themselves. Not to mention that state disarmament of the populace is a hallmark of every totalitarian regime; besides, Dienstbier's rhetoric is nothing new: "Germans who wish to use firearms should join the SA or the SS; ordinary citizens do not need guns, for in their hands they serve no purpose to the state." – Heinrich Himmler

Just under six weeks ago, I reported here about my broken arm, and shortly thereafter about its miraculous straightening; because the healing was progressing splendidly thanks to my flawless mental attitude, it seemed the cast would come off after just a month. However, a bit of a wrench was thrown in the works when I moved the arm rather roughly (even in the cast) and basically broke it again... but just like the first time, it was totally worth it and I have no regrets xD
After nearly six weeks, the cast finally came off; for a moment I was disappointed that the hand felt oddly stiff. But once I walked from the plaster room into the doctor's office, the doctor couldn't believe his eyes when I gave him the Vulcan salute, "live long and prosper" (my worst fractures are in the metacarpal bones leading to the middle and ring fingers)—he said he wouldn't have expected the mobility I have now until at least a month of rehab; true, I can't fully make a fist yet, but it's improving hour by hour.
The only defect is that when I curl my fingers into my palm, my ring finger deviates outwards and crosses over my pinky, which is a bit of an issue for ten-finger touch-typing; effectively I have only nine fingers now (hitting the keyboard with the ring finger coincides with the pinky; both fingers hit the same key), but luckily I possess master skills, so I can still hit 513 flawless keystrokes per minute even now; more than enough for the Sewers and work xD
Working with a mouse is slightly tricky for me right now—which will soon improve—as is gripping things (because when I hold something, my ring finger rests on top of my pinky)—which will probably stay that way; well, considering how amazing my life is and all the blessings God has bestowed upon me, I'd say a slightly crippled hand is still a pretty negligible downside to my overall existence compared to all those blessings. So I can only conclude that I'm still a pretty damn happy bastard; now I just need to get full mobility back, but if I can do on day one what should take a month of rehab, I figure it should be eaf. Thanks to everyone for their help in the Sewers and especially elsewhere. 110

Since you usually read about bad things in the Sewers, this time it will be my pleasure to report on something positive as well: In Texas, a century-old restriction barring residents from openly carrying firearms is likely to fall. That could now change, so anyone who isn't endangering or threatening anyone with a firearm will be permitted to carry it openly, even in hand; furthermore, the ban on carrying weapons on university campuses might be lifted. These changes could deter some criminals from committing violence, or at least make it harder for them, but above all, this is a step toward freedom; the state has no business telling people where they may carry a gun (or any other possession of theirs), nor how and with what they may defend themselves against criminals who don't respect such laws anyway and arm themselves regardless of bans. I wish our lawmakers would take inspiration from Texas in this regard.

Ninety-year-old Arnold Abbott in Florida spends his time in an interesting way: feeding the homeless alternates cyclically with stints in jail. Why? Because under local ordinances, people without a roof over their heads may only be fed by city-approved non-profits (which looks like quite a tidy racket), and only if they haul a mobile restroom along with them; Mr. Abbott does not meet these criteria, ergo he has to pay fines and go to jail for handing out food. During the latest operation by the heroic uniformed monkeys, the phrase "Drop the plate right now!" was even barked out, followed by law enforcement intervening to dump all the undistributed food into the trash right before the eyes of the hungry; in light of this, one cannot help but recall state propaganda using the poor and helpless as an excuse and justification for the state's existence—even though it is precisely for such people that the state is (typically for other reasons) the most destructive.

Two Afghans living in Sweden got a brilliant idea—they took an airsoft pistol and went out to rob people, figuring that in the dusk nobody would tell the difference anyway; until they ran into a victim who either wasn't fooled or assessed the situation as desperate, pulled out a knife, and wrecked them (one of them permanently). A commendable deed? Well, no good deed goes unpunished; and so the local court sentenced the robbery victim to two years in prison for excessive self-defense, offering the brilliant commentary that the victim shouldn't have defended himself, but should have tried to run away—and I'd really love to know how that smart-aleck judge would run away from bullets in a similar situation. Above all, I cannot grasp the perverted logic whereby a victim who eliminated an attacker so thoroughly that he will never be able to repeat his attack on anyone receives punishment instead of an award, especially one as senseless and barbaric as prison.

Czech Television has clamped down on so-called "non-payers," dragging them through the courts to squeeze out even more cash; and just who are these culprits? Well, they include anyone who has the sheer audacity to consume electricity without having submitted an affidavit declaring that they don't own a television set; even setting aside the sky-high insolence of automatically extorting fees from practically anyone who doesn't actively opt out, owning a television receiver is by law grounds for payment anyway, completely irrespective of whether the owner actually watches ČT. Forcing subjects to pay for services (especially state propaganda, whether in schooling or media) that they neither consume nor use is something of a state specialty; usually, however, it comes with some cover story about the apocalypse that would ensue without the state, whereas with ČT, nobody even bothered making an excuse anymore: Got a TV? Pay up!

French socialist comrades have come up with another brilliant idea of what to ban next: this time, it's broadcasting and watching European Football Championship matches on big screens in bars. Why? Obvious, of course: due to the threat of terrorist attacks. TVs in bars will be replaced by state fan zones guarded by cops; the result will be that, in addition to the lost profits of bar owners, the whole party will cost taxpayers over 200 million crowns. I don't care to dwell on what security outcomes this solution will produce (though I strongly doubt its effectiveness); the crucial point is that even if it genuinely made things safer, that is no argument for such repression. If we bought into this rhetoric, we could proceed identically in the case of all other dangerous entertainment.

As most readers probably know well, gun legislation in the Czech Republic is less terrible and repulsive than in most European countries; some even euphemistically describe this situation by saying that we have good gun laws. Personally, I disagree with such an assessment, because as long as firearms are not sold anonymously and free of registrations, permits, and restrictions, it constitutes repression and the initiation of violence by the state; pseudo-arguments built on doomsday scenarios that people would slaughter each other en masse don't hold water, primarily because if people truly craved killing one another so much, they could manage it even without legally regulated firearms. Nobody, except a few deranged individuals, wants to risk their own life just to murder people around them; but when such a person does come along and procures a weapon (which they can do even now, just with more difficulty), they inflict far more devastation in an unarmed society than in an armed one.
To my considerable surprise, Czech politicians don't even appear to harbor exceptionally prohibitionist urges regarding gun legislation (at least compared to politicians of other European nations); I have no doubt that if votes could be milked from it, their views would readily shift, but so far that isn't happening. Yet where harassment does not emerge at the national level, the EU will shove it in; and that is precisely how it seems to be going with firearms: The new directive restricts magazine-fed guns, and somewhat less strictly revolvers with non-detachable magazines; and while Czech politicians look quite disapprovingly on this concoction, it may very well do them no good, as other member states will easily outvote them... in other words, exactly what propagandists kept insisting before our EU accession would never happen is coming to pass: by diktat from above, we are losing fundamental freedoms.

So customs officers were searching for refugees on a train one day (Islam-bashers' wet dreams coming true), and lo and behold, what did they stumble upon? A traveling salesman carrying nine kilograms of ecstasy, plus a kilo of cocaine as a bonus; although the man hadn't attacked anyone and hadn't violated anyone's property rights, uniformed and legalized robbers not only stripped him of merchandise worth roughly seven to eight million crowns, but unlike ordinary thieves, they also plan to cage the poor fellow in a pen called prison for eight to twelve years and curtail his freedom there. And for what? The man was simply transporting goods that people are willingly interested in paying for, but the ruling class dislikes it; morally, such an act is no different in principle from mugging someone in the street, stealing their millions, and locking them in a cellar for a chunk of their life just for fun... yet most people applaud it simply because it was sanctioned by bigwigs whom they typically don't even respect.

The European Commission, together with Internet giants like Google, Facebook, and Twitter, published an online code of conduct aimed at preventing hate speech; if this was a voluntary action on the part of those companies, it is naturally entirely their business how they manage their property and whom they provide space to express opinions. However, if it was the result of coercion under threat of sanctions by the European Union, it is a gross suppression of freedom of speech. Since many do not see much of a difference (after all, both cases involve censorship), let me clarify: If a private owner of a medium censors its content, they are merely deciding about something that belongs to them (just as anyone decides who gets to speak in their living room), and consumers can reject it; if the state performs this censorship, it is a violent infringement upon someone else's property and typically a blanket oppression, since laws generally apply universally to everyone (including all media, neutralizing competition).
A crucial question therefore arises: How did negotiations between the European Commission and the aforementioned corporations actually play out? I can well imagine coercion, as we have seen in the past that the EU can throw legislative hurdles in the way of even the biggest giants; on the other hand, it wouldn't surprise me if corporate management was staffed by indoctrinated individuals who simply bought into European propaganda—after all, there is no shortage of such people in the world. Nor would I be shocked by a scenario where the European Commission offered those major players perks, though I consider that less likely; in such cases, the state typically offers suppression of competitors, which isn't very effective on the web and doesn't score political points, since people are quite sensitive to restrictions on internet freedom. Which option do you consider most likely, dear readers? Leave your thoughts in the comments.

The Ostrava tax office decided to bully the Raptor company a bit; it withheld its VAT refunds while investigating alleged carousel fraud, which was never proven. The catch, however, is that such conduct is not only utterly immoral, but even illegal; so Raptor took it to court, which ruled in its favor and ordered the tax office to return the loot with interest. This extortionist department refused to pay, which amusingly landed it in distraint proceedings (well, amusing if we ignore that we're paying for all of it from our taxes). However, I don't consider the worst part to be that the state essentially slapped a distraint order on itself, but rather the bureaucrats' spiteful desire to inflict harm, which reached such proportions that the tax office openly flouted the law and court decisions; and unfortunately, this is by no means the first recent case where state authorities blatantly disregard the very laws with which they crush their subjects.

Although we often hear many state employees grumbling against home births, these are still surprisingly legal under Czech law; there is, however, a small catch: you may give birth at home, but without a midwife. Dark humor? No, reality. Home births are allegedly too dangerous, so let's improve that by denying laboring mothers professional care; you ask why? I asked too, but the only answer that comes to mind is the state's need to make home births even more dangerous, thereby highlighting the necessity of our socialist healthcare system and cultivating fertile ground for yet another ban. When do you think it will come? And while we're at it, we might as well outlaw home conception too; what next, people fucking however they please?!

I'm not much of a hip-hop fan, but I can't help mentioning a few verses that the group Chaozz came up with years ago: "And who wages wars? Politicians, of course! They are the only ones who deserve a shotgun; or an anti-tank gun, because they're the only ones who want wars—normal folks would rather sleep in peace." There is great truth hidden in those verses, confirmed for instance by the events on the Western Front at Christmas 1914; millions of young men who had never laid eyes on one another were fighting in trenches, yet under the influence of state propaganda were senselessly slaughtering each other... at Christmas 1914, however, their humanity triumphed over indoctrination: That across many parts of the front, hundreds of thousands of soldiers maintained a holiday truce probably surprises nobody; but thousands upon tens of thousands of them even celebrated Christmas together—men climbed out of trenches, exchanged gifts with the "enemy," sang carols, tended to wounded together, celebrated Christmas.
Because this was quite a powerful experience for most involved, they wrote about it in letters from the front, which sparked public interest even back then; some newspapers even covered it. When word reached senior military officers, they unsurprisingly behaved like pigs—the "guilty" units were redeployed elsewhere (for instance, from the Western to the Eastern Front), and military units began to be reshuffled generally to prevent soldiers from establishing ties with the "enemy," because the state simply needs to bring out the worst in people and eradicate all that is good. Despite these efforts, those bastards failed to completely bury humanity, as similar incidents occurred in later years of the war; the truth is, however, that sadly nothing on such a scale was ever repeated again.

Although libertarians do not usually call for expanding state powers, when it comes to closing borders to refugees, I see quite a few exceptions around me, justified roughly as follows: "If we had more freedom (the legal ability to defend our property effectively, to discriminate privately based on religion, and so on), we could afford to let refugees enter Czech territory; but since we lack these freedoms and redistribution is running rampant, the state should close and guard the borders, or even ban Islam." What is pernicious about this reasoning? Instead of calling for curbing state power, we want to expand it so the government fixes the damage its own regulations created; this is a notorious statist trap of which examples abound—such as creating unemployment by driving up the cost of labor (various employee protections, minimum wage, etc.) followed by a "fight against unemployment" through further market distortion.
Libertarians in particular should spot the next logical fallacy in this reasoning better than anyone: while it is possible (and I assume so myself) that in a free society people would handle the current immigration crisis through natural free-market discrimination (whether in employment, service provision, or gated communities, the potential form of which can be found in the works of Hans-Hermann Hoppe), we cannot know for sure, because the market might arrive at a different solution. So when we ask the state to keep refugees outside borders, we are actually predicting the behavior of free people in the sense of: "They would deal with immigrants one way or another, so let's simulate that through state intervention." In essence, that is like saying that since charity and solidarity would probably exist in a free market, state redistribution is perfectly fine because it merely simulates these free-market mechanisms.

Both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate have passed an amendment to the Food Act; what can we look forward to? More harassment, what else; this time, cigarette manufacturers found themselves in the crosshairs, and by extension indirectly their customers—all smokers. Once again, those embarrassing warnings about the dangers of smoking on every pack will be enlarged; they will now have to cover up to 65% of the package surface and, additionally, feature disgusting pictures of dead children or sick people, as seen in certain other countries. Sadly, that's not all; manufacturing and selling flavored cigarettes will also be prohibited. Initially, an exception will apply for menthol cigarettes for a limited period; but even those will vanish from shelves in time. Since the bill passed smoothly through both houses of parliament, I don't think any improvement in the situation can be expected in the foreseeable future.
In theory, the purpose of this measure is supposed to be protecting public health, which has lately served as an excuse for utterly barbaric encroachments on our freedoms. Many argue that the state should and must care for its citizens' health because we have socialist health insurance, which makes one person's health the business of another. However, such an argument should not be used to justify even more state meddling, because its consistent application leads to sheer absurdities—such as the state dictating everyone's diet for their health's sake; the only sensible solution, of course, is to abolish forcibly shared healthcare costs once and for all and smoothly transition to a healthcare model where everyone decides on their own care for themselves.

Today, we look at an extremely fascinating court ruling in Italy: the court ruled that stealing food is not a crime when you are hungry. The judge acquitted a 36-year-old Ukrainian homeless man who stole from a local supermarket, stating that no one should starve in a civilized country. Not that all existing states aren't founded upon and directly funded by large-scale plunder, but until now they at least pretended that was something different and symbolically proclaimed that stealing is wrong; in Italy, however, they stopped giving a damn even about that and, in certain cases, permitted theft even for subjects. If you are poor enough, you may steal, supposedly so you don't go hungry. Considering the price of food in our "Western world," however, avoiding hunger is not all that difficult, as begging for food is essentially no problem.
Yet even if dealing with genuinely starving individuals, endorsing their theft sets a dangerous precedent; every homeless person can then ditch begging and simply go steal, with police and courts applauding them for it. Furthermore, it beautifully exposes how the state disregards the rights of store owners, who must suffer losses without any legal recourse. The fact that someone is hungry does not grant them the right to take someone else's property without the owner's consent; solidarity and helping the needy should be voluntary, not enforced by sanctioning theft.

The Ministry of Transport is planning another piece of bureaucratic bullshit: novice drivers will have a probationary driver's license for two years, during which they can lose their license with just eight penalty points, which amounts to one serious offense and one seatbelt or cell phone infraction; then they will have to attend driving school again, which many driving schools will certainly welcome with gratitude. Setting aside that the very existence of driver's licenses makes little sense, such ideas are pure grist for the mill of democratic "justice," which consists of the majority terrorizing the minority; and since there aren't many novice drivers awaiting driving school in the population, and they often don't even have voting rights, they make an ideal target for democratic bullying, in which Ťok thoroughly revels, as we've seen many times before. What else is there to say? Remember that what is legal is far from being right.

In February, the Ministry of Transport hatched an amendment to the law allowing uniformed monkeys to confiscate drivers' vehicle registration certificates right on the spot, turning them into prosecutor and judge rolled into one. While you could already read about this in the Sewers, you couldn't experience it firsthand, because Ťok's cops were internally ordered not to use this power until a decree specifying exactly when registrations could be seized was issued; and lo and behold, the decree is here! Under what conditions can harassment ensue? There are tons, but to name a few: missing exhaust components, rusty bodywork, leaking operating fluids, excessively worn brake rotors, excessive corrosion, and the like; do you notice how incredibly subjective most of these defects are? When, for instance, are brake rotors "too" worn?
The practical fallout from this amendment could be immense; given the aforementioned subjectivity and putting uniformed monkeys in the role of judges against whom there is no on-the-spot appeal (if they decide to seize your registration even when everything is clearly and indisputably fine, you're out of luck anyway—you have to leave the car behind and seek redress retroactively), it will be remarkably easy to shake down drivers to do whatever the officer pleases. This will apply especially to cases where the ape intends to issue a fine on the spot while the driver prefers to defend himself in administrative proceedings. I can hear it already: "Yes, of course it's your right, you don't have to make a statement, but I see a bit of rust here... are you in a big rush? Wouldn't want to have to leave your car here with us; but hey, we're all human, I'm sure we can reach an agreement, it's not worth the hassle over a few hundred crowns, is it?"

It has been a few years since the European Union, in its boundless wisdom, banned us from selling powerful vacuum cleaners, which undoubtedly saved the world, but victory is not yet won and more must be done; so the European Commission will heroically ban even more items—kettles, toasters, and hair dryers that fail to conform to the notions of all-knowing bureaucrats. At first glance, it might seem that such a solution will bring savings in electricity consumption, meaning everyone saves; that may be true, but nobody really considers the costs on the manufacturers' side, who will have to halt production of time-tested models and begin developing new ones. But who can decide whether it is worth it? In truth, there is only one way: let free individuals trade in a free market; in voluntary transactions, people always prefer whatever is advantageous to them. Any meddling by bureaucrats can only make things worse.
The funny thing about the whole matter is that the European bigwigs themselves evidently understand just how popular their bans are likely to be; the entire proposal has long been drafted, and its implementation is merely waiting for the referendum on the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union to take place. Long live propaganda and political marketing!

You could read about Erdogan's hypersensitivity regarding himself in the Sewers earlier; back then, however, he was still limiting himself to suppressing free speech in Turkey, which has now changed. How? Well, he went whining to Germany, where surprisingly they obliged him. What happened? When German satirist Jan Böhmermann composed and recited a very crude poem about Erdogan, pulling absolutely no punches, the establishment's reaction was swift: a Hamburg court quickly slapped Böhmermann down. First, he is prohibited from reciting his poem publicly, and second, he faces six months in prison and a fine equivalent to roughly seven million crowns. What is alarming about the whole affair is primarily that this was not a ruling by a Turkish court, but a German one, adjudicating under German "law."
Many—especially Islam-bashers—would certainly remark here about how weak Europe is caving to the Islamic world; but I don't believe that's the core issue, because the law under which Böhmermann is being tried and likely convicted existed in Germany long before Erdogan's whining. It is simply illegal to insult foreign heads of state, which I consider an utterly absurd law—likely a medieval relic from times when a simple subject wasn't allowed to open his mouth against the king either; although we now pretend to be an advanced civilization that honors free speech, when push comes to shove, we are no less barbaric than our ancestors or many citizens of Eastern nations—such as the aforementioned Turkey. For when it comes to the state demonstrating its power and dominance over the citizen, no punishment is too mild.

The Ministry of the Interior is on a tear: it built a recreational resort for its cops, whose swimming pool, tennis courts, and miniature golf course sit on someone else's property. How did that happen? The State Land Office restituted the land to its original owners, but somehow forgot to inform the Ministry of the Interior; it's wonderful to know that only top experts work in state administration. Yet I find something else even more absurd about the whole affair: the Ministry of the Interior intends to resolve the situation by suing the landowners because it wants to use the facilities for its cops. Isn't that comical? The very ministry theoretically responsible for upholding and enforcing the law in this country encroached on someone's land, and instead of admitting its error, it is trying to push through court that this is actually fine; can you blame people who believe state propaganda when they behave similarly?

Lawmakers passed the government bill on misdemeanor liability; what would you guess it contained? Correct: more tightening of the screws, repression, and steep increases in fines, sometimes up to tenfold. I won't cover all aspects of this amendment here, but only the one that caught my attention most: for insulting a police officer or official, you will now pay up to ten thousand crowns. Why? Well, considering the caliber of material the state employs in its ranks, it's hardly surprising that they don't enjoy much respect among normal, decent people; it must be obvious to anyone with half a brain that no fine, however high, can fix that. The more interesting question, however, is why subjects are forbidden from swearing at and insulting state representatives in the first place, when it has no practical impact on their work and insults in general are not punishable offenses. In truth, it is nothing other than another propaganda tool to accumulate power and flaunt supremacy.

You could read about Petr Hampl in the Sewers several times already; I consider him probably the most disgusting totalitarian on our pseudo-political scene—and not just because, by his own words, I ought to be hunted down like wild game and executed without a trial. He originally started his thus far unpromising political career in the Party of Free Citizens (Svobodní); after the European election debacle and a failed run for party chairman, he parted on bad terms with the Mach faction, soon founding the Czech Society for Civilization Studies (an anti-Islam association and such), becoming vice-chairman of Úsvit (from which he was kicked out after a while), then running for the Senate under Okamura; afterwards he was elected vice-chairman of the Bloc Against Islam, which he left to become chairman of the Alternative for the Czech Republic party, only to be elected chairman of the Angry Mothers movement a few weeks later... all within two years. Do you notice that incredible steadfastness of conviction, rock-solid character, and incorruptibility? Complemented, naturally, by an unyielding desire to serve the people xD

For those who noticed a drop in my activity (especially in the comment sections), I have a brief explanation: on Monday, I broke my arm quite badly in a motorcycle accident; so I'm not writing (or rather, writing very slowly), limiting my computer activities, and dedicating myself to recovery, which I consider my main priority.
Although it looked rather grim at first glance, in the end it might not be such a disaster; my hand was badly deformed and I basically couldn't use it, but at the hospital good fortune smiled upon me in the form of a top surgeon who managed to realign the bones and put them back into place without surgery (even without anesthesia, which was quite intense, but saved me a lot of time, energy, and overall health).
For this reason, the Sewers will run in low-power mode for a while; I'll try to provide articles, but I will have to skip discussions. Thanks for understanding.

Following up on the previous status report, I'd like to add a few details: While the hand was realigned brilliantly, the swelling was so massive that the cast couldn't be closed permanently; as a result, the bones shifted again, so surgery is unavoidable after all. On top of that came complications in the form of severe inflammation, so right now I am downing antibiotics and waiting for things to settle down enough for surgery.
Why am I writing this here? Because I would like to alert readers to the following:
1/ Typing and working slowly with one hand, so the Sewers will probably stagnate a bit; there might not be a new article every weekday for a while (though hopefully something will come out—I have a hot typist to dictate to; I just lack sufficient energy).
2/ I won't be taking part in discussions.
3/ I'll be grateful to other authors who can help me with writing; please send your contributions with a publication date a day or two in advance, and I will try to coordinate them.
4/ Once the swelling subsides, which according to the doctor should be around Wednesday, I'm heading into surgery, so I won't be around here until at least Friday.

In a city the size of Prague, there's always someone picking up a spray can or marker to scrawl something somewhere, typically on someone else's property; nobody ever paid much mind to it until a few politicians decided to raise their profile by scrubbing off anti-refugee graffiti. So over the past few weeks, everyone started obsessing over who is scrawling swastikas and similar nonsense where—the immediate suspects were naturally neo-Nazis and Islam-bashers, but soon false flag operation theories cropped up, and now even false false flag operation theories have surfaced. Absolutely everything is being dissected—the medium used, the placement of the graffiti, the author's vocabulary (Islam-bashers typically don't use the term refugee, but migrant or worse), and other aspects, just to establish whether "the bleeding-heart do-gooders are behind it" or "it's the work of Islam-bashers"; there's even a joke circulating on the subject: Why does a right-wing extremist wear a hood while spray-painting? So his dreadlocks don't fall into his face.
Are you waiting for a grand revelation of truth? Well, you'll probably get it, but likely not as you hope; I feel that everyone from both irreconcilable camps has become so crazed with collective guilt that they miss the fact that they're basically arguing over jack shit. Regardless of whether it was scrawled by an eager "hate-free" activist or a die-hard IVČRN fan, it's the action of a few individuals at most; sure, for Islam-bashers, a photo of Stropnický with a spray can would be an absolute sensation, just as a similar picture of Hampl would be for the Prague café—but why? So the camp the tagger didn't belong to could claim about the other that "they" did it; those "they," none of whom—apart from a handful of people—had any clue about the stunt, let alone participated in any way. Please, get a grip! Someone else's property should obviously be inviolable, but here it was damaged by a few individuals at most, not by everyone whose opinions you happen to disagree with.

What does a market actor do when identifying an opportunity to satisfy the needs of a large number of people? It rejoices, seizes it with both hands, and makes a profit. How does a public administration with a monopoly in the sector react in the exact same situation? It starts looking for reasons to do nothing. How so? Well, it gets its money either way (people are forcibly coerced into paying extortion), so why do anything extra when no profit comes of it? Logically, whoever earns more money the better they serve people has great incentive to deliver the best possible service; but whoever receives money irrespective of what they actually do for others is primarily motivated to do as little as possible. Despite how self-evident these principles are, crowds of people under the influence of state propaganda manage to pretend they don't exist; so I'd like to share a real-world example clearly illustrating how things stand.
Do you remember how, before the Blanka Tunnel complex opened, politicians promised public transit would run through it? Well, Blanka has been open for some time now and still nothing; why not? The public transit authority came up with a surprisingly candid justification: if city buses started using the tunnel, those routes would become extremely popular and massive crowds would want to ride them; but running so many buses is simply too expensive, so to save money, public transit won't run through Blanka. Yes, you read that right: public transit doesn't run through Blanka because it would simply be too good. A consistent application of this logic leads to canceling the most popular routes and introducing obscure ones that nobody wants to take; conversely, completely rejecting such an approach means a free market—entrepreneurs will be incentivized to operate precisely those routes people are willing to pay for, which are those that consume fewer resources than the utility they provide.

Venezuela is a land of unprecedented possibilities where, despite sitting on colossal oil reserves, oil is in short supply; the same holds true for ordinary drinking water, as state infrastructure collapses, which the government brilliantly resolved in an emergency by price-controlling bottled water—resulting in producers going bankrupt, ergo nobody has water in egalitarian fashion, meaning everything is in proper socialist order. Partly for this reason, President Nicolás Maduro has become a popular target for (not only libertarian) jokes; but Venezuela is one massive human tragedy, and Maduro is clearly running out of ideas on how to screw things up further.
His latest hit is introducing a two-day workweek for public sector employees; yes, you read that right—bureaucrats are only supposed to show up for work on Mondays and Tuesdays to save electricity, which the country is also lacking. Setting aside that for most Venezuelans it would be a blessing if bureaucrats didn't go to work at all and stopped doing harm, it demonstrates the utter helplessness of socialism: instead of the market stimulating production and finding efficient solutions, the government solves the problem by banning people from working. When food runs out entirely, will Maduro order everyone to go on a hunger strike? In socialism, anything is possible.

So I'm playing Grand Theft Auto, and suddenly BOOM: a crash involving three police cars, which went on to hit the vehicle of some unlucky soul... and lo and behold, it wasn't GTA, but reality on Liberecká Street in Prague; someone must have slammed on the brakes, the uniformed monkey behind him failed to stop in time, just like the one behind him, and then yet another one—you can really see the professional safe following distances they demand from other drivers. Unsurprisingly, none of the crews was rushing to an emergency call; they routinely drive like maniacs because many of them feel that not only the rules they enforce don't apply to them, but basic driving decency doesn't either. After all, how often do you see cops doing the very things they harass us for? Personally, about once a month. And when several of them congregate, it's hardly surprising when they take each other out; if anyone finds it superficial that I'm drawing conclusions from a single crash, feel free to look at the hard data.

A survey conducted in Britain revealed that residents there (and young people above all) love anal sex; and the government decided that something must be done about it, because this simply won't do. The Culture Secretary is allegedly downright appalled by how many young people engage in anal sex (personally, I bet his sexual partner dislikes it, which pisses him off to no end), so he must educate them not to; but how? His department already has a plan: supposedly they will restrict depictions of this practice in pornography... I wonder how he plans to achieve that, given that, first, it has long been by far the most popular category in porn, and second, the Internet exists. That "plan" will therefore (as always) take one of two forms: either disgusting harassment and Internet censorship, or bureaucratic busywork and burning taxpayer cash with zero impact; so let's hope for the latter—that it will "merely" be expensive and useless once again.

French lawmakers passed a bill criminalizing paying women for sex; now anyone who does so faces a fine of €1,500 to €3,750 (even higher for repeat offenders) and mandatory attendance at an educational course. The reason? Bruno Le Roux, head of the Socialists in the French parliament, says: "You cannot rent a woman like a car. Our society should no longer tolerate this." So the biggest whore of all, Bruno Le Roux, is in practice telling us this: "You are not allowed to have sex under terms of your own choosing; the state dictates the terms. And whoever we catch violating the state's terms for sex must forfeit part of their property to us; if they refuse to pay, we will force them by violence, and should they resist, we will gladly kill them." And I ask: what is the real filth that society should not tolerate? A man who pays a woman for consensual sex, or a man who initiates the mass violent robbery of property from those who don't dance to his tune?

You praise Pelikán once and he immediately breaks off his leash; following his sensible amendment allowing homosexuals to adopt, here comes an attack on our freedoms: we won't even be allowed to take the piss properly anymore, or rather overdo it. Why? The already obscure criminal offense of defaming a race or inciting hatred against a religion will be expanded under the amendment to include a ban on defaming a class defined by lifestyle (say, billionaires), education (for instance, those patriots who cannot write a grammatical sentence), income (such as paupers), or authority (probably Havlists); furthermore, the amendment prohibits inciting hatred against a group defined by sexual preference (and explicitly applies to asexuals as well). Damn it, where did all that constantly proclaimed freedom of speech go? And won't my favorite expression about jerking the pelican become illegal in the future because it might incite hatred against orthodox masturbators? Oh well...

Attorney Zdeněk Altner, currently wanted by uniformed monkeys, represented the Social Democratic Party (ČSSD) nearly twenty years ago in the dispute over Lidový dům; ČSSD promised him quite an exorbitant sum for it, yet paid only part of it—seventeen million was missing. The legal tug-of-war over the fee dragged on for a full sixteen years, during which it swelled thanks to—this is not a typical slip of "thanks to" instead of "due to"—contractual penalties to an unbelievable 337 million, which is a massive disaster for ČSSD (for that amount, the party could run three massive election campaigns); I'm amused by how quickly ČSSD leadership grasped economic laws that they stubbornly refuse to acknowledge in government—they have no money, so they lay people off, cut hours, and cut spending. Did it open their eyes? Not at all; socialists can relax—other people's blood doesn't bleed, so they'll continue managing our money just like before.
Yet that isn't the only thing ČSSD politicians came to understand; they also realized just how useless laws are... that is, when applying to them. So they refused to pay the money, wanting to take the entire matter to the Constitutional Court; the catch, however, is that legally this move does not stay the court's final ruling, which is unequivocal (ČSSD must pay 337 million) and cannot be appealed. So the Prime Minister stood before the nation and effectively said he didn't give a shit about the law; not in those exact words, but that was the unmistakable message. Why? Well, Altner is allegedly a notorious character and up to his ears in debt, so if money is wired directly to his Swiss account, creditors might not see a penny; do I hear that correctly? Is ČSSD inadvertently telling us between the lines that when a state court issues an idiotic ruling, we should just say "fuck it" and "correct" it as we see fit? If that is truly so, then for once I exceptionally agree with those socialists on something.

Petr Hampl, whom I have considered for some time the greatest evil on the Czech Islam-bashing scene (while Konvička strikes me as a deranged, frustrated crank, itinerant Volfová as a failed careerist, and Okamura as an orthodox populist, Hampl is in my view a genuinely evil person—and far from only because, by his own words, I ought to be hunted down like wild game and executed without trial), is leaving his leadership post in the Bloc Against Islam (BPI) and, despite having already launched his regional election campaign, is withdrawing his candidacy for governor of the Central Bohemian Region; on the godforsaken Vlastenecké noviny, one can find Hampl's video with the laughable rationale that the Central Bohemian Region is too large and decentralized (something he surely didn't know until now), while on iDnes we read that he doesn't have time (another thing he couldn't have foreseen)—and although media reported his departure on Friday afternoon, that morning even Volfová didn't know about it... everything points to a masterminded plan.
Do you wonder why the snake launched a campaign only to discover the shape of the Central Bohemian Region overnight, fleeing the BPI presidium like greased lightning and blaring it to the press just hours after first informing his closest associates? Well, I have a hunch. Someone I trust gave me very intriguing internal (and so far secret) information from Úsvit, which was supposed to heavily finance the Bloc Against Islam's campaign: Úsvit was allegedly tunneled out (again); in an account that should hold 60 million, there is now reportedly 59,000 crowns. This information cannot be verified yet, for if true, the party is guarding it jealously; but I trust my source, and the whole thing makes total sense—Hampl discovered the state of affairs and is abandoning the sinking ship before it blows wide open. Well, whoever builds their success on populism and collective guilt shouldn't be surprised to find themselves surrounded by stupid crooks and thieves.

The Ministry of Transport is harassing river paddlers again, because apparently last time wasn't enough; under a new decree, not only will life jackets be mandatory, but early in the season depending on weather, gloves, raincoats, and winter hats as well (holy shit...). But that's not all: rafts must also have a fire extinguisher (!) on board in addition to lights and a lifebuoy; the crowning glory, however, is a fifteen-meter rope—because when you capsize and are trying to rescue gear from the water, getting entangled in a rope—a fifteen-meter one!—is precisely what you want most! But even if the proposal didn't contain any absurdities or potentially hazardous items, I ask: what business does some Ťok have dictating what gear I take on the river? The worst part is that, for example, mandatory vests are (judging by online comments at least) received quite favorably... why?! If someone wants a life jacket, nobody is stopping them from putting one on; but why force it upon those who don't want it? Please, people, think!

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs decided that abroad, the Czech Republic should be translated as Czechia; and once again we have something to bicker about. Some like it, others don't, arguments and debates flare up, but... does it really matter at all? Even if the country started being called Shittia, nothing would actually change; I don't understand how anyone can take such nonsense seriously, except critically or as a joke. Could it be tied once again to patriotism, which teaches us to be proud of things we had no part in achieving and to hate people we've never met—and in this case, obsess over trivial bullshit? I'd be interested to know how much that change cost and will cost in salaries of bureaucrats and politicians, and the expense of all associated campaigns; personally, I wouldn't mind at all if the Czech Republic vanished completely and became part of another country—and if it brought lower taxes and less state harassment, I would definitely applaud it.

A uniformed monkey named Karel Kadlec got drunk last year and, with a blood alcohol level of 1.45 per mille, crashed into two cars; the court dismissed it at the time, ruling it was merely a misdemeanor, not a crime (interestingly, it took into account that to the responding cops, the man "did not seem under the influence"). Last week, the same drunken pig (he refused a breathalyzer test, but at the hospital tested over one per mille) entertained himself by ramming his Jeep into parked cars, wrecking more than fifty of them; and being a reckless daredevil to the end, he didn't even have third-party liability insurance. What will the court say this time? Perhaps it will consider that he taught at the police academy (which is hilarious in itself) and deem it just a misdemeanor again; much like when that uniformed chimpanzee who took out a biker and then kicked the injured man on the ground was, according to the judge, already punished enough by having to appear in court.
I couldn't care less how Kadlec gets punished (though he caused millions in damage, so in my view his property should be seized to the equivalent value to compensate victims, entirely apart from punitive sentencing), but here again we see in all its glory how things operate when the state acts as both defendant and judge; and it's fascinating how often people arguing against free-market justice object: "What if one of the disputing parties had ties to the judge? That wouldn't be fair!"—yet with the state, that apparently doesn't matter much. Not to mention that this whole charade is a slap in the face to everyone stripped of points for seatbelts and phone calls, or harshly penalized for drunk driving without harming a single soul; and by that I certainly don't mean Kadlec should be punished more harshly, but rather that all those victims of arbitrary police power are punished entirely excessively.

The devil Babiš is preparing a new tax bill that he plans to release before the elections; and what could be better than a populist tax-collection blueprint? Only fragments have surfaced publicly so far, but even those are quite something; besides the promised "expert realignment of the income tax framework" (holy crap... or how to rob conceptually and expertly) and scrapping the super-gross wage, we have another utter blockbuster: a clear definition of the švarcsystém (bogus self-employment) so that it can be unambiguously penalized. Naturally, changing tax laws will hit entrepreneurs mercilessly, forcing them to adapt at their own expense—such as by upgrading accounting software. In other words, more harassment, oppression, robbery, and threats of violence; because what else is it when one entity approaches another, demands their property out of thin air, and if they refuse and stand their ground, robs them via physical assault? And the crowds cheer, because they get a cut of the plunder. Disgraceful!

Matěj Stropnický (not Babiš's ass-licker from ANO, but his son from the Greens, who didn't mind Babiš's support before the election either, only turning against it afterwards) is a monumental prick; a few weeks ago, he reprimanded Tereza Sladkovská, my colleague from the Ludwig von Mises Institute, for working during her studies instead of collecting welfare benefits, and then declared it wasn't normal for eighty percent of Czechs to fly on vacation by plane. And because the sheer level of his assholery exceeded the tolerable limit even for Prague city councilors from ANO and ČSSD (not that they have any moral high ground to preach from), they made it a condition for reforming the collapsed coalition that Stropnický wouldn't sit on the city council; he agreed, but guess under what conditions? That the city buy out the Žižkov squatted social center "Klinika" for NGOs (Islam-bashers report heavily on that) and hike property taxes by ten percent; this is pathological: "OK, I'll step down from council, but only if you raise taxes." Just a massive prick, plain and simple...

Tonight, I accepted an invitation to the TV debate show Máte slovo ("You Have the Floor") regarding a blanket ban on smoking; I'll do whatever I can to prevent the show from revolving solely around how smoking harms health, focusing instead on property rights and prohibition as such. Having already had the chance to appear on the show (arguing against the euro), however, I know that despite its title, getting a word in edgewise can be excruciatingly difficult unless one behaves like a boor; it also depends heavily on one's debate opponents. If you can think of any solid arguments (especially concise phrasings or punchy slogans), or sharp rebuttals to typical statist defenses of the ban, throw them in the comments! It doesn't matter if they seem obvious or if I've written about them myself before—perhaps you'll come up with a great way to put it; considering how hard it is to get the floor there, above all I need to be concise. Thanks for the help!

Until now, Hradec Králové had two information centers and one virtual info point; but that wasn't enough—it was absolutely essential to build another, better, fancier, and seriously ultra-cool one: for forty million. And since the EU pays more than half (subsidies must be drawn regardless of what bullshit they produce), five million was left over for a stellar multimedia sphere, almost like something out of Star Trek; it displays all kinds of info about the city—only that and nothing else, it's unhackable... well, unless you count the group of teenagers who played porn on it. But the biggest kicker lies in the fact that it is a "Hradec Unto Itself" project: tourists are forbidden from using the info center! Why? Logically, of course... because that European money didn't come from a tourism fund; using it in any way not prescribed by almighty big Brussels (which I stubbornly continue to decline in the feminine) is entirely out of the question after all xD

A headline on iDnes caught my eye: "Fine for Ťok. Took advice on toll, but bypassed the law." Great—could Ťok finally be facing consequences for his actions? Not a chance! The very first paragraph disillusions the reader: "The Ministry of Transport must pay a quarter of a million crowns for awarding a contract worth up to 52 million crowns without a tender to Deloitte Advisory for consulting on selecting a toll operator." And the mockery continues: "The contract with Deloitte served its purpose, and the firm has essentially concluded its work within the negotiated procedure without publication (JŘBU) for the continued operation of the toll system. We hold a different opinion on the legality of our actions; however, the antitrust office's decision is valid and we will abide by it," responded the Ministry of Transport, which simultaneously stated that no personal sanctions would be taken. Why worry, when other people's blood doesn't bleed? And that's how the state fights corruption: someone awards a suspicious contract, and subjects pay the fine on their behalf!

Brno city councilor Martin Freund from the political movement Žít Brno decided to rent municipal apartments to randomly selected homeless people "for free" (or rather, for an amount equal to their state housing welfare allowance, so the tenants won't have to pay a single crown), claiming it pays off for the city even if they never find work, because when people have housing, that is a benefit in itself (I'm not exaggerating, that's literally what he said); and I ask: who is this "city" that it supposedly pays off for? If it's some bigwigs, I believe it; but if he means regular people, why must they be coerced by force into paying for it if it's so beneficial to them? I would also be curious to know how many homeless people Mr. Freund houses out of his own pocket; if it really pays off, why doesn't he do so and lead by example? I have already written tons of arguments demonstrating what nonsense this whole thing is, but here the proponent proves it best himself: because nobody needs to be coerced into what actually pays off.

My view on immigrants is currently very "out"; basically, I think roughly this: "No one should force anyone to support refugees. No one should prevent anyone from supporting refugees." The first sentence irritates the bleeding-heart "sunshiners," because after all, that's horrible discrimination, and since we already have a welfare state, why not expand its scope (and when I mention that the whole welfare state is wrong, they clutch their heads); the second sentence enrages the Islam-bashers, to whom anyone wishing to care for people in need on their own property and at their own expense is a plain traitor deserving severe punishment who needs to come to their senses.
As usually happens when I express my opinion in this vein (essentially saying the same thing over and over: laissez-faire, let everyone mind their own business on their own property at their own expense, let others do the same, and let the state stay out of it on either side), everyone always singles out the part that irks them (while one side interprets it as opportunistic xenophobia, the other as opportunistic treason) so they can beat me over the head with it; neither side typically pulls punches, since—despite my futile protests—they automatically lump me in with their opponents for failing to share their orthodox view.
Why am I writing about this? Lately, I often see various Islam-bashers lauding public demonstrations against refugees as acts of heroism; as someone who constantly enjoys criticism from both camps, I can assert that the exact opposite is true (speaking of expressions within the bounds of law; when the thought police get involved, the situation reverses). If any publicly voiced opinion on immigration comes close to heroism, it is standing up for refugees: first, the overwhelming majority of the population holds a more or less opposing view, escalating the risk of confrontation; but above all, Islam-bashers are far scarier than bleeding hearts. While bleeding-heart disapproval manifests (online or in person) typically as grumbling, Islam-bashers can be far more aggressive (I've received numerous profanities and threats from them, virtually and in person, a few times bordering on physical assault).
I wouldn't want this text to sound as though bleeding hearts are the good guys—it is precisely they who typically tap into various subsidies, collaborate with the state, and seek to censor their opponents, which I consider far more dangerous than the aggression of Islam-bashers; I simply wanted to point out that howling with the crowd while posing as a dissident is pretty cheap. True courage lies in saying things that the majority does not want to hear, even when facing the threat of getting punched in the face for it.

Zdeněk Pohlreich is a very skilled chef who—despite his strongly statist views—understands the workings of the market on a basic practical level, which probably has to do with being a successful entrepreneur and star of a television show where he teaches other restaurant and pub operators how to succeed; and today I'll write about one episode of that show: the chef visited a hotel restaurant run by municipal officials who described the property relations (literally) like this: "It's not a municipal hotel; it's a private hotel, but owned by the city." I don't know why, but that reminds me of the Stork's Nest. Other gems of explanation include: "Economically it makes no sense, but it's necessary," or: "We offer soup and a main course for 75 crowns because many city hall employees eat here." If you want to see more, look up episode 15 of season 6 on the internet.
And what intrigued me most about the spectacle? Well, even though Ano, šéfe! ("Yes, Boss!") had been filmed with all kinds of desperate characters, at least everyone understood that the goal of their business was to make money; this was the first episode featuring people who didn't even grasp this foundational premise, making up all sorts of "necessary economic nonsense" instead. Only a politician, a bureaucrat, or their subordinates could seriously come up with something like that; after all, how else can one know what is good for people other than letting them pay for it? Everyone pays for what they want and find useful; conversely, nobody voluntarily pays for things they do not deem beneficial. The market operates on this principle, whereas politicians and bureaucrats are typically characterized by misunderstanding it entirely, or at least ignoring it. Delusions in the form of "economic nonsense that is necessary" unfortunately permeate throughout society because they are propagated by the (state) educational system.

On Friday in the Sewers, I wrote that Robert Pelikán had actually done something positive; so today, let's remind ourselves once again what a bastard our Minister of Justice is. A few days ago, the Chamber of Deputies passed his amendment to the Criminal Procedure Code, under which not only tax evasion is a criminal offense, but preparing to commit it is as well; in practice, the law primarily means further expanding the powers of cops, who will now be able to initiate wiretaps and surveillance merely on the suspicion that someone is getting ready to evade taxes.
