Why? Because he was a drug manufacturer? So what? Because he produced substances that can harm people? Well, yes, but that hardly distinguishes him from manufacturers of countless other (state-permitted) goods that can ruin lives just the same (alcohol, cigarettes, knives, ropes...). Above all, he never forced his products on anyone; he merely manufactured and offered them. The choice to purchase and consume rested entirely with each individual. Yet the state decided to persecute certain producers and destroy their lives merely for offering a product to willing buyers. And what does the state do to them, beyond robbing them blind? It locks them in prison—a sanitized euphemism for medieval torment, where a human being is shoved into a tiny cage and held against their will, often for years on end. How does society view sick sadists who kidnap someone and hold them captive in a basement? Horrific, monstrous! But when the state does it? Perfectly fine!

Some time ago in the Sewers, you could read about the criminal prosecution of Konvička for speaking his mind out loud; the do-gooders applauded it back then, but they didn't yet realize that this was a double-edged sword: Žilková recently let slip on air some idiotic nonsense claiming that the raped women in Germany brought it upon themselves, that it's basically normal, and that deep down we all secretly crave giant black dicks anyway (I'm freely paraphrasing the gist of a long interview here, but I'm really not exaggerating much—just Google: "Žilková dobrovolně k novým samcům"), which are certainly sickening opinions, but even among the anti-Islam crowd a snitch appeared who filed a criminal complaint against her (just like when the bleeding hearts reported Konvička). The criminal complaint can once again be Googled (search in Google Images: "Žilková trestní oznámení"), though unfortunately the informant's name is redacted.
So Žilková has to go down to the police station; and I ask: Where is this freedom of speech that they tell us in school we supposedly have? And I answer myself: They're lying to us, there is simply no freedom of speech here.
Freedom of speech, after all, doesn't just consist in tolerating reasonable and logically substantiated statements, but above all in allowing people to publicly voice opinions that are completely foolish, disgusting, perverted, lying, illogical, hateful, reprehensible, and demented—basically something like the Žilková–Konvička duo. The moment the state starts dragging someone over the coals for such statements, self-censorship will naturally spread, not to mention that for such a thing to be carried out at all, someone is needed to decide what constitutes a "bad opinion"... do we really have an authority to whom you would entrust this power? And let me point out that this authority is no abstract "state" or "society," but very specific people—politicians and judges; do you trust them?

Yesterday I wrote about what capitalism is not, and didn't miss the opportunity to debunk some delusions of its critics. Today I would like to write a few lines about what capitalism is. To start off, allow me to quote a man whom I consider the greatest thinker of the twentieth century and probably of all time—Murray Newton Rothbard:
Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism; anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. The true anarchism will be capitalism; and the true capitalism will be anarchism.
If anyone happens to want a translation, that capitalist creation Google Translate handles it quite well (with one's eyes squinted).
So what does the term capitalism mean? It is a free market without state intervention. Yes, of course, capitalists can be ruthless businessmen motivated by their own selfishness and greed, which poses a huge problem when combined with the state—corruption, laws tailored to their businesses, subsidies, monopolies (which, by the way, do not arise without the state). In a free-market environment, however, that very same profit-seeking and greed drives those same people to satisfy the needs of others—how else could they obtain money without the state other than by persuading people to use their services and buy their products?
And what is the best way to persuade someone to buy something from you? Naturally by offering them something that person needs! Some might say that while this is a lovely theory, in practice things work quite differently. Yes, of course, you're right, in practice things work differently, but why? Because of the state, of course! In a free market, it genuinely works exactly as I describe; just look at places where the state doesn't interfere as much—Singapore, Hong Kong, and others—look at how they flourish! But what about socialist Sweden? Couldn't there be another way? No; just take a look at history: Sweden acquired its wealth during periods of wild capitalism; socialism was installed only after the country had already become immensely wealthy (and that growth was significantly slowed down as a result).
Capitalism is freedom and abundance; capitalism means the free market that took us from horse carriages to cars, from typewriters to computers, from empty pantries to full refrigerators, from hard toil in the fields to the freedom to choose a career in countless fields, from food being enormously expensive to negligible, from an occasional wash in a creek to luxurious bathrooms, from one outfit per person to overflowing closets, from an outhouse to a flush toilet, from journeys taking days or weeks to hours—in short, from poverty to riches! Make no mistake: this is not the work of a bureaucrat; behind it was greed, personal gain, and the pursuit of wealth... the very same qualities that the state turns into a catastrophe, the market harnesses for our benefit.

In recent years, I've observed that criticizing capitalism has become immensely trendy and popular, especially among young people (though by no means only among them). Well, fair enough, let everyone define themselves against whatever they see fit. What I find very sad and alarming, however, is that the vast majority of those who rail against capitalism typically have no clue what capitalism actually is. And the problem isn't simply that they "define it differently"—which wouldn't matter in itself if they adhered to such definitions consistently—but rather that they mostly criticize some grotesque monstrosity, while wanting to use the law to restrict real capitalism.
First, allow me to list a few examples of what capitalism is definitely not: Capitalism is certainly not Agrofert and Babiš—those are the products of socialist subsidies and regulations (biofuels...); capitalism is not private schools strictly hamstrung by state regulations; capitalism is seriously not private health insurance companies when health insurance is mandatory; capitalism is definitely not a (non-state) company that the state grants a monopoly on anything (water supply, for example). Where there is no free market, there cannot be capitalism; and if the state intervenes, then it is not a free market.
Some people argue that when big companies have non-market privileges, it's not the state's fault, but the corporations', because they bribe civil servants and politicians. Regardless of the outcome of academic debates over who is more to blame, it is completely evident how the problem definitely cannot be solved: by granting more power to the state. Even if it were absolute truth that it's solely and exclusively the fault of large corporations that corrupt politicians write custom-tailored laws for them, one cannot argue that the state will fix it (since the problem arose precisely because it does not); if states are corrupted by major market players, then regardless of who is to blame, the consequence of expanding state power can be nothing other than more corruption!
You can blame businessmen for corrupting politicians; but as long as there are businessmen operating in a market environment and politicians possessing the power to distort that environment, corruption will inevitably occur (after all, records of it are thousands of years old—it has evidently never been otherwise, nor could it be). The only solution, therefore, is either to strip businessmen of the ability to do business, or to strip politicians of the power to make decisions; and surely anyone who either remembers the first option or at least theoretically understands why it is a road to hell should also realize that the problem cannot be eliminated in any way other than by abolishing political power (increasing it will achieve the exact opposite). And for those who still don't realize it, I have one such picture...

I constantly hear people around me saying that immigrants are our greatest threat and that something urgently "needs to be done" about it; when I ask further, in 99% of cases that "needs to be done" means that politicians, the government, the police—simply the state—ought to act. Although direct statistics are inaccessible due to political correctness, in many countries one can observe a rise in crime that correlates with the arrival of migrants, which in my eyes is a sufficient argument (further strengthened by the concealment of direct statistics) for stating that immigrants are a statistically more dangerous group in our society. But are they really what threatens us the most?
An incomparably more dangerous group that initiates orders of magnitude more violence than all migrants combined consists of our nation-states and the European Union. Not citizens, not ordinary people, not "all of us," no "society," but states—which means politicians, bureaucrats, police officers, and other parasites living off our money, which they take from us under the threat of violence and call taxes. These people rob us, impose their will upon us, and if we do not submit, they haul us off by force and lock us behind bars in prison (even when we haven't harmed anyone; for example, merely because we refuse to pay them or don't want to let them meddle in our transactions); they are people who commit more violence in a single day than immigrants manage in an entire year. I am not saying that mass migration poses no threat; I am merely calling for reflection on whether it is wise, in addressing this problem, to expand the powers of a state that generates more evil and violence than all immigrants combined.

Many of Babiš's voters swear by the mantra: "Whoever is unimaginably rich has no need to steal." That's similar logic to: "Whoever is morbidly obese has no need to overeat." Of course, I don't mean to imply that someone who is rich is more likely to steal; I'm simply pointing out that assuming the opposite makes very little sense. In any case, what do the hard numbers say? In 2011, Agrofert's corporate income tax amounted to two billion CZK, while Agrofert collected a little over half a billion in subsidies; and as time went on, the first number fell while the second grew, until finally Agrofert's 2014 annual report showed that it paid 1.5 billion in income tax while siphoning almost 1.75 billion from subsidies. What a coincidence! Just like when, as Finance Minister, he waived 1.5 billion CZK in state fees for himself.
I am the last person to mind someone optimizing their taxes and trying to pay as little as possible to the state; however, it is outrageous when this is done by the very man who aggressively harasses everyone with EET, the VAT ledger statement, and lines his own pockets with subsidies that all taxpayers are forced to foot the bill for. In every society, there will be a certain percentage of people like Babiš—capable, smart, predatory, and ruthless. The difference, however, lies in how they manifest: while in a free market all those Babišes would be the scourge of their competitors and a boon to consumers (much like Rockefeller's Standard Oil), the state opens up an easier and far more attractive path for them to build their empires: instead of lowering prices, catering to customers, and outcompeting rivals, all they need to do is leverage the state's coercive apparatus and force everyone to pay by violence.

A wave of indignation was stirred up by Miroslav Donutil's piece recently broadcast on Czech Television (ČT)—a remake of Snow White in which the prince was a black man. Intrigued, I went to listen to the fairy tale, and it truly was dreadful, although the black prince was about the least of its problems in my eyes. Yes, of course, there were some mildly racist quips—for example, pointing out the drawbacks of Snow White's fair skin—but the hell with that, I personally am not overly sensitive to racism. What struck me far more, however, was the utter mental (and indeed spiritual, though I could forgive that) emptiness of the whole tale: not only was the struggle between good and evil removed, but so were all hardships; the protagonists simply faced no obstacles whatsoever. Snow White found the dwarves, cooked for them, they mined gold, she headed into town, met the black prince there, they got married, and had children. I'm really not exaggerating: there wasn't the slightest hint of a plot, of overcoming hardship or peril.
This complete toothlessness is no accident; it is a common hallmark of many modern fairy tales—above all, avoid taking a stand; the battle between good and evil is "out," and courage or problem-solving are likewise tossed aside. The main protagonist must show no initiative or influence over the events that simply drift past him (take Harry Potter, for instance: sure, things happen, but the main character exhibits no foresight or drive to take matters into his own hands—quite the contrary), because we must protect children from getting the impression that each of us is the master, driver, and engineer of our own destiny; things just sort of happen regardless of our actions. Whoever thrives was just "lucky," and otherwise "bad luck" is to blame—never the person himself. The motto of many modern fairy tales is: "He who does nothing makes no mistakes; so above all, don't stand out." How will such stories shape the generation raised on them? Compared to that, a black prince is seriously an entirely unproblematic character.

Facebook has blocked the "We Don't Want Islam in the Czech Republic" (IVČRN) page for the second time (and this time it seems permanent). The bleeding hearts applaud and celebrate, while the anti-Islam crowd feels censored and oppressed yet again. Personally, I find this move unfortunate, as I can't imagine any benefit from it other than escalating hatred between the two camps; creating a new page is no problem anyway. On the one hand, this will help IVČRN slightly (the ban is being covered in the media, giving them more visibility and an underground aura), but on the other hand, it also hurts them (it will take time to rebuild their follower base), so the net effect in my opinion will be practically nil. Why was the page blocked in the first place? Hard to say; the anti-Islam activists naturally claim it was due to political pressure in society, which might be true, but might not—it's entirely possible Facebook couldn't care less about IVČRN and they simply broke their rules. Both are possible.
However, I would like to address the claims that banning IVČRN is an attack on freedom of speech. In my view, it is nothing of the sort (much as I definitely do not endorse the ban). Facebook is a private company that decides what goes on its own servers, which is, of course, completely fine. While the essence of freedom of speech is that I can say whatever I want, no one is under any obligation to provide me with the platform to broadcast it! An attack on freedom of speech and an outright atrocity is when the courts drag Konvička over the coals for voicing his opinion; a server owner deciding what content is hosted, however, is a diametrically different situation. After all, by not publishing communist articles in my Sewers, I certainly don't deprive them of the freedom to express themselves on their own turf and on their own dime; but if I forcibly prohibited them from publishing on their own servers (whether on my own or through the state), that would unequivocally be an attack on freedom of speech.

Yesterday we dealt with German incest; today, naturally, it's the turn of German bestiality. Unlike incest, it is not a criminal offense among our western neighbors; however, many (led by the agricultural committee) are demanding that it be made illegal, as farms have even emerged in Germany that, among other things, profit from animal prostitution for those willing to pay for bestiality experiences. Is it disgusting? Of course. But should it be illegal? No! The reason is exactly the same as with incest in yesterday's piece: it is purely the business of the people involved; nobody else should interfere. An objection that this is animal cruelty that must be stopped? Well, I don't know exactly how these orgies work, but let's assume the animals aren't thrilled about it. Why, then, shouldn't this behavior be outlawed?
First, because the resources the state would use to enforce such a law were taken from people under the threat of violence against their will; it is thus swapping harming animals for harming human beings. Second, I could understand such a stance from vegans (not vegetarians) who hold that animals should have the same rights as humans; while I disagree with that, fair enough, it is a consistent view. But let no one who consumes animal products (or even eats meat) tell me that we must ban bestiality because of animal suffering. Factory-farming them under less-than-pleasant conditions for slaughter and processing is fine, but having sex with them is not? Come on! Surely no one can take that seriously. If we accept that animals exist to satisfy human needs and may suffer or be killed for that purpose, then one cannot consistently punish anyone for having sex with them; and if sex is a problem, then slaughterhouses must be an order of magnitude more serious a problem.

A bizarre event took place in Germany: the adopted Patrick Stübing entered into a romantic relationship with his biological sister Susan Karolewski without either knowing of their blood relationship (they didn't grow up together and only met as adults). When it was discovered, the state compounded their misfortune by slapping him with a two-year prison sentence, because the law is the law and ignorance of the law is no excuse—after all, what else can one expect from state authorities besides malice and stupidity? Fortunately, tons of good, reasonable people in Germany began fighting for the repeal of this senseless legislation; yet many people lose their minds at the mere thought of incest not being outlawed... and by no means only in Germany: even in the Czech Republic, people who are completely unaffected are speaking up, absolutely "certain" that if the Germans repeal the law criminalizing incest, total doom will follow.
Why are these people so blatantly wrong? First of all, because practically nobody has any interest in incest; whether it's illegal or not, virtually nobody will practice it, so in reality its legalization won't affect our lives in the slightest. And what about the handful of people who, for whatever reason, have sexual relations with close relatives? Well, it will naturally help them, because nobody will lock them up in prison. And why should they? After all, it's their business! Some object that it isn't, because the chances of having a disabled child are higher. Yes, that's true, but even so, it is still their business—if we start claiming it isn't, we've just found an argument for banning sexual relations between people with genetically inheritable disabilities; and not only that: following this reasoning, we could also ban sex for older people, since an older maternal age dramatically increases the likelihood of certain fetal disorders (such as Down syndrome). Do we really want to regulate this with laws too?

Instead of public schools giving students truthful information about drugs and explaining how each drug actually causes harm, they routinely portray all of them roughly as heroin. This ultimately does more harm than good, because once people discover that at least regarding some drugs this is just lies and fearmongering, they lose respect for the warnings about other drugs as well. In fact, I wrote an installment of my anarcho-capitalism series on this very topic quite recently. Personally, while I don't believe anything the state tells me, I also don't consider it wise to simply assume the exact opposite; ergo, I read extensively about drugs, picked out the interesting and relatively safe ones, tried them, and occasionally use the only class of substances that suits me—hallucinogens (otherwise I don't even drink or smoke).
My favorite drug, which I take about once or twice a year, is LSD; and after a particularly intense experience, I decided to write something about this substance and share information with readers that they never received in the state education system. Naturally, anyone can look these things up on the Internet, but whoever is interested in my perspective is welcome to dive in here.

Today marks exactly twenty-one years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses of the twentieth century—and in my opinion, of all time—departed this world just shy of his 69th birthday: Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism." The significance of his work lies in the astonishingly consistent unification of two seemingly unrelated schools of thought: the Austrian School of economics and anarchism. While his teacher, the brilliant economist Ludwig von Mises, proved the impossibility of economic calculation under central planning—thereby demonstrating beyond a shadow of a doubt the superiority of a free-market economy over a socialist one—he still assumed that the free market would be secured by the state. On the other hand, various anarchists pointed out the ethical indefensibility of the state as a monopoly on violence, yet their proposed solutions were typically various communist utopias devoid of any economic foundation.
In his life's work, Murray Newton Rothbard consistently merged these two currents into consistent anarcho-capitalism, recognizing that the state is the obstacle to both anarchy and the free market, while the absence of a monopoly on violence constitutes both anarchy and a free market. As he put it: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." He was a man of keen analytical intellect with an absolute sense of logic, yet simultaneously deeply emotional; an unrelenting hatred of evil—whose greatest modern embodiment is the state—permeated his entire body of work. He passed away before I was even ten years old; later, however, what he created profoundly shaped my life and opened my eyes. Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

The Chinese government has launched the Sesame Credit app (if you Google it, beware of confusing it with Credit Sesame, which is different software), whose purpose is to assess how good a citizen someone is and assign people a score accordingly. This score will subsequently be taken into account when dealing with authorities and the state in general, but it could also affect things like loan accessibility, pension amounts, and the like. Registration is not yet mandatory; however, the comrades plan for it to become mandatory by 2020. According to available information, the ultimate goal is for an account to be created for everyone at birth and remain with them throughout their entire life.
From the sources I reviewed, I wasn't able to pin down precisely how the scoring system works—or rather, my search yielded conflicting reports (some claim the app will track virtually everything, including social media activity: sharing pro-government posts earns you points, while sharing anti-government posts loses them; the app's developers, however, deny this). But whichever way it is, implementing such a system lays the groundwork for total totalitarian control. Over time, people will come to see it as completely normal, just like the Czech census has droves of defenders. And just as Babiš argues in favor of introducing EET by pointing out that Croatia has it too, I wonder whether I will live to see the first Czech politician justify the rollout of Sesame Credit by arguing that it produces wonderful results in China.

It has been nearly a month since I wrote about the young man who decided not to attend school, for which the state has been brutally persecuting him by repeatedly locking him in a psychiatric hospital. I warmly recommend reading that article to anyone who hasn't yet—it's quite intense. In connection with that piece, I find the readers' reactions fascinating, whether sent by email or posted on the various websites where the article appeared: while most people reluctantly mutter something about the asylum being perhaps a bit much (and some don't even concede that), compulsory schooling is in their eyes entirely proper, and above all, he brought it on himself—he should have just gone to school instead of being foolish. The comments are typically filled with contempt for the young man, calling him an idiot who wouldn't have been harmed by just going to school, but instead he had to stir up nonsense and really deserved a good punch in the face to open his eyes.
First, I was struck by the opinion: "Compulsory schooling yes, but the psychiatric ward is over the top." But how else is the law to be enforced if not through violence? Here, the inconsistency of statists is exposed in all its nakedness: they refuse to see that legislation inherently means violent coercion; yet you cannot have compulsory school attendance without coercing people to fulfill that obligation! Second, I find it remarkable how many people fixate on the victim's mistakes or foolishness while ignoring the aggressor's atrocities. What if I locked someone up because they refused to obey me? Would people also focus primarily on how stupid he was for letting himself get locked up? But for the state, of course, different rules apply. Third, it's intriguing how everyone constantly whines about a lack of ideals and admires romantic heroes who refuse to bow to terror, but when someone actually does so in real life, he is instantly labeled an idiot. And fourth, I find the defense of this wickedness—claiming the state is acting in the boy's own best interest—completely pathetic. Logic versus propaganda: 0–4.

Not only from libertarians, I occasionally read reflections along the lines of "the worse, the better," which generally assume that the current establishment (the bloated state, the EU) must soon collapse under its own weight because what politicians are doing is unsustainable. Yes, that's true: it isn't sustainable in the long run, and if socialism keeps expanding, it will eventually not only stifle our society's prosperity but could halt it altogether, so that we begin growing poorer, which will ultimately lead to collapse. But when? It took the Soviet Union nearly three generations, and it had far better conditions for collapse than what we have now. Why? First, it was genuinely completely centrally planned, whereas we are only partially so; second, the overall level of wealth back then was lower, ergo the road to absolute destitution was shorter; third, personal freedom (speech, religion, etc.) was lower; fourth, a positive example of "the West" existed (even if talking about it was forbidden).
The power of the market is fascinating: despite all the regulations and the massive ball and chain of the public sector, the private sector still manages to generate wealth. Historical precedent tells us that even once that ceases to be the case, it can take three generations for change to happen; if we factor in the time before we even start growing poorer, we are talking at best about our great-great-grandchildren being affected. I'm not saying the EU can't collapse sooner; on the other hand, it would easily be replaced by another variety of socialism. That's why I wouldn't pin too much hope on the slogan "the worse, the better." Supporting things that ridicule or cause infighting within the establishment while carrying minimal real danger is another matter (right now, for instance, the premier Czech clown named Zeman). So what is our only—albeit slim—chance? Tirelessly explain the benefits of liberty to people. Another year is here, and with it new armies of school-indoctrinated statists... so we've got work to do xD

I could wish you, my dear readers, much success in 2016; and it would be a very sincere wish, because you are mostly libertarians, so I want you to be successful and possess as many resources as possible to reshape the world in your image, and consequently in mine. But then I figured I'd do more: I'll provide a direct guide to how the world works xD. I don't really care for "lifestyle" articles; why? Well, I find them distinctly non-universal. Everyone has "their own" formula for success, not to mention that different people define success differently. Some time ago, however, I came across an article that I consider not only universal, but profoundly revealing. About what? A bit of everything... about life, and also about how the world works. Am I exaggerating? No, seriously, it is a gem among articles of its kind; part of its genius lies in how the author applies praxeology to everyday life—and he probably hasn't even read Mises and likely never heard of the Austrian School of economics.
And that is precisely why I'm publishing it in the Sewers: it is not written by a libertarian or primarily for libertarians, but it packages libertarian ideas in a different wrapping. To set reader expectations properly, let me reveal one more thing: for anyone whose life is a mess, who is dissatisfied with themselves, feels aggrieved, and essentially considers themselves a loser, this article can change their life (no exaggeration). For the successful (and I assume the majority of libertarians belong to this camp), it won't offer that much new, yet even so, in my view, it is well worth reading, as you will quite likely find many of your own thoughts expressed far better than you could phrase them yourselves. The article was originally in English, but for the reader's convenience, I translated it and incorporated key insights from the various links that pepper the original. So here it is: "Six Harsh Truths That Will Make You a Better Person"!

In 2014 (we don't have this year's statistics yet), 1,327 official vehicles driven by uniformed monkeys and 84,532 cars driven by normal people were involved in traffic accidents; in total, at the start of that year, 8,282 monkey vehicles and 7.8 million human vehicles were registered. It follows that during that period, about 1% of humans crashed, compared to 16% of the monkeys who were supposed to protect and serve those humans. Can a sixteen-fold accident rate be explained by higher mileage? The average human car travels fifteen thousand kilometers a year; while there are no exact statistics for police cars, to make up for the aforementioned disparity, the ape-squad would have to clock a quarter of a million kilometers a year, which would basically require replacing the entire fleet every single year—and according to the police department's financial reports, that isn't happening by a long shot.
Not to mention that even if mileage did explain such a staggering number of crashes, by the state's very own logic, that excuses nobody—or does the penalty point system somehow take into account who drives more kilometers? No. Are points wiped away based on crash-free kilometers? No. Why then should the cops be judged by a different standard? They simply crash sixteen times more often than everyone else and cause chaos on the roads.
Someone might argue that the uniformed monkeys are involved in so many accidents because they're chasing criminals and "road hogs"; but does a pursuit give them the right to endanger others? No. Not even the state grants them such a right, because under the law, while they may violate traffic rules, they may only do so without endangering anyone. Out of the 1,327 accidents they were involved in, they caused 661 and were deemed not at fault in 666 (and that assumes their colleagues and the courts aren't biased in their favor, which I highly doubt); thus, one cannot even claim that the monkeys are innocent victims being rammed by criminals.
And the moral of the story? Cops are aggressive, dim-witted brutes, dangerous to themselves (which is the absolute least of my concerns) and to everyone around them. The state tells us they are on the roads to protect and serve us, but in reality they are pests. And whenever I hear politicians talk about piles of corpses on the roads and "road pirates," I think they ought to sweep their own doorstep first, because the only real pirates are their own henchmen.

Especially lately, particularly in connection with the migrant crisis, we can read from many commentators that multiculturalism is evil, that it has failed, never worked, and will lead to our downfall; and I cannot disagree that if politicians continue forcing multiculturalism down our throats as they have done so far, nothing good will come of it. However, I get the distinct impression that authors of such pieces often suffer from a fairly fatal misunderstanding of the actual root problem, which in my opinion simply isn't multiculturalism; it is state-enforced multiculturalism.
What would multiculturalism look like without state backing? Well, lunatics like Kohout would probably continue going to the ghetto to kiss Gypsies, all sorts of left-leaning students would keep preaching it to us, writing articles about it, and a few might even take some refugees into their own homes; and my personal guess is that this move alone would cure quite a few of them of their multiculturalism. But what would be the real impact on an ordinary person? Practically none: we could all simply ignore Kohout, and the number of #welcomed refugees would likely be in the single digits or low dozens.
Why, then, is multiculturalism a problem? Because the state forces it upon us under the threat of violence. We are not suffering because of deranged eccentrics kissing Gypsies, but because of anti-discrimination laws, mandatory EU refugee quotas, expensive detention camps, forced integration programs, and NGOs hooked up to the state money pipeline—in short, because of politicians and bureaucrats paid with public funds who need to justify their own existence. Multiculturalism on its own, without state sponsorship, would be nothing more than a fairly harmless hobby of a few café-dwelling leftists (and without access to public money, there would be vastly fewer of them).
So we have two problem factors here: the state and multiculturalism. What would the state do without multiculturalism? Bureaucrats would simply find another pretext to prey on decent people. And what would multiculturalists do without the state? At most, they would draw pitying smiles from those around them. Unfortunately, I arrive at the exact same conclusion as so many times before: the primary cause of the problem is, once again, the state. And as so often happens, the situation looks different at first glance, leading many to actually see the solution in further state intervention (just in the opposite direction), when all it would take is for the government to leave people the hell alone.

I won't comment on the musical side of things, as I don't consider that essential for songs with a political message, but something else caught my attention: it always amuses me when someone is an ardent patriot, yet in the very act of boasting about it, makes heaps of glaring grammatical errors. Mr. Ortel, however, took it to another level: in "Mešita," which is not merely written but sung, and lasts just two and a half minutes, he failed at noun declension five times (and it wasn't for the sake of rhyme; the correct forms would have fit normally; some of these cases can be attributed to the Pilsen dialect, but by no means all). But patriots are impressed by violence far more than by any language, so they catapulted Mr. Ortel along with his band into top spots in the Český slavík music poll, boosting his fame even further.
When even D-FENS wrote about Ortel, I decided to explore their oeuvre a bit; and it was appalling—much worse than I had anticipated. I recommend the song "Hadr" (Rag) to readers, because it's something else; incidentally, that masterpiece also serves as the anthem of the Workers' Party. The greatest ordeal, however, is the track "Zůstaň mým domovem" (Remain My Home)—I have rarely heard anything so cringeworthy in my life; I simply have no words for it, you have to hear it (and see it; the music video captures all the misery). This song is best described by this quote from George Carlin (I'm not sure if he was the original author): "Nationalism teaches you to take pride in shit you haven’t done and hate people you’ve never met." Unfortunately, accomplishing something in life takes time, energy, resources, and effort, whereas belonging to a nation can be done effortlessly by anyone, making it much easier to take pride in the latter. That is why patriotism is so popular: it is basically the ideal ideology for losers.

I've pushed a few changes to the codebase of the Sewers, but I've already received several follow-up or confused questions about what's going on, so allow me to comment briefly: first, I added an RSS feed—nothing much to explain there, whoever uses RSS readers can add my feed; second, I made a few theme tweaks that might not be entirely obvious at first glance. Unregistered visitors have it easy: a new menu item has simply appeared (» appearance «) where they can choose how the Sewers should look for them; the setting will be saved in browser cookies. Registered users have it slightly more intricate: in addition to the » appearance « option, they also have » edit account details «, where they can make the same choice, but this setting will be stored in the database with their user accounts rather than in cookies.
What's the difference? Whatever you set in the » appearance « menu will be saved only in that specific browser; conversely, through » edit account details «, you can set the appearance that the Sewers will have wherever you log in from. In the event of a conflict between settings, the user profile setting ("edit account details") wins, although it contains an option (the very first one) that can override this (i.e., the user's theme will match whatever was chosen in the » appearance « menu). You can use this, for instance, to mute the sounds of the Sewers while at work (the black-and-white imageless theme is also soundless), which some readers asked for. And as I just verified theory in practice, giving a website a makeover via CSS is remarkably easy, so if anyone has an idea or request for another theme, feel free to write to me; if several similar suggestions come together, or if I like something, I'll implement it.

Although I'm no big fan of hip hop, I have to ask: Have you ever heard libertarian rap? If not, Google "Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek Round Two"; not only does it capture reality with astonishing accuracy, but the creators also had an incredible eye for detail (watch the video carefully, it's worth it), and the ending drives home the sad point brilliantly. On top of that, it's hilarious—I was roaring with laughter, and along with me all the other five and a half libertarians who understood it. And what about collectivist rap? Be my guest and Google "Revolta: Povstaň s láskou"; this piece describes the problems of our society in an incredibly emotional and fairly accurate way, yet proposes completely moronic solutions (such as food self-sufficiency, putting power in the hands of the youth, nationalizing banks, demolishing shopping malls, and the like)—and most people, practically anyone who listens, nod along in agreement, because understanding it requires absolutely nothing.
Unfortunately, these two works illustrate the current state of individualism and collectivism in society with absolute precision: while libertarian ideas are logical, deeply consistent, rigorous, and true—yet virtually nobody takes them seriously because understanding them demands actual effort—collectivist ideas are typically populist, inconsistent drivel that looks good at first glance, but dissolves into absurdity upon deeper logical analysis; yet everyone understands them, and many even consider them an ideal (the sharper ones sometimes add that it is an unreachable ideal). Add to that the fact that libertarians are often oddballs (like myself) who struggle with the superficial, inaccurate soundbites so vital for populism, and we find ourselves holding the finest product around, yet without any advertising, so we aren't selling anything. What are we to do about that?

While I don't celebrate Christmas in the traditional sense (with my family, we typically enjoy a nice day characterized by great food, visits, and playing video games together, but without stressing over cleaning, baking cookies, "mandatory" gift-shopping, and the like), as an anarcho-capitalist and a Christian, I think it is awesome; why?
Christians managed to take this originally pagan holiday, turn it into great PR, and transform it into a commemoration of the birth of the Lord Jesus, whom God sent to redeem us from sin and suffer for our transgressions—for which I personally am immensely grateful to Him (despite the lighthearted tone of this entire text, I mean this sentence in all seriousness)—even though Jesus apparently wasn't even born in winter (all the noteworthy astronomical events around year zero that could have been the Star of Bethlehem, whether 1P/Halley or not, fall into other seasons); libertarians ought to take a page out of Christians' book regarding their approach to PR xD
In modern times, Christmas has additionally become a very consumer-driven occasion (and I'll make money off this year's holidays as well, since I'll celebrate the entire break, including today, with well-paid work), which is a wonderful thing: rarely do so many voluntary exchanges take place at any other time of year. Among other things, I make a living programming ERP systems for giant retail and wholesale chains, some of which manage to generate up to 80% (!!) of their annual revenue in December. So to those who complain that the spirit of Christmas has been replaced by consumerism, I say: the primordial purpose of Christmas was celebration (even festivities having nothing to do with Jesus), so stop philosophizing and enjoy it; and if you miss spirituality, pray—I personally do so not only at Christmas, and I warmly recommend it.
And for those who don't want to pray, so you don't walk away empty-handed, I have at least a photo brimming with Christmas atmosphere, and also a Christmas song from the best band that ever was, is, and will be (the endless visual kitsch is obviously not their doing, but I suppose that comes with Christmas), which reminds me to mention Ding Dong Merrily On High in a rendition pleasing to the male eye (I can't help myself, Chloe Agnew is irresistible). And so that not only the straight majority but also the gay minority—whom many of my brothers and sisters in Christ unfortunately can't stand (despite officially professed tolerance)—can find something to enjoy, I'm also sharing Carol of the Bells by Pentatonix (in case anyone hasn't noticed, this is a cappella singing without any musical instruments; yes, indeed, these guys are incredible).
If there is still someone among my readers whom I haven't infected with the Christmas spirit and convinced that Christmas is divine (which surely everyone must see clearly by now), I can lovingly rake through the last remnants of dark humor for you; and if even that fails, then perhaps only (at your own risk, because that gentleman clearly has issues, and whoever clicks the following link might end up with them too) Řezník's take on the matter summarized in the "song" Fucking Christmas—a sentiment I fundamentally disagree with, but since this is the holiday of love and understanding, I decided to share it, because he was censored in Český slavík and even dragged into court over his music, which is disgusting (well, so is his music, but nobody is forced to listen to it), so I'm giving him at least this Christmas shout-out xD
And that's all from the Sewers for today, so MURRAY CHRISTMAS.

What goes around comes around; and when it comes to collective guilt, that holds twice over. If we divide people into "us" and "them" (based on anything other than the actions of specific individuals) in order to curtail the liberties of "the others" because of the wrongdoing of some of "them," we hand brilliant ammunition to "their" populists, who preach collective guilt as well. And the more we act that way, the more "they" will perceive things the same way, which in turn vindicates the rhetoric of "our" populists, and the whole dynamic can escalate ad absurdum. Applying this to refugees, we find that by restricting their liberties, we genuinely drive them into the arms of various terrorist organizations. But beware! There is no good idea that cannot be distorted and abused; and unfortunately, that is what the bleeding hearts are doing: they divide society into "us" and "them" in the exact same manner, but curtail "our" liberties for "their" benefit, boldly claiming that if they don't, "they" will become radicalized.
Do you know what German bleeding-heart politicians are calling for right now? They want to ban New Year's Eve fireworks, allegedly so as not to traumatize refugees, because consumer fireworks might remind them of war; and they justify restricting our freedoms by claiming we must yield so as not to radicalize anyone. But don't they realize that this is precisely what they are doing? After all, the principle cuts both ways, and who started it is completely irrelevant. By restricting the liberties of local residents, those locals will naturally begin to feel threatened, and more and more of them will insist on an "us versus them" divide, which in turn leads to the exact same sentiment on the other side. How is it that the bleeding hearts understand this principle clearly in one direction, while the anti-Islam crowd understands it in the other, yet neither group can pause to reflect that there isn't the slightest reason why the exact same thing wouldn't apply to both sides? Well, collectivism has never gone hand in hand with logic. So when will politicians ban fireworks?

Bureaucrats in the European Union are drafting legislation according to which social networks would be banned for anyone under thirteen, while youths aged thirteen to sixteen would only be allowed access with parental consent. What can one say to that? First, surely we can all see what an outrage this is, as the state once again declares its intention to raise children in place of parents; if this continues, in a few generations it will be the norm that raising children is the domain of the state, and if anyone dares suggest that parents should do it, they will be branded an extremist. Second, I hope it is also clear to everyone what absolute bullshit this is, given that we can all imagine how enforceable such a law is in practice.
There are essentially two ways this can turn out if the bill passes (it hasn't been approved yet): Either there will be some state-run registry of parental consents or a similar madness, or the law could be deftly wielded as a stick to beat inconvenient dogs—which would be a disaster in either case; or it will simply boil down to adding another checkbox for parental consent alongside the terms-and-conditions box—in which case it will be comically toothless, further cementing the notion that breaking the law is the norm, which would be just fine. We thus have three possibilities: (a) the bill doesn't pass, (b) the bill passes and someone actually starts enforcing it, or (c) the bill passes and becomes a complete joke. Option (b) is horrifying, but strikes me as unlikely; personally, I'd bet on (a). Readers' guesses are warmly welcome in the comments.

I recently heard Miloš Zeman speaking again on the topic of compulsory voting, of which he has long been an ardent proponent. Because only about half of the electorate participates in this democratic process, the ruling elite finds that insufficient and wants more; and when they want something, nothing is easier than simply ordering the people to do it. The reality of the matter, however, is that only the president truly wants it, and he lacks the power to push it through; ergo, we will most likely not see compulsory voting in the foreseeable future. That said, it cannot be ruled out entirely down the road, as there are countries where citizens have this obligation (paying a fine if they refuse to participate).
At first glance, of course, such an idea struck me as monstrous, since such a law is morally indefensible; the question is, what would the practical repercussions be? First of all, it would undoubtedly turn people against the ruling class, which is always a positive. Furthermore, in my view, such a law would create fertile ground for ridiculing democracy more effectively. In Germany, for example, there is a political party called "The Party" (in the original, "Die PARTEI"), which has a single plank in its platform: "We will do nothing." Understandably, it doesn't enjoy huge support, but mandatory voter turnout could change that.
Not to mention that one could potentially exploit compulsory voting by founding a party whose primary promise would be the repeal of compulsory voting; beyond that, it could also run on a libertarian platform, ideally smuggled in Trojan-horse style: the official platform would simply be repealing mandatory voting, but in the event of electoral success, it could pursue some liberalization in parliament, or at least use media attention to spread libertarian ideas. The question, of course, is how many of the roughly 50% who abstain do so out of pure laziness versus principle, which would greatly determine where those votes would go if forced to the ballot box.
So while we can certainly be glad that voting isn't mandatory here (one less potential bureaucratic nuisance), personally I wouldn't dread its introduction that much. Our situation couldn't deteriorate significantly as a result (aside from yet another idiotic government edict, of course); on the other hand, such a law could ultimately yield some liberalization, or at least weaken the state in the eyes of its voters and further stoke their anger. The question, of course, is how much that would actually change things. What do you think, dear readers?

Exactly one month ago, I published an article here titled "Political Correctness Out the Wazoo," which now turns out to have been a hasty title, as it leaves little room for escalation in subsequent headlines. But who could have known back then that things would get even more correct in just a month? Yes, you're right: anyone could have known. And what happened now? The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam renamed historical works of art whose titles were deemed politically incorrect by modern standards: for instance, "Mohammedan" became "Man with a Beard," "Hottentot Whore" will henceforth be "Smoking Woman of the Khoi Tribe," "Head of a Moor" is in Newspeak "Head of a Man," "Negro Servant" was renamed "Young Servant," and over two hundred other artworks were similarly desecrated... do you think in the next upgrade we'll see alterations to the skin color of the depicted figures so that the ratio of black and white people among the rich and poor is balanced?
So the state funds culture out of taxpayers' pockets under the pretext of caring for it better than those terrible private individuals, yet it apparently doesn't understand even what any barbarian math-and-physics student like Urza gets—namely, that a work of art includes its title, and altering it defiles the artist's message. Or is someone seriously going to tell me that when some prick renames the painting "Hottentot Whore" to "Smoking Woman of the Khoi Tribe," no information is lost, along with part of the artist's expression? And worse still: historical context and the zeitgeist of the era from which these works originate are erased; but it is "necessary" to imply to students on mandatory school trips to the museum that political correctness has existed since time immemorial. Recently, I saw a cartoon of parliament captioned: "You idiots, Orwell wrote 1984 as a warning, not an instruction manual!" But it's slowly ceasing to be funny, because renaming works of art is precisely the job description Comrade Winston Smith had...

Bitcoin probably needs no introduction here; what libertarian wouldn't be thrilled about a currency beyond state control? A tremendous amount of writing has already been dedicated to this topic, with authors not only describing Bitcoin, but also offering various predictions about the future of this virtual currency from both economic and technical standpoints. While I share their enthusiasm to a large extent, I also believe that one critically important factor is often overlooked amidst the excitement: the fucking state. Even if several politicians hadn't already declared their intent to ban Bitcoin should it reach mass adoption, such a move by the state is more than predictable—after all, what government willingly surrenders its monopoly on money?
Manufacturing public demand for a ban will be a trivial task: it will be enough to uncover and sensationalize in the media a real or fabricated ring of pedophiles transacting in Bitcoin (it doesn't even have to be true; simply flooding the media with it will suffice). Immediately, a swarm of "experts" will pop up confirming that Bitcoin is not just the currency of pedophiles, but also of terrorists, thieves, and tax cheats. And law enforcement? Well, some will object that due to decentralization, it's practically impossible to seize bitcoins from people, which is true; on the other hand, it is very easy to prohibit merchants from accepting Bitcoin, and anyone accepting the currency in an online shop will be thrown in the slammer. An outrage? Sure, but who cares aside from libertarians? Of course, it's right to keep trying to resist, but I fear Bitcoin faces the same fate as Bernard von NotHaus. Does anyone have a more optimistic perspective? Please share it in the comments.

Some time ago, I dumped a comment into the Sewers that several people wrote to me suggesting I should publish as a full-fledged "article." Since I felt it was rather long for the Sewers, here I outline its core point (in slightly more general terms): how we lose our freedom.
Phase One:
We possess a certain freedom (of speech, movement, enterprise, bearing arms, etc.); people are not (yet) willing to give it up, and anyone who tries to restrict it for the sake of some bureaucratic nuisance gets told to get lost, begins losing voters, and is shunned by his peers. If someone were somehow to pass a law abolishing this freedom out of the blue, anyone who promises to repeal the legislation will score gains in the next election.
Phase Two:
The prohibitionists present a powerful emotional pretext to curtail this freedom (a terrorist attack, mass child abuse, radiation, biological weapons, and so forth—basically anything that stirs strong emotions, even if its connection to the freedom in question is utterly marginal). If it represents a major intrusion into our lives, they promise the change is only temporary. I presume we are all familiar with arguments like "after all, during wartime this and that is allowed or done" (using war as a benchmark of moral high ground is laughable in itself). Hysteria completely drowns out any reasoned debate, and the ban passes.
Phase Three:
Once people have grown accustomed to the freedom being somewhat restricted, social engineers propose reducing the number of murders, rapes, robberies, and the like by curtailing this freedom just a little bit more. While these attempts occasionally fail, over time they eventually succeed (notice that once a regulation is introduced, practically no one ever repeals it). Once that happens, with the public no longer paying much attention, that freedom starts being chipped away over every petty triviality and bureaucratic whim. Although initially unthinkable, by this point it leaves virtually everyone indifferent (aside from a few crazy libertarians).
Phase Four:
Processes (in both the public and private sectors), services, goods, and norms emerge that are predicated upon that freedom being restricted in some way. These are then used as arguments for why that freedom must remain suppressed. Even when the original pretext disappears, or proves to have been nonsense from the very beginning, in reality it no longer matters. Nobody cares about the freedom anymore; moreover, "everyone knows" it must be restricted, because otherwise "things wouldn't work" (due to all the established processes that rely on that restriction).

The Ministry of Health amended the Public Health Protection Act (yes, we have such a law too, because our bodies belong to the state) so deftly that students in schools are not allowed to come into contact with motor fuels (greetings to apprentice auto mechanics) or weak acids and ethanol (cheers, chemistry students), meaning that chemistry Olympiads are completely done for as well. The Ministry of Education promised a remedy, but didn't give a damn, so nothing happened. Like true consummate professionals, Minister Němeček and Minister Valachová first and foremost bicker over who is to blame: according to Valachová, Němeček screwed it up with an idiotic amendment, while he defends himself by claiming she had the draft in advance and should have commented on it. As for the problem itself, that can naturally wait, because one can always set up an interdepartmental committee, draft a proposal, and send it to public health officers, who also have plenty of time. Can you imagine acting like this at your job?
Yet this tragicomic incident is merely the tip of the iceberg, a symptom of something far deeper. Beyond the existence of such blatant filth as the Public Health Act undoubtedly is (by which the state declares that we don't own our health—and therefore not even our own bodies—but rather politicians do, usurping the right to decide), we face yet another issue: the entire concept of our legal system is turned on its head. A law took effect that is blatantly wrong, as everyone knows, including those who drafted it; yet everyone is forced to obey it, because if a teacher were now to conduct experiments with students using prohibited substances (the very same ones allowed just a month ago), he'd end up behind bars. Someone might argue that it has to be this way, because otherwise, every instance of unlawful conduct would require evaluating whether the violated law happened to be nonsensical in that specific situation. And what do I say to such an objection? "Exactly! That is precisely how it should be!"

Just on Friday, I poured out a piece in the Sewers about misguided public debate, only to find out shortly afterward that elsewhere (specifically in Turkey), they took it to the next level (which we can also view as a glimpse into our dark future). A certain Bilgin Çiftçi compared Turkish Prime Minister Erdoğan to Gollum from The Lord of the Rings, for which he could face up to two years behind bars. The court doesn't give a dog's shit about freedom of speech; instead, five expert witnesses from film studies and psychology were summoned to the trial (the judge reportedly hadn't read The Lord of the Rings), tasked with issuing an expert verdict on whether Gollum is truly an evil character, since Mr. Çiftçi's defense counsel argued that might not be the case, ergo the comparison was not necessarily defamatory. Bizarre? Indeed.
I assume the vast majority of Czechs would find the case utterly absurd and consider the question of Gollum's virtue completely marginal compared to the fundamental suppression of free speech—which is what actually matters. On the other hand, those very same people are then capable, in debates over restaurant smoking bans, of completely overlooking the crucial trampling of the owner's freedom to decide about his own establishment, and instead bog themselves down in debates over the health risks or smell of cigarette smoke—which is just as irrelevant as analyzing Gollum's character. How is that possible? Well, these people have already undergone state brainwashing regarding the regulation of businesses, but not yet regarding the societal harm of insulting a public official. But rest assured that if it becomes an issue, someone will push it into the school curriculum, and after indoctrination through the educational system (the media can't even hold a candle to it), within a single generation Czech courts could be earnestly debating the moral character of Jabba the Hutt, to whom Zeman is so fondly compared.

Sometimes I put on the talk show "Máte slovo" on my second monitor (mostly as background noise) if there's a political topic in that episode. Today, they discussed an amendment to the already totalitarian "Significant Market Power Act," tightening the law even further. The show's hot topic was supermarkets securing discounts from food manufacturers leveraging their strong market position; however, the law states that an entity possessing "significant market power" may not demand a lower price without "just cause" (that's actually in there). The debate then unfolded with proponents of regulation accusing retail chains of buying food at low prices from a dominant market position, while supermarket representatives denied it—and everyone implicitly assumed that this must be wrong.
Why is this dreadful? Well, for the same reason the debate on smoking bans in restaurants was atrocious, centered entirely on whether cigarettes harm health and how badly smoke smells (the single key takeaway from that debate that I still remember to this day was that smoke in a pub spreads just like urine in a swimming pool). And that is precisely how virtually everything is debated (far beyond just that talk show): whenever adopting a regulation on anything is discussed, the debate is essentially reduced to whether that "anything" causes harm or not; if the answer is yes, regulation is automatically assumed to be justified, ergo right. And that is why, dear libertarians, we must tirelessly point out the heart of the matter: liberty, property rights, and the true cost of regulatory laws (not merely economic, but above all moral)—because no one else is going to do it for us.

In connection with migration, we often hear the comparison that a state is like a house: just as a property owner decides whom to welcome into his home and whom not to, the state should supposedly decide who is allowed across its borders and who stays out. While such a comparison might seem intuitive at first glance, in reality it is one of the falsest analogies I have ever encountered; what makes it especially unique is that the claim being compared actually contradicts the very premise it draws from.
How so? Well, if the state determines who is permitted to cross the border, it simultaneously prevents me from inviting into my home whomever I see fit (since in some cases it keeps them out of the country entirely). Isn't that paradoxical? The analogy rests on the premise that it is good for me to decide for myself whom I let into my house, yet this very principle, used as the benchmark, would be overridden by the principle the analogy seeks to justify: I can hardly invite whoever I want into my home if that person isn't even allowed across the border.
Another flaw with this analogy is that while a house typically has a rightful owner who makes the decisions, the state does not. A far more accurate analogy would be an apartment building in which I own an apartment: Can my neighbors, by majority vote, forbid me from having a guest over whom they happen to dislike? Hmm... suddenly that's not quite so clear-cut, is it? Not that they couldn't establish such an agreement in advance, but if no such rule existed when I purchased the apartment, it suddenly becomes a rather murky matter, and I highly doubt anyone would still use the analogy in that form (even though it is more accurate in every respect).
Yet even more than a house, a state resembles a city; and here we find ourselves on very thin ice indeed, as having the residents of a city vote on who is allowed to come there to work, for example, is virtually unheard of. By no means take this text as a defense of EU refugee quotas—because even more absurd than neighbors telling me who can visit my home would be them ordering me whom I must take in; I am merely pointing out that comparing national borders to private property boundaries makes virtually no sense, and in fact contradicts itself.

A rather unpleasant nuisance has spread around here: Prague cops are bragging to the media about how, after a multi-month operation, they caught wicked taxi drivers. And what did these villains do? Well, they dared to agree on a voluntary transaction with a customer before the ride (two kilometers for a grand, which works out to about a 98% margin) and subsequently didn't turn on the taximeter. The state, however, violently mandates that all exchanges take place according to its own (moronic) rules. Six cabbies and one bureaucrat who tipped them off about inspections have been charged, with the uniformed monkeys even boasting about tailing them around the clock, requiring ten detectives and dozens of decoys per target just to prove each victim broke the law by at least five thousand CZK, since anything below that threshold is merely an administrative infraction rather than a felony (and not every sting worked, as the drivers rarely offered that kind of deal).
Even leaving aside the moral dimension—namely the disgrace of the state interfering in voluntary exchanges—what actually happened here? A detective (counting a fresh recruit) makes about 25,000 CZK a month; let's conservatively say the multi-month sting lasted two months; let's assume the decoys worked for free; let's ignore equipment and cab fare expenses. We find that the state blew 3.5 million CZK (a conservative lower estimate) on detective salaries alone, just to—holy shit, to do what!? To convict six people of offering someone a ride at a mutually agreed (albeit steep) price, and one guy for covering for them. Bravo! Three and a half million to charge seven people with a victimless crime—and the bastards even brag about it in the media!? Are you wondering if they've completely lost their minds? Well, Google it and read how the press kisses their asses for it, followed by ecstatic comments from the moronic mob... because why wouldn't we blow millions just to stop someone from making a 98% margin? And that, dear children, is democracy: rule of the people!

Minister of Labor and Social Affairs Marksová truly lives up to her name: the minimum wage, which is already set to rise in January from 9,200 to 9,900 CZK, she wants to increase by another thousand the following year, and up to 12k the year after that. The explanation goes as follows: "Nowadays, if people exceed the income threshold even slightly, they lose their housing benefits. It's quite a lot of money; it doesn't pay for them to work." On the one hand, it's nice that she noticed the inverse relationship between welfare benefits (also dispensed by her ministry, incidentally) and people's willingness to work; on the other hand, I can't help wondering how much stupidity or malice it takes for someone to propose raising the minimum wage as a "solution" instead of slashing those benefits.
I don't know what Ms. Marksová thinks the minimum wage is, but it certainly isn't a law that increases wages, let alone prosperity; the minimum wage simply means that the state forbids people from working for compensation below what politicians dictate. The state creates nothing with this, protects no one, but simply outlaws labor below a certain price point. Whoever cannot generate that much value (plus all the taxes) for an employer simply won't be hired by anyone, as the employer would lose money. Calibrating welfare benefits so high that people don't feel like working is foolish; but "fixing" the situation by outlawing work under certain conditions... that is completely pathetic. So I ask: Does Marksová know what she's doing (which would make her quite a monster), or is she just completely brainless? What do you think?

For years I've maintained that nothing on the Czech political scene can surprise me, as it is populated purely by crooks and nothing good can be expected from them; and for years, unfortunately, reality has proven me right time and time again. When suddenly... the ODS almost pulled off a surprise; and if they persist in their efforts, they might even shock me in a positive way. At a moment when Babiš's EET is looming inexorably, and it seems only technical glitches and government ineptitude could stop it, the opposition ODS steps onto the scene—and not with some embarrassing "we tried our best, but the government outvoted us," but by genuinely throwing a wrench into Babiš's gears (well, so far more like a tiny spanner). Now I only hope and plead with the ODS to see this through and obstruct relentlessly, infinitely, ad absurdum. If you do that and shove Babiš's fucking cash registers right up his ass by filibustering the bill until the end of the parliamentary term, I will tip my hat to you with utmost respect!

The perennial comparison of Islam to Nazism and Muslims to Nazis is among the most popular Islam-bashing arguments; not that such a comparison doesn't make sense in certain special situations—some of the smarter crusaders against Islam use it mostly sensibly—but in the vast majority of cases it is nothing more than brainless parroting of these opinions by dumber folks who are capable of nothing more than rewriting completely random texts simply by substituting occurrences of the corresponding words. One could even write software in half an afternoon that could do this automatically, and the output would be roughly just as stupid. Where, then, do such comparisons fall short?
First of all, although Islam shares some features with Nazism, it also has a number of entirely different characteristics. The main difference lies above all in the fact that while Nazism is a very young and specific ideology, Islam is nothing but one huge mess, a religion many hundreds of years old with countless interpretations and a holy book with loads of translations (six 'major' ones and heaps of others). In reality, Islam encompasses a whole range of different currents (from aggressively totalitarian Salafists to benevolently frivolous Sufis), which Nazism simply does not have. For that reason, it is completely absurd, for instance, to compare 'moderate Muslims' to 'moderate Nazis' (since there were in fact no Nazi factions preaching anything diametrically opposed to the teachings of Hitler himself; had they existed, then such a comparison would make sense).
Moreover, even in cases where the comparison does make sense, abominations often stem from it. This typically happens when someone tries to push through a ban on Islam by arguing that Nazism is also banned. The problem here lies, first and foremost, in the fact that banning a totalitarian ideology is itself a totalitarian practice; one simply cannot defend against totalitarianism with totalitarianism (meaning not even Nazism should be banned). If we sacrifice freedom of speech, expression, the press, or religion, we ourselves become those whom we want to ban! The argument that bans on totalitarians are not themselves totalitarian practices is completely absurd; there is no objective yardstick to determine what ought to be banned, ergo someone must exist who decides—and that is precisely where totalitarianism lies.
I am definitely not claiming that comparing Nazism and Islam is necessarily wrong under all circumstances; political Wahhabism, for instance, truly does resemble Nazism. But one cannot indiscriminately and thoughtlessly claim across the board that they are one and the same thing, because that is plain and simple not true. The differences are sometimes negligible, other times enormous, so before comparing one to the other, it is wise to reflect on what the outcome is supposed to be and whether the comparison doesn't completely lose its meaning in that specific area. Please, let us not blind ourselves to logic in the name of fanaticism.

Based on an EU regulation from a few years ago, the Czech state forbade its subjects from hosting traditional pig slaughters unless they have a special permit; unfortunately, by all accounts this permit cannot be obtained simply by going down to the authorities; rather, you more or less need to own a slaughterhouse. Conventional neighborhood pig slaughters are simply a thing of the past; and commercial pig slaughters organized by pubs likewise. However, the whole thing also has a silver lining—the state lacks the resources to actively monitor compliance with this law, so the only way it can harass anyone is if somebody snitches on them first.
The downside is that such scumbags can indeed be found among us. In 2014, the state raked in one hundred and twenty thousand crowns in fines, all from natural persons (corporations most likely didn't dare, since you need to advertise it, which increases the risk of being reported), who were probably snitched on by their neighbors. Shame on them! Shame on every bastard capable of ratting out his neighbor for slaughtering his own pig; this can't even be excused by any bullshit about the 'danger to society' of such an act—this is pure, unadulterated filth, for which those involved deserve the utmost contempt.
On the other hand—although I failed to track down the exact number of such snitches—given that a single fine for an illegal pig slaughter can climb up to three hundred thousand and the state collected one hundred and twenty thousand for the whole year, we can assume there were likely just a handful (or a small dozen) of cases; even if the average fine were only ten thousand, that would be twelve people, or one per month, which isn't that many for a population of ten million. Overall, I like the certain indifference of people in this country toward breaking laws; although people mostly consider taxes to be right in the abstract, on a personal level tax evasion and working under the table are not socially condemned all that much (unlike in Germany, for example, where it is viewed similarly to robbing a neighbor).
In any case, it is a downright shame to follow such laws that the state doesn't enforce; it is enough to convince snitches not to snitch. So if you know any such human garbage, be nasty to them, ostracize them, convince those around you to do the same, just teach them a lesson so they think twice next time. And the fewer people collaborate with the police, the better, so spread information around you about all the evil the police have caused or done (for
examples
one doesn't need
to look far
). The state is evil; and whoever is willing to commit dirty deeds for it, let decent people show them that this is not the way.

The War on Drugs has (always) been failing; Murray Newton Rothbard and other brilliant visionaries predicted this long before this war properly even began, people immune to state prohibitionist propaganda realized it within a few years, others understood it after a few decades, and today basically everyone knows it, including little kids—even former rulers are now admitting it. I am convinced that the current ones know it clearly too, but they make their living off of it, so it's easier for them to pretend it makes sense; besides, what would all those poor drug-squad cops do then?
The Global Commission on Drug Policy assessed the state of affairs in a report in which it found, with surprise, that drug policy costing millions of dollars out of taxpayers' pockets has failed, because while missing its mark entirely, it instead creates organized crime and causes the death of thousands of people; members of this commission include, for example, former UN chief Kofi Annan, former NATO Secretary General and former EU High Representative for Common Foreign and Security Policy Javier Solana, former US Secretary of State George Shultz, and former presidents of Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia. The former powerful, whose power no longer depends on the drug war, have no reason to lie anymore...
Right in the introduction of their report, it states: 'The global war on drugs has failed, with devastating consequences to individuals and societies around the world.' It also says in the same place: 'Political leaders and public figures should have the courage to articulate publicly what many of them acknowledge privately: that the available evidence strongly demonstrates that repressive strategies will not solve the drug problem, and that the war on drugs has not, and cannot, be won.' What matters is that those past leaders, who criticize it today, plucked up that courage; I'd also be curious to know how they guessed what current leaders say in private—could it be rich personal experience? xD
The whole thing belongs to the vast category of things that would be laughable if they weren't so tragic. It's one thing that strictly logical explanations of why the war on drugs simply would not work existed decades ago, but since that was inconvenient, they were quite understandably ignored. However, we face a completely different situation today: on top of those explanations, there is now empirical evidence that this war does far more harm than good—yet politicians persist in this activity anyway, because the real goal isn't the declared results, but more power, expanding the state, and last but not least, a wonderful revenue stream from taxpayers' pockets.

When I last wrote in the Sewers about Pelikán's Ministry of Justice, which fights against it truly relentlessly (against what? Well, against justice, of course xD), I had no idea that I'd be grumbling about Pelikán here again in just two days; on November 18, the gentleman in question tweeted the following statement: 'Whoever publicly incites hatred toward any (...) religion (...) shall be punished by imprisonment for up to two years.' And on that very day—what a coincidence—Konvička was indicted for the crime of incitement to hatred. Of course, it doesn't look at all like the Minister of Justice had any personal interest in the matter and was even publicly bragging about it; he would never do that, would he?
What does Konvička say today? 'There is an obvious attempt to criminalize the government's political opponents, and that effort is clearly evident in the date the indictment was drawn up.'
What did Konvička say a while ago? 'The only thing that will help is pressure on politicians, elected officials, and journalists to do everything to stop Islamic expansion.
